See the dazzling images that won Astronomy Photographer of the Year

New Scientist September 17, 2026

The astonishing diversity of the cosmos is on display in the 2026 Astronomy Photographer of the Year competition, organised by the Royal Observatory in Greenwich, London. From our own solar system to distant nebulae, these images showcase the many wonders we can observe from the ground on Earth.

The overall winner (above), The Quiet Predator, was taken by Ali Alobaidly in Kuwait. It shows a dense nebula 650 light years away, in the constellation Cepheus. This cloud of dust, called the Shark nebula, contains a few bright stars that make their surroundings glow blue. The nebula is so dark and distant that it took Alobaidly more than 28 hours of observing to create this image.

The runner-up in the competition (above) is Beyond the Wormhole, taken by Kfir Simon in Israel. While the image may evoke a hole in space-time, it actually depicts the centre of the Helix nebula, which is about 650 light years away in the constellation Aquarius. Beyond the central star that formed the nebula when it shed its outer layers thousands of years ago, extraordinarily distant galaxies shine through the dust and gas.

Advertisement

In the Our Moon category, Venusian Pearl on the Moon (above) took the prize. Petr Horalek took this photograph in the Czech Republic as the moon passed in front of Venus in the middle of the day. He captured this relatively rare event, called an occultation, just as Venus slipped behind the crescent moon.

The runner-up in the Our Sun section is, unsurprisingly, an image of the sun. However, Anatomy of the Chromosphere (above), captured by Peter Ward in Australia, isn’t a simple photograph. It represents two different wavelengths of light, one of which captures emission from hydrogen along the sun’s edges, represented in red, while the other shows emission from calcium, shown in lilac. Together, they reveal the structure of the sun’s chromosphere, which is the layer just above its visible surface, but below its corona.

Comet C/2025 A6 (Lemmon) jets across the sky in this highly commended image by Julien DeWinter and Landon Boehm, taken from Texas. When it was captured, in October 2025, the comet was almost at its closest point to the sun, about 101 million kilometres from Earth. That proximity to the sun caused remarkable activity on the comet, creating two long plumes, one made of dust and the other of electrically charged plasma.

With a more earthly setting, the winner of the Skyscapes category is Botswana Star Trail, taken by Stefano Pellegrini. It captures the movement of stars above a grove of baobab trees over the course of 340 camera exposures, each lasting 30 seconds.

The winning images from the competition will be exhibited at the National Maritime Museum in London from 18 September.

Robots clash in first naval engagement between uncrewed sea drones

New Scientist September 17, 2026

In the first-known naval engagement between uncrewed vessels, a Ukrainian robot boat sank a Russian opponent in the Black Sea.

The action between the remote-controlled uncrewed surface vessels (USVs), or sea drones, took place earlier this month. A video released by the Ukrainian Navy shows its USV, identified as a Sargan-3000, firing a 12.7-millimetre heavy machine gun at the Russian vessel, which appears to be of the Orcan type, until it sinks.

Both sea drones are propelled by water jets. The Sargan is around 7 metres long with a top speed of over 80 kilometres per hour, while the Orcan is about 5 metres long and can reach 64 km/h.

Advertisement

Fully autonomous drones have killed human soldiers for the first time

This is the first-known clash of its type in the history of naval warfare, according to independent naval expert H. I. Sutton. But it didn’t come as a surprise.

“It was inevitable that there would be USV-on-USV combat,” says Sutton. “We have seen the same in the air, and on the ground.”

Ukraine developed USVs after scuttling its only major warship early in 2022 to prevent its capture. In October 2022, Ukraine carried out a successful attack with seven sea drones, damaging a Russian frigate and a minesweeper at the Sevastopol naval base in Crimea.

Since then, Ukraine has moved from improvised USVs based on speedboats and jet-powered watercraft to advanced designs, including the Magura and Sea Baby series. In conjunction with shore-based anti-ship missiles and aerial drones, Ukraine’s uncrewed vessels have sunk or damaged a third of the Russian Black Sea fleet. The remainder is now largely confined to port behind booms and other defences.

Subscriber-only newsletter

Initially, Ukraine’s USVs carried explosive charges for one-way attacks. More advanced versions are now armed with surface-to-air missiles, with one Ukrainian USV being the first ever to shoot down a helicopter, in 2024. Others are fitted with machine guns and unguided rockets. Some Ukrainian USVs are miniature aircraft carriers, launching aerial drones.

From 2024, the Russians copied Ukraine, building small, fast USVs with explosive warheads to attack ports, bridges and shipping. The Russian Orcan in this month’s action was likely to have been heading towards the Ukrainian port city of Odesa as part of a campaign targeting cargo ships.

“It was a small vessel with an explosive charge and no gun turret, intended for an offensive operation ramming a larger vessel,” says Sutton. “The Ukrainian one was armed with a machine gun, showing that it had a more defensive role. So, it was to be expected, although not guaranteed, that the Ukrainian one would win this duel.”

Ukraine is racing to design faster, more capable interceptor drones to tackle Russia's new generation of jet-powered Shahed attack drones

Sutton says the action is likely to drive further evolution of USVs on both sides. Just as helicopters being used against sea drones led to the design of new models equipped with surface-to-air missiles, attack USVs may start carrying machine guns or other defensive weaponry, or travel with escorts.

This first robot naval action is unlikely to be the last. “Probably in future we will see Ukrainian USVs interdicted by Russian ones close to Russian naval bases,” says Sutton.

Naval experts believe the Black Sea campaign is a special case, saying that its lessons may not apply in other theatres of operation where actions take place over much greater ranges and timescales. But the continued rise of robot boats is another sign of warfare’s changing face.

Beautiful new cat species is first to be named in a century

New Scientist September 17, 2026

A new cat species has been scientifically described – the diminutive, spotted tilcayo from Bolivia.

Several species of small cat in the Leopardus genus live in South America, including the ocelot, margay, kodkod, Geoffroy’s cat and the tiger cat or oncilla. The similar appearance of these nocturnal and hard-to-spot cats has made separating them into distinct species difficult.

This is particularly true of tiger cats, which are about the size of a house cat, and are found in Costa Rica in Central America, and across a vast swathe of South America including Bolivia, Brazil, Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador and Peru. Historically, there have been many local and scientific names for them, but they all got subsumed into a single species, Leopardus tigrinus.

Advertisement

Tiny orange frog around the size of a pencil tip is brand-new species

Genetic studies have since divided the species into four, resurrecting three of the species names that scientists once used before they were all lumped together under the name L. tigrinus. This process saw the official recognition of the southern tiger cat (Leopardus guttulus) in 2013, Leopardus emiliae in 2017 and the clouded tiger cat (Leopardus pardinoides) in 2024.

Now, Eduardo Eizirik at the Pontifical Catholic University of Rio Grande do Sul (PUCRS) in Porto Alegre, Brazil, and his colleagues have analysed the complete genomes of 38 individuals from the Leopardus genus, including 26 tiger cats from across their known range.

The genomics revealed a fifth distinct species living in the Bolivian Yungas forests on the east slopes of the Andes mountains. The researchers describe it under a completely new name: Leopardus tilcayo, naming it after the local term used for this cat.

Subscriber-only newsletter

“We’ve discovered a new species of cat that had not been scientifically named before,” says Eizirik, adding that this is the first time this has happened for a century.

“There are more cat species. Who can’t love that?” says Leslie Lyons at the University of California, Davis. “They’re hard to find and see, so it’s not surprising that some of the early taxonomy needs to be modified now we have more data.”

L. tilcayo has a combined head and body length of between about 42 and 50 centimetres and weighs between 1.5 and 2 kilograms. The genomes revealed that it diverged from the lineage containing L. tigrinus and L. pardinoides nearly 1.4 million years ago.

Domestic cats originated in North Africa and spread to Europe in the past 2000 years, according to DNA evidence, while in China a different species of cat lived alongside people much earlier

Telling the new species apart visually is not easy. “The five tiger cat species are all cryptic species. They’re morphologically very similar,” says team member Jonas Lescroart at University of Antwerp in Belgium.

The researchers also found that in the Peruvian Yungas forests, on the west side of the Andes, there is a distinct group of cats in the L. tigrinus lineage that they describe as a novel subspecies, L. tigrinus antisuyo.

There are so many barriers in South America that can geographically isolate animal populations from each other, including mountains and rivers, that more cat species may be waiting to be found, says Lyons. “It’d be rather cool if we could find another species out there.”

L. tigrinus is listed as vulnerable by the IUCN Red List, but the new species and subspecies will have to be evaluated and protected as distinct units, says Eizirik, especially as the forests they live in are shrinking as agriculture expands.

Short bursts of exercise can boost your cognition

New Scientist September 17, 2026

Tiny bursts of exercise once an hour could boost your cognition at school or at work, adding to the evidence of how important it is to take occasional breaks.

“Exercise improves pretty much every domain you can think of, including cognition over the long term. The interesting thing here is that this is immediate,” says Mike Trott at the University of Queensland in Australia, who wasn’t involved in the research.

It is well known that exercise is good for our overall health, cognitive powers and mental health, but it can be hard for adults to hit the World Health Organization’s recommended minimum weekly levels of physical activity of 150 minutes of moderate-intensity activity or 75 minutes of vigorous activity. About 31 per cent of adults fail to hit these targets, so interest is rising in “exercise snacks”: sessions of physical activity that last no more than 10 minutes, performed at least twice a day.

Advertisement

Exercise may relieve depression as effectively as antidepressants

In the past few years, studies have found that short bursts of exercise can help keep your heart healthy or add years to your life. To see if they can similarly boost our brains, Yongming Li at Shanghai University of Sport in China and his colleagues reviewed 25 randomised controlled trials investigating the cognitive effects of exercise snacks.

The review included a total of 1115 people of all ages, with the mean age of participants in the studies ranging from 8 to 78 years. They involved people sitting for hours, interrupted by a couple of minutes of exercise either every 30 minutes or every hour.

The exercises included yoga, chair-based stretching, climbing two flights of stairs, walking on a treadmill, resistance exercises, stationary cycling, or high-intensity exercises like running on the spot for a minute or leg raises and jumping jacks.

Free newsletter

The researchers found that these short bursts of exercise gave a modest immediate boost to working memory, cognitive flexibility, attention span and the ability to ignore impulsive reactions, assessed across the studies by a statistical measure known as Hedges’ g. With this measure, 0.2 indicates a small effect, 0.5 a medium one and 0.8 or above a large effect. Overall, the measure for the study was 0.24.

The cognitive benefits were stronger if the exercise habit continued for several weeks (g = 0.51), and if it happened in school or in the workplace (g = 0.61).

It is hard to interpret the overall effect size because the youngest and oldest people in the study were at very different stages of cognitive development, says Mark Hamer at University College London. However, he thinks the findings are plausible.

We now have a greater understanding of how exercise slows cancer

“It’s interesting with the kids in particular and this concept of trying to break up lessons, which could involve a teacher getting the kids to stand up or jump on the spot,” he says.

The review also found that gaps of an hour between exercises provided slightly more of a boost than gaps of 30 minutes, which makes sense biologically, says Trott.

The leading hypothesis for how exercise affects the brain is that it makes the body release dopamine and noradrenaline, increasing blood flow, he says. This gets everything working a little bit better, and studies show that, over longer periods of time, this can boost the size of the hippocampus, which is involved in memory, and the performance of the prefrontal cortex, which is involved in focus and decision-making.

We all know that walking is good for us, but growing evidence reveals that the right hike can exponentially enhance the health benefits

“The immediate effects of dopamine and noradrenaline last for over an hour, so if the exercise snacks are more frequent than that, any extra effect is going to be really small because you’re still riding the wave of the first one,” says Trott.

Current health messaging about taking breaks during the day is generally based on evidence of cardiovascular and metabolic effects, and the exercise snack work adds to evidence of how beneficial it is to break things up frequently, says Hamer. “Even if that’s just by standing up or going up and down the stairs.”

Ancient skeleton shows woman in imperial China had her nose amputated

New Scientist September 17, 2026

A woman who lived in China about 700 years ago had her nose cleanly sliced off, perhaps as punishment for stealing horses or cattle. She lived for at least a few years after the incident and may have worn a prosthetic nose over the hole. The archaeologists who found her remains, buried face down in a cemetery, think this may be the only known physical evidence of punitive nasal amputation from ancient China.

“I suspect she lived a difficult life, facing stigma and social challenges,” says David Shaye at Harvard University, who wasn’t involved in the study. “Facial deformities can profoundly affect identity, social interaction and a person’s place within a community. In this sense, this archaeological finding connects very directly with challenges that people continue to face today.”

Ancient Chinese legal texts describe cutting off a person’s nose as one of the “Five Punishments”, along with decapitation, limb amputation, castration and facial tattooing. By the end of the Yuan dynasty, which ran from AD 1279 to 1368, the law prescribed it mainly for theft of high-value livestock, or for repeated offences involving the theft of less valuable animals.

Advertisement

High-tech archaeology shows we aren’t the first to endure hard times

Yet despite ancient texts documenting thousands of cases, there’s never been physical evidence of it actually happening, says Qian Wang at Texas A&M University.

In 2018, surveys ahead of construction of a trade school in central China’s Henan province uncovered a cemetery containing 299 tombs. Fei Yan at the nearby Sanmenxia Institute of Cultural Relics and Archaeology and colleagues rapidly excavated the site and stored the skeletons at Zhengzhou University. An archaeologist there, Yawei Zhou, noticed one skull had a strangely wide nasal opening with missing bone and healed edges, suggesting the woman’s nose had been cut off during life.

By 2024, Wang had joined the investigation. The researchers identified the remains as belonging to a woman by features of the pelvis and skull, while tooth wear and skeletal indicators put her age at 40 to 45. Radiocarbon dating of her right femur placed her death between 1298 and 1404, spanning the late Yuan and early Ming dynasties. The design of the tomb itself is consistent with the Yuan – the Mongol dynasty founded by Kublai Khan.

Subscriber-only newsletter

Isotope analysis of the skeletal remains suggested the woman ate mostly millet and little animal protein, consistent with relatively low socioeconomic status.

CT scans revealed that large amounts of bone and other tissue around and inside her nose had been cut away, apparently from bottom to top, says Wang. The healed and remodeled edges showed she survived for years afterwards, although probably with difficulty breathing and moving her upper lip.

The woman must have had good medical care: the fact that she survived suggests caregivers controlled bleeding, prevented infection and probably managed her pain, says Wang.

“If initially bleeding was controlled, the wound would slowly heal on its own over several months,” says Shaye.

A bizarre skeleton from a Roman grave has bones from eight people

Small lumps of extra bone – known as bone spurs – formed around the nasal opening. These could reflect chronic inflammation, but it’s also possible they chronicle pressure from an artificial nose. “This woman had a normal diet for a commoner and might have worn a nasal prosthesis to cover the scar – indicating that she tried to get back to normal life,” says Wang.

Only later, examining the lone photograph from the hasty excavation, did the team realise the woman had been buried face down, says Wang. None of the other bodies in the cemetery was buried this way. The practice is sometimes associated with punishment during the Yuan dynasty. Wang suspects she was buried isolated from her family or community, possibly face down to hide her disfigurement.

DNA from plague bacteria has been identified in graves from 1338 in Kyrgyzstan, and these pathogens appear to be the ancestors of those that caused the Black Death

“We believed there was a discriminatory attitude,” he says. “It could be a decision of disapproval.”

Wang adds that there may be other explanations for the woman’s injury, including disease, accident or even self-mutilation. However, the researchers found no telltale signs of such alternatives. If their interpretation is correct, the skeleton provides the first physical evidence of punitive nasal amputation in ancient China.

Beyond showing that a gruesome punishment described in historical texts was actually carried out, the discovery offers a rare glimpse into how the ancient Chinese punished, treated and ultimately regarded convicted criminals, says Wang.

Plug-in solar panels still have safety risks in the UK despite legalisation

New Scientist September 17, 2026

It is now legal to buy and use plug-in solar panels in Great Britain, but safety concerns surrounding them haven’t yet been addressed by the UK government. This is according to one of the leading engineering institutions, which says the legalisation has been rushed through without creating proper legal standards and has created an increased risk to life.

With plug-in solar panels, you simply buy a kit, place it in a sunny spot and plug it into a wall socket. There’s no installation cost, no certification and no planning permission. The devices are popular in many European countries and the UK government legalised them on 27 August to boost renewable energy generation and cut down on household bills.

Prior to this legalisation, Mark Coles, the head of technical regulations at the UK Institution of Engineering and Technology (IET), told New Scientist about several potential issues. One surrounded residual current devices (RCDs), the safety devices found in fuse boxes that sense when current is leaking to ground – a sign of electrocution or a short circuit – and almost instantaneously cut power. Most RCDs used in the UK aren’t suitable for current flowing in both directions and so could malfunction if used with plug-in solar panels.

Advertisement

Another of the IET’s concerns is what happens if there are multiple kits in use in an area and a power cut occurs. In theory, the plug-in kits should also shut down in order to prevent “islanding”, when one home’s power stays live. But if they are still generating power, then they could deceive each other into thinking the grid is live and keep running. The problem then is that power can jump past the fuse box and electrocute maintenance workers in the area fixing the outage.

The IET made these concerns clear to the UK government both before and during the consultation by the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNZ) that ended on 30 June. But Coles says the issues weren’t addressed and now present a risk.

“It was a done deal before it went out, I’m sure,” says Coles. “It’s been rushed. There needed to be time to develop a proper standard for these things, because we feel under certain circumstances that there’s an increased risk to life.”

Plug-in solar is coming – how dangerous is it and is it worth it?

Coles says the risks emerge only when there’s a perfect storm of problems, but that this will inevitably lead to an injury or a death over time if plug-in solar panels are widely adopted.

Extensive scientific studies have been carried out to determine how quickly damage is done within the human body from electric shock. Based on that research, UK RCDs are required to trip and cut off current within 40 milliseconds. But there are no similar standards for plug-in solar panels, which Coles suggests could – if things go wrong, and in very limited circumstances – take longer to shut down.

“You could be exposed to the electric current for longer than you should have been,” says Coles. “You’re in the danger zone.”

The IET’s advice is to get an electrical inspection prior to committing to plug-in solar in order to minimise risk.

Free newsletter

A DESNZ spokesperson told New Scientist that “we have funded an independent contractor to fully test the electrical safety of plug-in solar devices on UK electrical house wiring practice, which found these products to be safe”.

The department added that it had looked at testing with older household electrical safety devices and found no evidence that their ability to provide protection was affected when used with the type of plug-in solar systems sold in Europe.

Coles agrees that tests were carried out, but says that they focused on plug-in solar kits sourced outside the UK, because none was legal here at the time, and with brand new RCDs. That has two problems: legal RCDs in the real world can be much older, and of older design, and there was no clear definition or regulation for plug-in panels that were tested, meaning that ones now for sale may act differently.

“They spent this money on getting these units tested, but these units were non-standard units,” says Coles. “So it’s not like I’m testing something that’s been made to a product standard and I’m seeing how it conforms to this product standard. So I don’t see the point of spending the money. From our point of view, it’s being rushed.”

SpaceX’s Starship will orbit Earth for first time during next flight

New Scientist September 18, 2026

SpaceX’s reusable rocket, Starship – the tallest and most powerful ever launched – will orbit Earth for the first time within days. And because it will also release working Starlink V3 satellites, it will be the first commercially useful Starship mission.

The company has announced that a launch window will open at 7.15am CDT (1.15pm BST) on 22nd September, during which Starship will launch from the company’s Starbase site in Texas.

The flight – Starship’s 14th – will reach an altitude of 275 kilometres and complete six orbits of Earth over 10 hours, with re-entry and splashdown targeted in the Pacific Ocean, to the west of Chile.

Advertisement

SpaceX’s 1 million satellites could avoid environmental checks

This will make it by far the longest and most ambitious test flight of Starship to date. All 13 previous Starship test flights have been, at best, sub-orbital.

Starship is made up of two parts: an upper stage, confusingly also called Starship, and a lower stage, called Super Heavy. Currently, SpaceX is testing the latest third generation of each section using a fail-fast, learn-fast strategy more common to Silicon Valley than the conservative world of space exploration.

SpaceX is several years into its development programme for Starship, intended to be a rapidly reusable and extremely powerful launch vehicle that will take over the rollout of the company’s Starlink satellites and be a central part of NASA’s Artemis moon missions.

Free newsletter

The 14th flight will also see 26 Starlink V3 satellites launched for the first time. Thousands of these new devices will join the existing constellation of satellites that provides internet connections around the world. Until now, Starship test flights have launched only dummy test satellites.

Davide Amato at Imperial College London says that an orbital test is indicative of confidence within the company that the rocket will at least survive the journey to orbit and the release of satellites. But he says that re-entry, where the company has faced problems during recent tests, may be another matter.

“In short, they’re making good progress towards introducing Starship as a successful commercial launcher,” says Amato. “Whether Starship will be ‘revolutionary’, as promised by their CEO, will depend on whether they will be able to achieve a high launch cadence and on whether their design is cost-effective.”

SpaceX is about to launch tallest and most powerful rocket in history

Leah-Nani Alconcel at the University of Birmingham, UK, says that the 14th test flight will be a key step for SpaceX. Not only will the release of V3 satellites help the company update its Starlink constellation – the new satellites fly in a lower orbit than existing Starlink satellites and have higher data capacity – but their larger size than previous models will go some way to showing whether Starship is up to the task of launching its proposed Starmind data centre spacecraft, which are substantially larger.

“I don’t think it’s a huge jump in operational complexity for the launch vehicle, but demonstrating the Starlink V3 delivery to orbit is a significant step,” says Alconcel. “It may not be as flashy as the ‘chopstick catch‘ for the vehicle stages, but it would be a big boost to their commercial capabilities to have both the already-established high-cadence Falcon 9 and a proven Starship in their repertoire.”

A rocket launched last year is thought to have smashed into the lunar surface this morning, creating the moon’s newest crater

Three of the satellites due to be released on this flight have been modified to include cameras that can scan Starship’s heat shield whilst in orbit and transmit images to engineers on Earth.

During the 13th test flight, the booster stage made its ascent as planned, but during descent only eight of the 13 engines intended to slow its fall reignited, causing it to make a hard splashdown into the ocean rather than the planned gentle simulated landing on water. Neither the booster nor upper stage will attempt to make a controlled landing on the 14th flight.

Only two Starship flights have taken place so far in 2026, with flight 14 due to be the third. The upcoming flight will also be the second since SpaceX’s flotation on the stock market, which made controversial founder Elon Musk the world’s first trillionaire. The number of flights has fallen far beyond bold estimates made in previous years; SpaceX officials hoped to launch as many as 25 Starship test flights last year. In reality, only five test flights occurred that year.

SpaceX didn’t respond to a request for an interview, but the company says on its website that “there have been several modifications to hardware and software to address issues seen on the previous flight”.

Physicists are scrambling to make sense of possible dark matter signal

New Scientist September 18, 2026

We may have finally spotted a dark matter particle – but figuring out exactly what kind of particle it was is a daunting task. Even as researchers race to confirm they really did detect an unknown particle, physicists around the world have already started working out what sort of dark matter particle it might have been.

The potential particle in question was found at the LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) detector in South Dakota and announced on 1 September. The detector uses a huge tank of liquid xenon to look for signatures of dark matter particles smashing into the nuclei of xenon atoms, which are expected to produce a burst of light in response to any collision that would then be picked up by the arrays of cameras surrounding the tank.

The LZ group recorded only a single burst of light, and there is about a 1-in-200 chance that the signal was a fluke event rather than evidence that dark matter was there – but nevertheless it is tantalising.

Advertisement

Unexpected hints of dark matter should breathe life into particle physics

What makes the signal even more intriguing is that it was at a higher energy than would be expected if the particle were a standard weakly interacting massive particle, or WIMP, the simplest proposed type of dark matter. “It’s an anomalous event,” says Henning Flaecher at the University of Bristol in the UK, part of the LZ group. “It’s not what you would expect from the most general dark matter models.” The fact that this high-energy event was spotted, with no accompanying lower-energy collisions, makes it exceedingly unlikely that this particle, if it exists, is a “vanilla” WIMP, he says.

In the weeks since the announcement, theorists have released scores of papers digging into the data, searching for answers. “The large number of papers is less a statement that theorists believe the event is a [true] dark matter discovery and more a reflection of the fact that, if it persists, its energy already tells us quite a lot about types of physical processes that could produce it,” says Juri Smirnov at the University of Liverpool in the UK.

Many of those papers debate the possibility that the particle could be what is called a higgsino, a type of non-“vanilla” WIMP. It arises from a theoretical framework called supersymmetry, in which every known particle is proposed to have a “superpartner”, with some similar properties but different spin. In supersymmetry, the higgsino would be the superpartner of the Higgs boson.

Subscriber-only newsletter

A higgsino is the simplest WIMP explanation still available to explain the LZ signal, according to JiJi Fan at Brown University in Rhode Island. “It gives rise to a wealth of signals that could be searched for at different experimental frontiers.” Plus, a higgsino detection event is predicted to be unaccompanied by a host of lower-energy collisions, matching the signal detected by the LZ group.

However, the higgsino has its problems. The most basic model of that sort of particle that could explain the LZ detection seems to be ruled out by constraints from other experiments. This doesn’t mean the particle couldn’t have been a higgsino, but it does suggest the higgsino in question would need to have had a much higher mass than expected.

Many other models have been proposed to explain the detection, though. Among them are several models of dark matter particles originating in extra dimensions. While this may seem an unnecessarily complicated line of enquiry, these models were already being studied to solve other problems in particle physics, says Lisa Randall at Harvard University, a co-author of one such paper. “In some sense, the data looks like it’s calling out for something like this: it avoids the pre-existing constraints and fits quite naturally.”

Particle collisions are inherently quantum, but much of that character is lost when we turn them into classical data. Sarah Alam Malik explores whether preserving more of it could help us spot signs of dark matter and other new physics

An extra-dimensional dark matter candidate could both fit the LZ detection and explain why the fundamental particles have the masses they do, a long-standing puzzle, she says. Other models propose a whole dark matter sector, with multiple types of dark particles.

Right now, there is no way to tell which, if any, of these models might be correct. “I don’t think the data currently justify saying one of these is ‘the’ explanation,” says Smirnov. Some of them do come with additional predictions, though, which will be particularly useful when trying to pick through so many ideas, he says.

As the LZ team and other teams at detectors around the world continue to analyse their data, looking for additional events to confirm that the dark matter particle was real, all of these ideas could help them know exactly what it is they are looking for. “Anomalies could come and go, as we all know,” says Fan. “My take is that they provide us with some concrete targets to think: is this expected? Are there new territories/questions in theory or experiments we should cover? No matter whether the LZ event is confirmed, some of these topics would lead to long-term research.”

Fishapod fossil shows early elbows came in a variety of forms

New Scientist September 18, 2026

An ancient fish that lived just before the first four-legged animals walked on land had a pointed forearm bone and a hinge-like elbow joint, adding to the growing evidence of trial and error in early arm formation.

The 350-million-year-old animal was one of several “fishapods” – creatures with fins that had evolved some limb-like features. It might have used its fins for actions other than swimming, such as moving along the bottom of rivers.

“We keep uncovering more and more variation in the shapes and geometries of these bones,” says Thomas Stewart at Pennsylvania State University. “The more we study the diversity, the more we realise there’s just a range of unusual forms of animals living in and exploring their ecologies.”

Advertisement

Extraordinary ichthyosaur fossil shows its last meal was a pterosaur

In the past two decades, scientists have found fossils from dozens of distinct species of finned tetrapodomorphs, or fishapods. These animals lived in water and had fins that contained bones similar to those found in the limbs of today’s four-legged animals. The most iconic fishapod – Tiktaalik roseae – has been nicknamed the “crawling fish” because it could probably use its fin-limbs to crawl out of water, capturing an important step in the evolution of vertebrates.

But the story of how fish evolved into land animals is anything but a straight line, Stewart says. For instance, Qikiqtania wakei, which he and his colleagues described in 2022, was a fishapod that appears to have initially evolved weight-supporting fins but then evolved to be a full-time swimmer.

Now, the team has analysed another unusual fishapod. So far, the animal is known only from fossils of a single isolated fin that was discovered on Canada’s Ellesmere Island. The researchers CT-scanned the fossil and compared its arm-like bones with those of 16 other known fishapods. The isolated fin didn’t quite match any of them, suggesting it came from a distinct species.

Subscriber-only newsletter

The radius – which, in humans, runs from the elbow to the thumb side of the wrist – was long and triangular, coming to a sharp point at its far end – where the wrist would be in a tetrapod. Other bones and tissue would have led from here to the fin’s tip, but the shape of the radius itself would have provided little support for pushing against the ground, says Stewart.

At the elbow end, the radius lacked the rounded knob seen in other fishapods, but instead was narrow and “shaped like a bean”. The upper arm bone was missing, but the radius’s shape suggests the joint between them would have worked like a simple hinge that largely bent back and forth in a single plane. This is more restrictive than the elbows of other fishapods: they could twist and rotate their elbows, like we can, to provide greater flexibility of movement.

The fossil also contained the intermedium, a small bone seen in fishapods that scientists suspect eventually evolved into part of the wrist. In the fossil from the unknown fishapod, the intermedium was relatively longer than in Tiktaalik and its close relatives.

Hidden fossils reveal secrets of oceans before major mass extinction

Exactly what the animal was doing with its unusual fins isn’t clear, says Stewart. The restricted movement of the elbow might have been a kind of experiment in evolving appendages that could have served this particular animal’s needs, in its environment. But this doesn’t necessarily mean the elbow joint was perfectly suited for its role.

“When animals begin to explore new kinds of movements, they might be kind of awkward,” he says. “They might not be the best at it, but they’re still good enough. It’s a matter of sufficiency, not optimality.”

Julia Molnar at New York Institute of Technology, Long Island, says she was excited to see the new specimen. “The question of when and why the fin-limb and water-land transitions occurred is still very much up for debate,” she says. “I would not be surprised if this wide variation in radius shape represents different approaches to the problems and opportunities of this changing world.”

Palaeontologists have found new evidence that the early ancestors of amphibians, reptiles and mammals did not have a larval stage with external gills like modern frogs or salamanders

Importantly, the variations shouldn’t be interpreted as different attempts to evolve limbs for a future life on land, but rather to suit their own current environment, says Brian Swartz at the University of California, Berkeley.

“A fish like this one might use its fins to ‘walk’ in shallow water or push through vegetation,” says Molnar, “allowing it to escape large aquatic predators and prey on smaller fish and arthropods at the water’s edge.”

Journal of Vertebrate Paleontology DOI: 10.1080/02724634.2026.2708076

Our brain evolved from two primitive nervous systems that merged

New Scientist September 18, 2026

Our brain may be a hybrid of two ancient nervous systems that were packaged together hundreds of millions of years ago. This is based on the finding that the front and back brain regions in people and several other species develop from two distinct cell types in embryos, instead of sharing the same developmental origin, as previously thought.

“Our research suggests that evolution took two existing neural systems and pushed them together spatially,” says Kyle Loh at Stanford University. “Having the brain as one organ would probably be more efficient, but we rely on this primordial way to make the brain as two separate pieces.”

Human brains may have got bigger for no particular reason

Loh and his colleagues studied early stages of mouse embryo development and found its brain develops from two types of early progenitor cells, proliferative cells with a limited capacity of self-renewal. One type expresses a gene called OTX2 and turns into the neurons found in the front part of the brain, comprising the forebrain and midbrain. The other expresses a gene called GBX2 and becomes the neurons in the back part of the brain, the hindbrain.

Advertisement

The researchers then conducted experiments using human cells in a dish and found that the neurons of the hindbrain and those of the forebrain and midbrain also develop from different progenitor cells. “We’ve shown for the first time that the front of the brain arises from a totally different progenitor cell than the back of the brain,” says Loh.

This explains why it has been so hard to grow human hindbrain tissue in a lab. “It was actually a summer student’s failed experiment that got us into this,” says Loh. Researchers have typically tried making hindbrain neurons from the progenitor cells that are destined to become forebrain and midbrain neurons, which doesn’t work, he says.

Subscriber-only newsletter

Armed with this knowledge, the team was able to grow functional human hindbrain motor neurons in a dish for the first time by starting with the correct type of progenitor cell.

The hindbrain coordinates fundamental life-sustaining processes, such as breathing, sleeping, eating and the beating of the heart, whereas the forebrain is the centre of higher-level thought. Conditions like amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), the most common type of motor neuron disease, and spinal muscular atrophy cause speech and swallowing difficulties because they affect the hindbrain. Recently, scientists also discovered that GLP-1 drugs like Ozempic and Wegovy suppress appetite in mice by acting on the hindbrain.

Now that it is easier to grow human hindbrain neurons in a dish, it should assist ALS and spinal muscular atrophy research, and allow us to investigate the precise mechanisms of how GLP-1 drugs work in people, says Loh.

When does your brain reach adulthood? We’re now understanding the many ways the organ continues to mature decades after society first deems you an adult

The researchers also studied early-stage embryos of chickens, zebrafish and acorn worms, and found their nervous systems are similarly derived from two different types of progenitor cells. This suggests our shared two-origin brain system arose at least 550 million years ago.

But jellyfish, which we diverged from around 600 to 700 million years ago, have two separate nervous systems. These may have joined up in our distant ancestors because it improved their overall processing power, says Loh. “You get more efficient communication when things are closer together,” he says.

Having our brains develop along two separate pathways might also have facilitated the evolution of complex thought, says Loh. While the hindbrain was taking care of all the basic functions for keeping us alive, “evolution could play around with the forebrain, and make mistakes and give rise to all the fancy things like memory and creativity”, he says.

Nature Neuroscience DOI: 10.1038/s41593-026-02433-7

NZTA orders nationwide stand-down of heritage train services after Te Awamutu railway death

New Zealand Herald September 20, 2026

The fatal incident occurred yesterday at Te Awamutu station.

All nationwide heritage train services have been halted following the death at Te Awamutu railway station last night.

Police confirmed late last night that a person died after “an incident involving a train” at about 6.20pm.

“Sadly, one person died at the scene,” Senior Sergeant John McCarthy said.

“This is a tragic incident, and we are providing support to whānau and those who acted immediately to try to help.”

Email correspondence seen by the Herald confirms that all rail heritage services have been cancelled today by order of the New Zealand Transport Agency Waka Kotahi (NZTA).

“Due to a serious rail incident in the North Island, the network regulator has initiated a mandatory, nationwide safety stand-down for all services operating under a rail heritage licence,” the notice reads.

“While this incident is entirely separate from our operations here in the South Island, standard safety protocols require all movement to pause until an initial investigation is completed.

“The safety of our passengers and crew is our absolute priority, and we strictly adhere to these regulatory requirements.”

KiwiRail referred queries about cancellations to NZTA, which has been approached for comment.

Contact the New Zealand Herald newsroom

One passenger who had plans to travel by rail from Dunedin to Christchurch told the Herald they were informed by service provider Mainlander at 2am that their 8am trip was cancelled.

“We got a note under the [hotel] door at 2am saying all historic services have been cancelled.

“It’s really awful for the family involved and so they [Mainlander] just need to do what they have to.”

Replacement coaches were arranged for passengers, with the traveller describing about 300 to 400 people packed into buses.

“The Mainlander team here are wonderful and looking after everyone as well as possible.”

The journey was expected to take just under eight hours.

Police said there was no ongoing risk and asked members of the public to avoid the railway station.

WorkSafe said it had been notified and an inspector was making initial inquiries to understand what had happened.

A Christchurch cafe is selling what could be New Zealand’s most expensive coffee, with single cups going for $100.

Rook Cafe on Hereford St in the central city recently sourced some rare “Geisha” beans from Panama.

Contact our South Island newsroom

This morning the special beans from the renowned Mount Totumas estate in Chiriqui were being used to brew $100 cups of coffee.

The first customers, Maxwell and Tallon, split the cost of a cup, saying it was “very exciting”.

“I mean, it’s just such a rare variety from like a very specific area, from a very specific farm, and you get the trustworthiness of Kyle [Cabangun], who’s just a fantastic barista, so it’s a once-in-a-lifetime chance really,” Maxwell said.

A self-confessed coffee aficionado, he has had expensive cups before, “maybe $20 to $30 per cup, but this is definitely the most expensive I’ve had”.

He wasn’t quite sure what to expect, but said: “From what I’ve smelled, it’s probably going to be something floral and really beautiful and nice.

“It’ll be really interesting to see what it comes out like, particularly with the brewing method that he’s chosen.

After watching the “nerve-wracking” process of it being made, Maxwell sat down to enjoy his coffee.

His first reaction was that it tasted quite “floral” but he was interested to see how it changed when the temperature fell.

“But first thoughts: really good. It’s fantastic so far.”

Tallon agreed but added: “It’s quite a lot to think about, when you’ve got a $100 price tag in the back of your mind. But it’s really nice, I can’t wait for my second sip.”

Another early customer, Lily, said it was “worth every cent” and a “once in a lifetime opportunity”. She also described it as “floral”.

“It’s lovely, really lovely,” she said.

Rook had presold a number of cups, but early birds like Lily can still grab a taste of the limited supply, with only 14-15 cups likely to be available.

Cabangun prepared the beans in a hand grinder to avoid losing any coffee before using a paper filter and adding hot water.

They compared the price tag to that of high-quality wine.

“Coffee, if anything, is harder to grow and produce than wine,″ Cabangun said.

“This cup of coffee is some of the highest-quality coffee you’ll probably ever try. Coffee is graded on a scale of 0-100, and this sits at 94-96 on that range.”

Mike Thorpe is a senior journalist for the Herald, based in Christchurch. He has been a broadcast journalist across television and radio for 20 years and joined the Herald in August 2024.

Christopher Luxon says he’s “all in” on National’s plan to break up the supermarket duopoly – but if the Commerce Commission rejects the idea, “we won’t be doing it”.

Speaking on Newstalk ZB’s Mike Hosking Breakfast, the Prime Minister disagreed with Hosking’s claim that National – supposedly the party of enterprise and hard work – was “picking on industries you think are a bit suspect”.

“We’re also a party of competition,” he told Hosking, adding that the supermarket sector in New Zealand was “fundamentally not competitive”.

He said he could not think of another country where 82% of the market was dominated by just two grocery players.

National believed its policy would see supermarkets competing better on price, choice, range and location – but there should be a very high bar to intervene and it should be taken out of the hands of politicians, he said.

That was the reason for giving the Commerce Commission the final sign-off, in the form of a six-month review after the election.

“If they say no, then we won’t be doing it … It’s such a big intervention that you should make sure that it’s reassured by the very best competition experts you’ve got.”

Luxon acknowledged coalition partner Act didn’t agree with the policy but said there was an emerging consensus across Parliament and “it may well be agree to disagree”.

Luxon is making his media rounds this morning, as parties ramp up their campaign promises ahead of Election Day on November 7.

The past week has seen National and Labour compete to see who can crack down the hardest on the supermarket duopoly, with both claiming their plans will lower food prices for Kiwi shoppers.

National last week announced it wanted to carve off Foodstuffs’ Pak’nSave brand from its New World and Four Square brands, leaving the country with three nationwide supermarket chains. The move would first be reviewed by the Commerce Commission to see if it would bring down prices.

Labour, meanwhile, wants to separate Foodstuffs’ and Woolworths’ wholesale and retail arms, letting smaller grocers purchase stock from any wholesaler they choose.

The grocery sector is promising to fight any restructuring plans.

On the weekend, National also announced it would ban digital screen use for kids in early childcare if re-elected, as well as tightly restricting young students’ screen time at school.

That policy would minimise individual device use for Years 1-3, as well as bringing in age-appropriate limits for older students. It would also require the writing component of primary students’ twice-yearly assessments to be completed on paper.

The Act Party has promised to “make farming fun again” by cutting red tape, including climate regulations, from the agriculture sector.

And New Zealand First will campaign on a 15-point health plan including reviewing intravenous vitamin C and embedding nutrition in the school curriculum.

Last week also saw investigative journalist Nicky Hager teasing a new book, though the subject matter remains a mystery.

Hager has invited journalists to the book launch on Tuesday night in Wellington.

He has previously released two books on the internal workings of the National Party, The Hollow Men (2006) and Dirty Politics (2014), while his 2002 book Seeds of Distrust went behind the scenes on Labour’s genetically modified corn scandal.

Explainer: What Labour’s capital gains tax means for properties worth less than they were bought for

New Zealand Herald September 20, 2026

Labour’s proposed 28% capital gains tax comes with a little-known rule that could make a key difference for people who bought property at the peak of the market.

The party has stressed its “simple” tax would only apply to gains made after its July 2027 valuation day and would not impact any gains made beforehand.

The tax only applies to investment property, which includes all second homes like baches or someone’s only home if they have not lived in it for a period of four years or more.

It means property that has ballooned in value over decades would not suddenly be slapped with a massive tax bill if owners decided to sell up after 2027 – only gains after that year count.

But there is a caveat for properties purchased at the peak of the market that could make the purchase price relevant in calculating a property’s tax bill.

It relates to those whose property has dropped in value but then climbs again slightly before sale.

Say someone bought a second house at the peak of the market for $1 million, which has dropped to $800,000 by the July 2027 valuation day, but then inches up to eventually sell for $850,000.

In real terms, the owner would have lost $150,000, but would they be taxed on the $50,000 increase between valuation day and sale?

Despite not having a clear answer in its policy document or website, the Labour Party has clarified that a property owner in this situation would not be taxed on the $50,000 increase between valuation day and sale.

A party spokeswoman said in order to calculate the amount of CGT owed, Labour would use a “median rule”, as recommended by the Tax Working Group report.

“This makes sure a valuation on one particular day doesn’t create an artificial gain or loss – you pay tax on the gain you actually make,” the spokeswoman said.

The Tax Working Group recommends a median rule as a way to avoid taxing artificial gains.

Estimate the taxable gain and possible tax bill if the property is sold after Labour's proposed valuation day.

The median rule makes $900,000 the effective cost base. The estimated taxable gain is the sale price minus that amount, capped at zero.

* Estimate only. This calculator models Labour's announced 28% tax on taxable property gains after 1 July 2027 and applies the Tax Working Group's median rule. It does not include deductible costs, improvements, losses, ownership shares, existing tax rules or other individual circumstances. Labour's proposal is not yet law and its final design could change.

To calculate the taxable amount, officials would take the median, or middle number, of the purchase price, valuation day price, and sale price and subtract that from the sale price, to calculate the taxable amount.

This means the purchase price can be used to ensure owners are not taxed on gains they did not make overall.

House prices peaked in late 2021 but have since dropped by about 15% in nominal terms and roughly 30% lower after inflation.

New data reported last week suggested that price peaks are unlikely to be reached again until late 2029.

Nick Goodall, head of research for property intelligence firm Cotality, estimates that three-quarters of residential property investors who purchased during the peak would be impacted by Labour’s median rule if the tax were to be implemented.

It equates to about 19,500 residential properties from a total of 26,000, Goodall’s estimates suggest, noting the tax excludes the family home.

“This is likely one of the factors that has led to Labour projecting a relatively small amount of revenue to be gained from the proposed CGT in the first year, ramping up after that,” he said.

The party is modelling $100m in revenue from the tax in its first year, climbing to more than $1.3 billion after 2030.

Goodall said investors will likely delay selling their property due to the new tax, predicting about 18,000 residential sales in the first year of the tax being implemented, down on a normal year of 30,000-35,000.

Cotality estimates that about 29,000 first-home buyers entered the market during the 18-month peak period, with about 3600 thought to be in negative equity, meaning they owe more on their property than what it is now worth.

Ethan Manera is a Wellington-based journalist covering Wellington issues, local politics and business in the capital. He can be emailed at ethan. manera@nzme. co. nz.

Wallabies have been eradicated in one forest and a lake restored – but catfish, crabs and some pest plants are spreading in the Bay of Plenty, a new report shows.

The Bay of Plenty Regional Council says it is “winning” the battle against invasive species despite the mixed results.

The council’s pest control report for 2025/26 was released last week.

It found 92% of pest management programmes were on track and no new pests became established.

A major success was the elimination of wallabies from Endean Forest, near Rotorua.

Wallabies were introduced from Australia more than a century ago and spread unchecked. More than one million are now thought to live in the wild in New Zealand.

An aerial 1080 operation was carried out on Endean Forest in August 2025. A year later, surveillance cameras no longer detected wallabies in the forest or surrounding area.

The operation aimed to stop the pest from spreading west into the Mamaku Plateau.

Across the Bay of Plenty, 2295 wallabies were culled during the year, including 33 in areas targeted for complete eradication.

Lake Ōkāreka was another success. The lake’s health score rose from 36% in 2013 to 70% by 2025.

More than a decade of weed control has resulted in hornwort, one of New Zealand’s worst aquatic weeds, being undetected since 2015.

Two other invasive weeds, egeria and elodea, are also no longer detected, while lagarosiphon remains at low levels.

Council biosecurity manager Hamish Lass said the wallaby “elimination” was significant because it prevented population spread into the Waikato.

“It also supports the effectiveness of aerial 1080 as a tool to eliminate wallaby,” he said.

Lass said Ōkāreka was now “very close” to being free of invasive aquatic weeds.

“The lake’s strong ecological recovery shows what can be achieved through long-term investment, strong partnerships, regular surveillance and rapid response.”

However, one of the more significant concerns in the report was the surge in brown bullhead catfish in Lake Rotorua and Lake Rotoiti.

A total of 19,589 catfish were caught during the year, compared with 5477 the previous year, despite fewer nets being deployed.

The report said catch rates had increased substantially and noted most fish caught were juveniles, indicating strong ongoing breeding.

Lass said the council was “concerned” the population appeared to be increasing despite “ongoing control efforts”.

“While control operations removed nearly 20,000 catfish during the year, the data suggests the population remains resilient and may be growing.”

Meanwhile, the Asian paddle crab population in Tauranga Harbour is now so high that “containment is no longer realistically achievable”.

Lass said the focus had shifted to monitoring, targeted removals, community engagement and understanding the long-term impacts of the species on the harbour ecosystem.

Several widespread pest plant programmes are also struggling against infestations.

Woolly nightshade remains the region’s largest plant pest programme, with infestations spread across 1723 properties. Recorded pest cover increased by almost 29,000sq m during the year, reaching more than 335,000sq m.

Wild kiwifruit also expanded, with infestations increasing by more than 28,000sq m to almost 359,000sq m across 1074 properties.

“The wide-scale distribution of these species, the fact they are spread by birds, coupled with fast growth rates, makes them very challenging to manage,” Lass said.

He said the current budget and staff numbers were “not considered adequate” to make significant progress in managing these species.

Additional increases were recorded for yellow flag iris, Darwin’s barberry and apple of Sodom. The council attributed some of the growth to improved surveillance uncovering previously unknown infestations.

The report highlighted successes in controlling other invasive plants, including the near-eradication of sporobolus grass from Tauranga Moana estuaries and significant reductions in lantana, old man’s beard and Italian buckthorn infestations.

Overall, the council completed 4403 property inspections during 2025/26, received 1094 public inquiries and found no new exclusion pests (pests not currently known to be in the region).

Lass pointed to 92% of pest management programmes remaining on track and the absence of any new exclusion pests becoming established as evidence of success.

“Overall, the regional council considers the Bay of Plenty to be winning the battle against invasive pests and weeds.”

Mathew Nash is a Local Democracy Reporting journalist based at the Rotorua Daily Post. He has previously written for SunLive, been a regular contributor to RNZ and was a football reporter in Britain for eight years.

Whangārei Hospital was at critical capacity seven times longer this winter

New Zealand Herald September 20, 2026

Whangārei Hospital's emergency department has been in Code Red seven times longer this winter than 2025, the official information shows. Photo / NZME

Pressure at Whangārei Hospital’s emergency department this winter has been laid bare in documents released to the Northern Advocate.

The data showed the emergency department (ED) was in Code Red seven times longer in the first two weeks of July than the same period in 2025.

Code Red was the highest level in the ED’s escalation system and showed significant pressure, such as high patient volumes, limited bed availability or staff shortages.

In July, nurses said they feared someone would die in the ED waiting room because of the pressure the hospital was under, but Health New Zealand Te Whatu Ora was unable to directly answer how busy the ED was.

An Official Information Act request showed Whangārei Hospital ED was in Code Red for 1470 minutes from July 1 to 14, 2026.

That was seven times the 204 minutes for the equivalent period in 2025.

Health NZ noted Code Red did not mean the ED had reached “capacity” or couldn’t take more patients.

“If emergency care is required, people should go to an ED. Across the country we actively manage pressure and people should continue to expect that if they need emergency care, they will be seen and treated.”

Dr Gary Payinda, a Northland ED doctor speaking in his personal capacity as an ASMS member and Labour Party candidate, said the system was in crisis.

Patients suffered because they were unable to get timely care and staff suffered “moral injury” if they were unable to care for patients at the expected standard, he said.

It was made worse by a lack of openness about a hiring crackdown and incorrect messages about thousands more nurses being hired, Payinda said.

Data revealed by Labour showed there were just 54 more nurse fulltime-equivalents (FTEs) hired nationwide in March 2026 than March 2024. In Northland, the number decreased by 67 FTE.

“Staffing dropped during a period of time that we were in frequent overwhelm,” said Payinda. “It’s a crisis that makes you lose some faith.”

Payinda said the pressure on Whangārei Hospital ED was not due solely to influenza season.

“We were at times hitting almost daily ED capacity, up to 180%, before the flu struck. The flu was just the straw that broke the camel’s back.”

While pressure on the ED was reducing, Payinda said there would be a summer surge as Northland’s population increased and more staff were needed.

“It’s not one-off or random, it’s a system whose capacity is worn-down and eroded.”

But Whangārei MP, National’s Dr Shane Reti, said Whangārei Hospital ED – like emergency departments across the country – was under pressure from the worst influenza season in a decade.

Increased sick leave among clinical staff also created challenges, he said.

“I want to acknowledge that pressure and thank the doctors, nurses, and other health professionals at Whangārei Hospital who have turned up day after day for their patients through a very tough winter.”

Thankfully, weekly ED presentations due to respiratory infections peaked in the week ending August 16 and were now below the 2025 winter peak, Reti said.

The latest statistics, covering January to March 2026, showed 84% of Northland ED patients and 74% nationwide were admitted, discharged or transferred within the Government’s six-hour target, he said.

This was part of a national turnaround in emergency department performance under the coalition Government, Reti said.

“When National left office in 2017, 89.2% of patients were admitted, discharged, or transferred within six hours. By 2023, after six years of Labour, that had fallen to just 67.5%.

“Under this Government, patients are spending less time waiting in emergency departments, and there are more staff on the frontline.”

Reti joined Health Minister Simeon Brown last week to turn the first sod of Whangārei Hospital’s new acute services building – including expanded ED – and 158-bed ward tower.

He acknowledged it would take time to deliver the project, set to cost more than $750 million, but said it was a long-term investment, giving the growing community the facilities it needed.

Reti said Northland had a lot of new health infrastructure open in the past three years including a new $50m paediatric facility, $3m whānau house, $35m child health centre, $60m radiotherapy centre and $18m car park extension.

Health NZ also put measures in place in Northland to help EDs manage winter demand this year, Reti said.

Measures included:

“Whangārei should be proud of its hospital and the people who work in it,” Reti said.

Denise Piper is a news reporter for the Northern Advocate, focusing on health and business. She has more than 20 years in journalism and is passionate about covering stories that make a difference.

Councils are getting hazard warnings, residents should pay attention too – Editorial

New Zealand Herald September 20, 2026

Damage caused by a storm and flooding in Te Araroa, Gisborne District. Photo / Corey Fleming

Disaster can strike anywhere and, when it does, the public cannot depend on external protections or preventive measures.

If people haven’t already, now is the time to review plans and preparations for a disaster.

A Herald investigation looked into what natural hazards councils around the North Island have been warned of, after a review of the deadly Mount Maunganui landslide found Tauranga City Council had received multiple warnings about the hazard over years.

From Northland to Greater Wellington, scientific evidence of flooding, tsunami, landslides and earthquake risks shows disasters aren’t just something that happens to someone else somewhere else.

Doubtless, the South Island also faces its own hazards, which local authorities are also hopefully taking into account.

Natural hazard warnings from scientists can be all too easily dismissed as scaremongering, but one must consider where the harm is in being too prepared.

If preparation and prevention are done right, then most people might never know about it.

The harm of local authorities being unprepared is all too clear – six lives were lost in the Mauao landslide.

An independent review in 2024 into the response to Cyclone Gabrielle, in which 11 people died, found local officials were “overwhelmed” by the “severity, speed and scale” of the disaster.

Review head Mike Bush was clear at the time that his review was not a “blame-apportioning exercise”, and it shouldn’t have been.

His finding that New Zealand’s emergency management system was not fit for purpose and “sets up good people to fail” showed that even the experts could find themselves unprepared for the worst-case scenario.

The public should have high expectations of local authorities. However, it is fair to say they are not perfect and in some cases may not be prepared for all eventualities, whether because of the opportunity costs of significant investment or because a risk has not been identified yet.

The best thing people can do to give themselves a good chance in a disaster is to make sure they have their own preparations in place.

An evacuation route, an assembly point in a tsunami, flood or earthquake, methods of transportation and supplies in an accessible grab bag are all important aspects of personal preparedness.

It is timely that the National Emergency Management Agency’s national earthquake drill and tsunami evacuation, ShakeOut, takes place next month.

It can only be a good thing if more people are ready with a disaster plan.

The Guardian Sun, 20 Sep 2026 21:30:38 GMT

Proposal one of many at conference responding to concern voters unaware of party’s policies or what it stands for

The Liberal Democrats say they will tax big tech to finance a new online crime agency, as they try to address concerns that not enough voters know what the party stands for.

The plan, to be announced at the party conference on Monday by the Lib Dems’ home affairs spokesperson, Max Wilkinson, would create a new Online Crime Agency focused on offences including child sexual abuse material, trafficking in drugs and weapons, and deepfake AI-generated pornographic images.

The planned budget of £250m a year would be paid for by an “online crime levy” on large AI and technology companies. Wilkinson is to tell the conference it is “time they picked up the bill” for offences they had enabled.

Ed Davey, the party leader, on Sunday set out a proposal to cut fuel duty by 10p a litre for a fixed three-month period, as well as reducing the bus fare cap from £3 to £1 and other transport-related cost of living policies.

The party is increasingly concerned that, although it won its best election result in a century in 2024, it does not have a distinctive enough message to reach voters in an increasingly fragmented and noisy political landscape.

Polling conducted to coincide with the conference in Brighton, released on Sunday, showed Lib Dem policies are less well known than those of Restore Britain, which launched as a political party only in February and has one MP – Rupert Lowe – compared with the Lib Dems’ 71.

The research by More in Common, which was presented at the conference, showed widespread uncertainty among voters about what the Lib Dems stood for. Just 39% said they had an idea, lower than for every other major party, including Restore Britain, which was formed by Lowe after he split from Reform UK.

Other parts of the research showed just 16% of voters said they had heard from the Lib Dems in recent months, against 66% for Reform, while 3% said they had seen Davey on social media, compared with 20% for the Reform leader, Nigel Farage.

In a round of media interviews on Sunday morning, Davey pushed back against the idea that the Lib Dems, who are static in national polling at about 12%, risked being forgotten in the political conversation amid the rise in prominence of Reform and the Greens.

His party, Davey insisted, was making a genuine difference, and not just generating coverage without substance.

“I’m talking about real change, not just talking about the bubbles,” he told the BBC’s Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg show. “We have been winning council elections for eight years in a row. That has never happened before – it’s the most successful period that we’ve had.”

While there is no talk among Lib Dem MPs about a challenge to Davey, some say they are frustrated the party’s message is too vague and its support too reliant on tactical voting in a limited number of places, mainly in the south of England.

One Lib Dem MP told a conference fringe event, at which More in Common’s findings were presented, that the party needed to expand the geographical and social range of its influence.

Specialist courtrooms to prioritise rape cases in England and Wales

The Guardian Sun, 20 Sep 2026 21:30:26 GMT

Funding boost for facilities and fixed dates for trials designed to encourage more survivors to come forward

Specialist courtrooms prioritising cases of rape and other serious sex offences are to be introduced across England and Wales, with campaigners welcoming the move as potentially transformative.

The changes, designed to encourage more survivors to come forward, will include the provision of private entrances and waiting rooms, and facilities equipped for recording evidence in advance and observing sentencing remotely.

Announcing the move, Andy Burnham said victims of rape and serious sexual offences had felt let down by the justice system for too long, adding that prosecution rates for rape remained “shamefully low”, with many victims waiting years for justice.

“These changes are long overdue and will make a significant difference, but focusing on prosecution alone will not be enough,” the prime minister said.

“So as well as ensuring victims get justice, we will step up action to prevent these horrific crimes from happening in the first place.”

A multimillion-pound cash injection is intended to make sure every crown court in England and Wales has at least one room set up specifically to hear rape and serious sexual offence cases within two years.

Rape and serious sexual offence cases will also be prioritised in courts more widely, the Ministry of Justice (MoJ) announced. Such trials will be given a fixed date, as opposed to being placed on floating lists where they can be moved at short notice and delayed by months.

Among those welcoming the announcement was Labour’s Charlotte Nichols, who told the House of Commons this year she was raped after an event she attended as an MP and waited 1,088 days for her case to get to court.

Nichols said: “Today marks a hugely important milestone, helping to improve the experience of victims and survivors of sexual violence in the court system who are all too often retraumatised by seeking justice.

“I’m proud that substantive, meaningful change has come from waiving my anonymity to speak about my own experiences, and am hugely grateful to the prime minister and lord chancellor for taking forward these measures, as I know the difference they would have made for me and so many of the survivors I have worked with in recent years.”

The MoJ cited Nichols’ “immense strength and bravery” in its announcement.

While welcoming the announcement, there was a warning by the victims commissioner, Claire Waxman, that the crown court backlog of rape and sexual offence cases was now “significantly worse” than when she first called for specialist courts in 2021.

She said: “Tens of thousands more victims are now waiting for their cases to reach trial, and specialist courts alone will not be enough to tackle the scale of the delays or deliver the swift justice victims deserve. Indeed, court delays could prevent many rape victims from accessing the specialist courtrooms that are being set up to support them.”

Further changes announced include new trauma-informed training for court staff and a pilot scheme giving victims of sex offences a single point of contact to ensure their needs are met during the court process.

Separate from the funding for courtrooms, there will also be £43m to support survivors through the national rape and sexual abuse support fund for the next two years, including through counselling, therapy, outreach and group activities.

The new measures also include the creation of a rape justice taskforce, drawing figures from across the criminal justice system to tackle the rising rate of postponed rape trials and confront the myths that cause victims to withdraw from cases.

The Conservatives’ shadow justice secretary, Nick Timothy, said tackling delays in rape trials was long overdue, but that the courts backlog had been “used” by the Labour as justification for controversial plans to significantly restrict the right to jury trials.“If resources can be found to accelerate rape trials, why are they persisting in their attack on this ancient right to jury trials?” he said.

In 2022, an announcement by Boris Johnson’s government of three specialist courtrooms to prosecute rape cases was dismissed by legal blogger the Secret Barrister as a “gimmick” that did not address the chronic underfunding of the justice system.

Changes in the new provisions include many of the reforms that campaigners and charities have been calling for over many years.

“Taken together, they reflect the urgency of ensuring that courts are fit for purpose and properly meet the needs of victims and survivors, which is crucial to securing justice,” said Ciara Bergman, the chief executive of Rape Crisis England & Wales.

“We’re particularly pleased to see measures that will improve trial efficiency and ensure survivors are better able to participate in, and observe, proceedings.”
