The Split Up review – this soapy divorce drama is loads of lavish, nonsensical fun

The Guardian Sun, 20 Sep 2026 21:00:25 GMT

Sanjeev Bhaskar plays a patriarch handing over the family firm in a spinoff of The Split. It’s full-on sudsy fun right from the off

I do like a soap that doesn’t hang about. That works itself up to a creamy lather and invites you to shut the bathroom door against real life and dive into a hot bath with it immediately for a much-needed break.

The Split Up delivers full-on sudsy fun from the start. From the team behind The Split, it’s another glossy tale of a family-run family law firm specialising in the never-too-complicated divorce cases of any high net worth individuals in their vicinity. This time, it’s written by Ursula Rani Sarma instead of Abi Morgan, the family is British South Asian and the location is Manchester not London, but beyond that it’s very much business as usual. A case of the week functions as the still eye of the ever-growing storm composed of the love lives, personal concerns and professional ambitions of the interrelated lawyers and their friends, colleagues and enemies – who are often, of course, one and the same thing. Mild glamour meets much plot; viewer happiness ensues.

The new clan, the Kishans, comprises recently widowed patriarch Dhruv (Sanjeev Bhaskar), who is preparing to hand over the firm he has spent decades building from scratch to his charismatic, highly competent daughter, Aria (Ritu Arya), who is as driven and ambitious as he was at that age. But Dhruv is older now, and driven and ambitious youth does not seem quite the unassailable asset it once was. Caution and consolidation perhaps have their place, too. He ponders this quietly. Aria is too busy laying plans, busting divorce balls and dealing with her portion of B-plots to notice immediately.

The main complication to Aria’s narrative is her dad’s unilateral decision to add financial specialist Luke (Dimitri Leonidas) to the firm. Of all the forensic accountants in all the world … Luke is the one Aria had a one-night stand with at a conference a couple of years ago. His re-entry into her world delights her not, and would delight her boyfriend, Neal (Danny Ashok) – who was also her boyfriend at the time – even less. Aria and Luke had better keep their former association hidden and their relationship going forward strictly professional. That’s a very good plan. Like most good plans, it fails on first contact with the extremely hot enemy.

In the mix we also have Aria’s sister, Maya (Aysha Kala), who is a lawyer. Perhaps wisely, she took herself out of the melee a while back and just pops in now and again to lend a hand, in between raising a handful of kids and enjoying a strong and happy marriage, despite the long hours and late nights her husband (Tom Forbes) is putting in at his demanding job. Viewers hope that this is a sign of his unflagging commitment to providing for his family, but viewers have been here before.

Rounding out the family is little brother Kav (Arian Nik). He is gay, which is fine by Dhruv, but he is also requiring multiple goes at passing his law exams, which is not. Journalist-influencer Ashok (Mawaan Rizwan) is keen to take his mind off things. Though he is also keen to glean gossip about the firm’s celebrity clients. Viewers hope no personal-professional lines are crossed. But viewers have been here before.

Amid the familial and genital shenanigans (and they are not one and the same – this is not exactly a family show, except that it’s a show about a family, but it’s not THAT unfamilyish a show), the Kishans do occasionally muster some billable hours. In the first episode, these are mostly invoiced to Tash and Alex (Jane Horrocks and Lenny Henry, respectively), hosts of a wildly popular podcast about making marriage work, called Marriage Works, until one of them was caught in flagrante with a younger woman. Twist – it was Tash! The lady half of the couple! She doesn’t want a divorce, she wants an open marriage. Aria wants Alex to protect his assets. Alex wants Tash to be happy. Aria wants to eyeroll, hard, but Alex is an old friend of her father and she resists. In episode two, the guest star is Jameela Jamil, as another internetty type about to be screwed over by whatever the Modern is for “absolute bounder” until Aria rescues her too.

But ultimately, the cases of the week are very slight, forgettable things, clearly of little interest to anyone involved and the site of most of the weak spots in the script (“Our friendship is our legacy, that’s the real loss here”). It’s the multiplying personal dramas and the nicely drawn tensions and tendernesses between the Kishans – who are all depicted with wit and warmth – that will keep us coming back. It is great fun: lavish nonsense with just enough truth in it to stop it becoming utterly preposterous. Come on in, the water’s lovely.

The Split Up is available on BBC iPlayer

Evenepoel wins fourth world time trial title in a row, Reusser retains her crown

The Guardian Sun, 20 Sep 2026 20:28:21 GMT

Remco Evenepoel dominates men’s event in Montreal

Marlen Reusser denies Zoe Backstedt in women’s race

Remco Evenepoel etched his name into the history books with a dominant fourth successive men’s world time-trial victory in Montreal on Sunday.

The 2024 Olympic champion came into the race as the overwhelming favourite and he did not disappoint. Evenepoel was already more than 30 seconds ahead of the rest by the second intermediate time check, just over halfway along the 39.2km (24.4 mile) route.

By the time he reached the finish line, the 26-year-old Belgian had put almost a minute into second-placed Filippo Ganna of Italy, with the French rider Paul Seixas taking third another 15 seconds back. Evenepoel has not lost a time trial since the 2025 Tour de France.

Evenepoel becomes the first man to win the time trial world title four times in a row, while also equalling the record number of overall titles held by Germany’s Tony Martin and the Swiss rider Fabian Cancellara.

He has enjoyed his best season to date so far this year, winning the Amstel Gold Race, Clásica San Sebastián and Grand Prix de Québec, as well as finishing second behind Tadej Pogacar this year at the Tour de France.

Ganna started slowly and was only 10th at the first time check, but by the third he had moved up into second spot. But he could not make any headway into Evenepoel, who did not stop increasing his lead from the start to the finish.

The young Swedish rider Jakob Soderqvist, the under-23 champion in this discipline last year, was second to Evenepoel at the first two time checks but faded over the last 10km and finished fifth. The teenager Seixas gauged his effort better and put in a strong ride over the final 10km to finish third.

Earlier on Sunday, Marlen Reusser retained her world time-trial title as her expected main challenger, Demi Vollering, finished a disappointing eighth.

Reusser secured an ultimately comfortable victory in Montreal, winning her second world championship after triumphing last year in Kigali – but not before the young British rider Zoe Backstedt gave her a scare.

Backstedt had been quickest at the first two intermediate time checks on the course but Reusser powered away in the second half of the race to beat the 21-year-old by 40sec. Germany’s Franziska Koch finished third, a further 6sec back.

“It’s a good present,” said Reusser, who was competing on her 35th birthday. “I also thought, win or not, I have something to celebrate.

“From the side of pacing and understanding how fast you should go and how you should also cope with these challenges on the way, I was really nervous. I was not really sure, because we don’t have time trials like this often … I’m used to doing 20km.”

Reusser has been virtually unbeatable in races against the clock in the past few years. The Swiss cyclist is a four-time European champion and has won time-trial stages at the Tour de France Femmes and Giro d’Italia Women.

Backstedt had been a junior and twice under-23 world champion in the discipline, but this race was around 12km further than any previous time trial in which she had competed. Koch’s bronze medal continued a dream season for the German, who won Paris-Roubaix in April. Vollering, the European road race champion, was never in the running for a medal.

Elsewhere, Mathieu van der Poel warmed up for his bid for a second world road rice title with a long-range solo break on the final stage of the Tour of Luxembourg .

The Dutch star broke clear just over a couple of kilometres into the 177km stage and held on in front all day to win by more than a minute. Van der Poel’s run is thought to be one of the longest solo breaks in the history of cycling.

The 2023 world road race champion will be one of the favourites in Montreal next weekend, where the reigning champion Pogacar will be missing because of injury.

“That was not the plan before the start, but I found myself alone from the start of the race in fact, and I just rode my tempo the whole day,” Van der Poel said. Italy’s Davide Piganzoli finished fourth on the stage to secure overall victory.

More than a dozen arrested in connection with 2021 assassination of Haitian president

The Guardian Sun, 20 Sep 2026 20:17:44 GMT

Jovenel Moïse, 53, was shot dead in July 2021 in a killing which sparked chaos in Haiti

Eighteen people have been arrested in association with the 2021 assassination of the Haitian president Jovenel Moïse, according to US officials.

Moïse, 53, was shot dead on 7 July 2021 at his private residence by a hired group of about 20 military-trained Colombian mercenaries. His security detail did not intervene to protect him.

“Today’s multi-location and international arrests underscore the FBI’s continued commitment to bringing all participants in this plot to justice,” FBI special agent Brett Skiles said on Sunday.

The suspects have been taken to Florida to stand trial.

In the same post on X, federal prosecutor Jason Reding Quinones said: “18 transported in military plane from Haiti to face American justice in the southern district of Florida.”

“Five years later, we are still bringing defendants before American courts, and we are not finished,” Quinones wrote, adding that 30 suspects have thus far been indicted in the killing.

In May, four men were convicted in a federal court in Miami of charges including conspiracy to kill or kidnap Moïse, conspiracy to provide material support and violating the US Neutrality Act to engage in an illicit military operation abroad.

The men face possible sentences of life in prison.

All four were linked to CTU, a private security firm based in Florida, and lured into the plot by the prospect of securing lucrative contracts in the event of Moïse’s ouster, according to federal prosecutors.

Eleven people have already been indicted in connection with the assassination in US courts, which have jurisdiction over plots hatched on American soil.

Five of them have been sentenced to life in prison, including a former Colombian soldier, a former Haitian senator, a Haitian Chilean businessman, a retired Colombian soldier and a Haitian American.

Haiti has descended into deeper chaos since Moïse’s killing, and currently has no president.

It is preparing to hold its first presidential and legislative election since 2016, as well as a referendum on the constitution, on 13 December – if security conditions allow.

Gangs control about 80% of Port-au-Prince, and violent crimes such as kidnappings for ransom, armed robbery and carjackings plague the impoverished nation.

A UN-backed armed force tasked with helping local police combat gangs will not be fully staffed by October as planned, its spokesperson said earlier this month.

Announced by the UN security council last year, the Gang Suppression Force was expected to ramp up between April and October to a planned capacity of 5,500 uniformed personnel and 50 civilian staff.

As of July, it comprised fewer than 1,000 personnel from Chad, Mongolia, Jamaica, Guatemala, El Salvador and Sri Lanka. More recent figures have not been disclosed.

The investigation found all three women were dropped off by taxi at Madeira Drive, the road running along Brighton Beach, at 10.20pm on 12 May, wearing everyday clothing.

No evidence was found to suggest they visited any nightclubs or local businesses in the area at the time and the investigation concluded all three women entered the water near to where their bodies were found, the police spokesperson added.

A spokesperson for the force said: “The purpose of the police investigation was to identify any evidence of criminal offending linked to how the sisters came to be in the water or their subsequent deaths.

“We can confirm the thorough police investigation has not found any evidence of a crime being committed or involvement by a third party.”

Additional details such as the sisters’ specific movements before their deaths and their potential reasons for entering the water will be considered during the East Sussex coroner’s inquest.

Ch Supt Adam Hays said his force had been “acutely aware of the speculation surrounding this incident” and “concerns raised by black communities surrounding the deaths of black people in or near bodies of water”.

He said: “Jane, Rebecca and Christina’s tragic deaths sparked a national outpouring of grief, and I would like to thank everyone who supported our investigation by coming forward with information. We will now support the coronial process and ask that the sisters’ family continue to be given privacy to come to terms with their loss.”

After the sisters’ deaths, their father, Joseph Jacobson, said there were days when the grief felt unbearable but that he held on to the memories they had shared and “the bond that death can never take away”.

In a statement released through Sussex police, Jacobson said: “Jane, Christina and Becky were more than daughters to me: they were my joy, my strength and the beautiful light that filled our family with happiness and love.

“Each of you was unique and precious in your own special way. Your smiles brightened dark days, your laughter brought comfort and your presence made life more meaningful. Though your time on Earth was short, the impact you made will remain in our hearts for ever.”

A GoFundMe online fundraiser for the women’s funerals has received more than 2,200 donations from members of the public, totalling nearly £46,000.

In a potential sign of growing tensions before the UN general assembly in New York this week, Donald Trump cut short a weekend visit to the Camp David presidential retreat on Sunday with no official explanation, and a new security alert was issued by the state department to all US citizens in the Middle East.

Keeping his options open, Trump reportedly told a Fox News reporter “very big things are going to be happening in the not-so-distant future” and that the options he was considering were “wiping Iran out, letting them rot economically or making a deal”.

The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps warned that if an attack does take place, “all US bases and interests in the region will become targets of continuous, effective and painful attacks without any limitations or considerations”.

Iran’s leaders also pledged some of the reprisals could extend as far as US naval forces in the Indian Ocean, and accused some Gulf leaders of “double-dealing” by allegedly giving a green light to the US attacks.

The outburst of sabre-rattling appears to have been prompted by attacks on the Saudi capital, Riyadh, by Yemen’s Iranian-backed Houthi rebels. The barrage on Saturday marked the first time the capital’s Aramco oil facilities had been subject to such a sustained attack since the Saudi-Houthi ceasefire broke down in June. Riyadh insisted it had intercepted the missiles, but local photographs show smoke pouring from the Aramco facility. The port of Yanbu, vital for Saudi oil exports, was also targeted.

The US largely regards the Houthis as a proxy Iranian force and argues that the group’s attacks on Riyadh would not happen without Tehran’s approval, a claim Iran denies.

Trump last week provoked profound questions about the level of US commitment to its Middle East allies when he spurned a call by the Saudi crown prince, Mohammed bin Salman, asking the US to come to Saudi’s direct military help.

The Saudis wanted US aid after the Houthis suddenly captured strategic ports along Yemen’s west coast overlooking the Red Sea, giving the Houthis control of the Bab al-Mandab strait, the narrow waterway that takes commercial shipping through the Red Sea towards Asia.

On the other side of the Arabian peninsular, the strait of Hormuz between Iran and Oman is already effectively closed to western traffic and the pressure on European energy supplies is growing by the day, leading states such as France to take emergency measures to prevent fuel shortages.

In an attempt to keep the US out of its war with Saudi Arabia, the Houthis had given commitments to US officials that they would only target Saudi-related shipping in the Red Sea, a commitment that Trump appeared to regard as sufficient to ensure essential US interests would be protected and that the US need not become involved militarily.

Pressure on the Pentagon budget and dwindling munitions supplies due to the Iran conflict have also made the US reluctant to broaden the theatre of war. Successive bombing campaigns have not dislodged the Houthis, whose lighting advance to the Red Sea coast took the Saudi-backed Yemeni forces by surprise.

Trump appeared to disregard the wider security threat by telling Fox News: “The US is in constant contact with the Houthis and they have agreed not to go to war with the US.”

The Houthi government said 318 ships passed through the strait from 10-18 September.

The Iranian judiciary accused the centre of conducting “illegal acts that violated diplomatic conventions”.

Andy Burnham faces a weakened Trump – but the president remains unpredictable

The Guardian Sun, 20 Sep 2026 18:45:23 GMT

PM hopes to be firmer with US leader than his predecessor without provoking diplomatic warfare, as the Iran war weighs on the UK economy

No international relationship has more power to determine the success of Andy Burnham’s premiership. So you might imagine the stakes for the prime minister’s first face-to-face meeting with Donald Trump on Tuesday would be high.

Yet Burnham may prove to be a lucky general. The balance of risk has shifted. Trump is unpopular at home, where inflation remains high, and is mired in an intractable conflict in Iran that has the potential to sink his midterm dreams.

When Keir Starmer first visited Trump in February 2025, the situation could not have been more different. The notoriously unpredictable president had just won the US election and was at the height of his powers – and was showing muscle on Nato and Ukraine, and with threats of tariffs.

Starmer’s “keep calm and carry on” strategy helped keep Trump on board the defence alliance and also protected the UK from the worst of his aggression over trade. But it came with a cost: he was often left looking obsequious and at odds with the national mood.

Burnham defended his predecessor’s approach but in June signalled he would take a different direction. “Obviously the relationship is important to the UK, but not to the point where we just go along with anything they say,” he said. “We’ve got in trouble in the past when that happens.”

Downing Street insiders expect Burnham to be a bit more forceful when he feels there’s a need to stand up for British interests. But there is no suggestion he will follow the more combative approach of Mark Carney, the Canadian prime minister.

Instead, one source said he would probably take a “third way” between Starmer and Carney, pushing back more than his predecessor publicly and privately, but avoiding open diplomatic warfare. A second source said the prime minister had three ambitions for Tuesday’s talks: bond with Trump, make the case for Ukraine, and avoid any drama.

Early clues about how the talks might go from the White House perspective have been mixed. In June, Trump suggested Burnham was “extremely liberal” (not as a compliment) and dismissively described him as the “mayor of a town”.

The US president remains angry the UK did not join his strikes on Iran, and has attacked the country as a “dying” nation “on the edge of disaster”. More recent comments that he might not help if Argentina again tried to seize the Falklands, and that he would love to see a united Ireland, suggest his displeasure has not abated.

But that will not necessarily translate into a strained personal relationship with Burnham. The pair have spoken on the phone twice and are said to have got on. The prime minister’s laid-back, confident style is likely to go down well with Trump, who has already shown with the New York mayor, Zohran Mamdani, that he can warm to leftwingers.

On policy too, government insiders point to small reasons for hope: Trump responded warmly to reports the UK government was going to “open up” the North Sea (although the decision to drill at two fields has been delayed) and has – so far – been relatively restrained when asked about the UK’s planned West Bank settlement trade ban.

Their meeting will be fraught with tension over both matters, and other areas – such as defence spending and the Iran war – have potential for further clashes.

It will help Burnham that Tuesday’s talks will be held on the comparatively neutral ground of the UN, rather than at the White House. As such, he will avoid the jeopardy of an Oval Office press conference that Trump could easily derail.

Trump may also decide he has had enough fights for one day. His meeting with Burnham will follow his address to the UN. Last year Trump told world leaders their countries were “going to hell” over their immigration policies. The UK meeting may end up as just a sideshow.

after newsletter promotion

Burnham’s views on Trump have also shifted since he took office. As mayor of Greater Manchester, he said the US president would not be welcome in the city, blaming his “poisonous” politics. After winning his seat as an MP in Makerfield, he warned against the “divided, dark politics” of the US.

But over the summer, Burnham appeared to shrug off potential divisions, telling reporters that “everyone says things as politicians”. The new prime minister said he would “say what I feel” to Trump but – crucially – would also try to “find a connection” with the mercurial president.

With Trump now weaker domestically, political power in the US is starting to shift to who comes next. Burnham is walking into the room with a president who is running out of time. Yet Trump is in power for two more years, and he is nothing if not unpredictable.

Burnham’s priority may be on domestic affairs, but his closest aides acknowledge that the biggest weight on the UK right now is Trump’s war in Iran. While the war continues to wreak damage on the British economy, Burnham will struggle to deliver his promises of change.

So for the time being, the power still rests with Trump, and Burnham may yet find he has to navigate a perilous path as Starmer did before him.

Friedrich Merz vows to stay in office after CDU ‘disaster’ in German state elections

The Guardian Sun, 20 Sep 2026 18:33:02 GMT

Far-right AfD wins in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and leftwing Die Linke on course for victory in Berlin

Germany’s embattled chancellor, Friedrich Merz, has vowed to stay in office and fight for future-proofing economic changes despite heavy losses for his conservatives in two state elections, one to the far right and the other to a leftwing party.

Preliminary results indicated Merz’s Christian Democratic Union (CDU) tallied just over the 5% threshold to enter the state parliament in the coastal region of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, its worst-ever state score, which he called a “disaster”.

The anti-immigration, Kremlin-friendly Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) party extended a streak of strong showings by coming in first in the former communist region with nearly 38%, more than doubling its previous score.

In the capital, Berlin, one of Germany’s 16 federal states, the far-left Die Linke looked on course to win with about 25% of the vote, ahead of the incumbent CDU by a five-point margin. The AfD made headway there too, with a clear double-digit result.

The deeply unpopular Merz has been fighting for his political survival after a humiliating series of setbacks with voters this year.

Speculation about his ability to hold on as chancellor reached fever pitch after Saxony-Anhalt state’s AfD chapter routed the CDU with a record 44% for the party in an election two weeks ago.

The Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania result marked the third time the AfD has emerged as the strongest party in a region, although the party seemed likely to remain shut out of power in the state because of a “firewall” of non-cooperation agreed by the other main parties.

In a rare speech on a state election night, Merz admitted the CDU had been bitterly deprived of “tailwinds from Berlin” in both of Sunday’s races. But he said he would remain chancellor and party chair and continue a reform drive on fronts including taxes, healthcare, pensions and reducing bureaucracy.

Merz said the German economy was facing “profound upheaval”, while public discourse had become “harsher and more irreconcilable”.

“Trust in our country’s institutions is waning and is being actively undermined by radical parties on both the left and the right,” he said.

But he added: “Germany is capable of reform. I would even go so far as to say that these reforms are the antidote to the poison of authoritarianism, which is penetrating ever deeper into our society as the fascination with authoritarianism grows.”

A jubilant AfD co-leader, Tino Chrupalla, mocked Merz before his speech, saying voters had given his own party a “very clear result” and called on the chancellor to resign.

About 2.5 million people were eligible to vote in Berlin and nearly 1.3 million in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.

The stinging blows from the latest elections had been expected to put pressure on Merz at a minimum to cede the CDU leadership, which would have in effect ruled out a run for re-election at the next national poll, due in 2029.

Merz’s eroding support has created a sense of instability in Europe’s top economy, which is struggling with deindustrialisation, sluggish growth and soaring energy costs.

If the AfD’s surge led Merz to abandon the chancellery prematurely, it would give the far right further momentum as France, Italy, Spain and Poland head into elections next year with nativist parties on the march.

Germany has high constitutional hurdles to replacing a chancellor against their will and any appointed successor would need to demonstrate a ruling majority. A failure to do so could trigger a new election.

The AfD is the biggest opposition force in parliament and is leading national opinion polls with about 30%. It has called for Germany to quit the euro, end support for Ukraine and carry out mass deportations of “irregular” migrants, while citing the “destruction” of the CDU as one of its central goals.

The CDU’s debacle in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania – a small, relatively poor state – is particularly bitter for Merz as it was home to the constituency of his arch-rival, Angela Merkel. While she governed Germany for 16 years, Merz appears to be on the ropes after no more than 16 months.

Merz took office in May 2025 at the helm of a coalition with the centre-left Social Democrats (SPD) promising to restore the German economy to strength and slash the AfD’s support.

A failure to make decisive headway on either front has produced profound disappointment in his leadership, with only one in 10 Germans saying they are satisfied with his performance. An inability to connect with voters appears particularly marked in the former communist east, where the AfD is strongest.

In Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, the Social Democratic party state premier, Manuela Schwesig, distanced herself during the campaign from a key pension change backed by her party in Merz’s coalition government.

She was expected to hold on to power in a left-leaning coalition even if the AfD came out on top when all the votes were counted. Despite leading the polls for months, the far right failed to garner enough support to govern alone and the remaining parties have ruled out working with it.

A confirmed win by Die Linke in Berlin, where the far-left party has called for expropriation of corporate landlords to fight rising housing costs, could see its candidate, Elif Eralp, become the capital’s first leader of Turkish origin.

The Guardian Sun, 20 Sep 2026 18:29:03 GMT

World No 294 lets victory slip in agonising fashion

JJ Spaun triumphs by two shots at Wentworth

We will come to JJ Spaun and Jeremy Clarkson later. Only those without an ounce of compassion in their body could feel no sympathy for Manuel Elvira. The Spaniard, without a professional win to his name, stood on the 18th fairway at Wentworth’s West Course with one of golf’s most extraordinary stories in his grasp. Having just eagled the 71st hole and found the short grass on the friendly par five, the 30-year-old who began tournament week as the world’s 294th ranked player knew a birdie would seal the PGA Championship title. A par would force Spaun into a playoff.

What happened next was a form of sporting torture rather than the realisation of a fairytale. Elvira pulled his layup into a bunker, flew the green, fluffed a chip into another sand trap and missed a bogey putt from 4ft. He did exceptionally well not to burst into tears. The disastrous 18th meant Elvira finished in a four-way tie for second place. Even Spaun, a winner on his Wentworth debut, had to be bashful at the manner of success.

“It is devastating that I hit the wrong shot on the layup and left myself the toughest shot in the fairway bunker,” Elvira said. “I wasn’t able to pull it off. I have played some of the best golf probably of my life.”

Beware the jilted golfer. Spaun arrived in England carrying a grudge at being overlooked for next weekend’s Presidents Cup where the US will take on an international team at Medinah. His omission was odd even before this victory. Rory McIlroy, during post-tournament media duties, had assumed Spaun was part of Brandt Snedeker’s team. Americans have now won three of the last six editions of the DP World Tour’s flagship event.

“I played with a huge chip on my shoulder,” said Spaun. “I definitely had something to prove this week but everything happens for a reason.” Spaun was already a major champion. This win means it is seriously difficult to believe Spaun will be ignored again when the US take on Europe in Ireland at next year’s Ryder Cup. His game can travel.

Spaun and his family have become regular visitors to the Cotswolds after developing a fondness for the television show Clarkson’s Farm. To add to a wacky closing scene in Surrey, Spaun’s wife was waving a Clarkson mask around as the champion was confirmed. “I’ve kind of blossomed into this player I never thought I could be,” Spaun said. “To take my game across the world – more specifically here in England, a place that’s dear to my family’s heart – the stars kind of aligned for me to come out on top.”

Spaun’s fourth round of 67 included four birdies in the final five holes. Seventeen under par proved sufficient to take the trophy by two strokes. Those alongside Elvira were McIlroy, Aaron Rai and Adam Scott.

McIlroy’s weekend involved missed opportunity. One realises how special a talent the Masters champion is when reaching 15 under par despite missing chance upon chance. McIlroy’s 68 included four birdie misses from 10ft or closer. His irritation at what might have been can be partly offset by the making up of decent ground on Patrick Reed in the DP World Tour’s order of merit race. Reed versus McIlroy promises to be quite the spectacle between now and mid November.

Christopher Kane and Mulberry make swaggering joint comeback at London fashion week

The Guardian Sun, 20 Sep 2026 18:14:14 GMT

Appointment of Kane as creative director signals the return of serious style ambition for former It-bag brand

With spicy leather mini-dresses and shoes with miniature axes for heels, two beloved British names made a swaggering joint comeback at London fashion week.

Fifteen years ago, Christopher Kane and Mulberry were two of the biggest shows on the line-up. Kane was the brilliant young designer who could find fashion in the most unlikely places: rubberised lace minis were inspired by “Princess Margaret on acid”; while illustrations from the 1972 classic The Joy of Sex appeared on slinky slip dresses. Mulberry was London’s home-grown It-bag brand: anyone who was anyone had a Bayswater or an Alexa.

The pandemic hit independent designers hard, and Kane placed his brand in administration in 2023. Mulberry hit the ropes after price hikes misfired, fighting off a takeover bid as profits plunged. But a new chief executive and a renewed focus on Britishness and craft is fuelling a revival at Mulberry, with sales up 23% in the first quarter of this year. The appointment of Kane as creative director signals the return of serious style ambition at Mulberry, and gives a new platform for Kane’s talent.

On paper, it is an unlikely match. Mulberry is rooted in its Somerset factories and makes understated practical bags; Kane has a flair for bad-girl party dresses learned on the streets of Glasgow where he grew up.

Where they meet is leather. There were leather sheath dresses and elegantly spare leather car coats, as well as heeled loafers featuring Mulberry’s signature postman’s lock. Kane builds each collection around one visual motif – Frankenstein, gorillas, the reproductive organs of plants – and for this collection, took the castellated leather flaps of Mulberry’s Bayswater bags and turned them into notched hems and necklines. This was punchy, full-throttle fashion, accessorised with money-making bags and shoes.

Climbing the party-branded stairs of the Brighton Centre with a Liberal Britain tote bag over his shoulder, Cody Butler looks quite at home at the Liberal Democrats’ annual jamboree.

But asked how he is finding it, the 21-year-old replied: “Odd.” The former Tory activist resigned as chair of the One Nation Conservative Network and left his old party in July, arguing that centrists, remainers and members worried about the climate crisis and conservation were no longer welcome in the party. A week ago, he joined the Lib Dems.

“There is no easy way to describe joining a new political party, because it’s like finding a new family,” he said. “I was brought up in a Conservative association. I was the local Tory boy. So it’s great, but odd.”

Butler is one of several youthful former Tories who have publicly defected to Britain’s third party and are in the process of setting up a new group: the One Nation Liberals. It’s a growing group, with other potential defectors believed to be waiting to see if they can survive in Kemi Badenoch’s increasingly rightwing party.

Butler has been joined by Josh Bancroft, a former Tory councillor on Cannock Chase council, who left the party to join the Lib Dems earlier this month. “Moderates like me have been forced out of the big tent over the past few years,” he said. “My politics haven’t changed, but the party has.”

The 26-year-old said moderates looking for the exit have grown in number since Badenoch embarked on a purge of the Conservative parliamentary party.

In July, the Tory leader warned that anyone who supported net zero targets or Britain’s membership of the European convention on human rights would be blocked from standing as a candidate in the next election. The former minister Gavin Barwell lost the whip, and another former cabinet member, Grant Shapps, was blocked from standing again for the party.

“The Conservatives have taken leaps to the right and left me and millions of voters behind,” Bancroft added. “The Liberal Democrats can be and should be their new political home.”

Bancroft and Butler have been welcomed with open arms into the Liberal ranks, with one MP joking that Badenoch had become the Lib Dems’ most effective recruiter. During a Q&A on the first full day of the conference, party leader Ed Davey repeatedly mentioned Badenoch, referencing her decision to freeze out members and MPs who support net zero policies.

“Unlike Kemi Badenoch, who thinks there wasn’t a problem with this summer’s heatwaves, we actually realise you have to take action on climate change and we’re leading that debate,” he said.

Despite being stuck at about 11% in national polling, many Liberal Democrat activists and MPs in Brighton are talking with atypical swagger about cementing the foundations of the so-called orange wall. They point to the 72 seats they won in the last election, making them the largest third party in British politics for over a century. And of the 27 seats where the Lib Dems came second in 2024, 20 were taken by the Conservatives.

He appears to have concluded that he needs greater security in central midfield – hence Sander Berge and Shea Charles, with Alex Iwobi moved out to the left wing. There were round pegs in round holes for Fulham, which was not completely the case for United, albeit they were able to welcome back Luke Shaw on the left side of their defence.

With no Benjamin Sesko because of a recurrence of his shin issue, Carrick was without his only pure No 9. His solution, once again, was to use Cunha as a false 9 and ask Bruno Fernandes to play close to him. It was a box midfield, with Youri Tielemans and Kobbie Mainoo further back.

Arbeloa got his wingers, Oscar Bobb and Iwobi, to come inside to good effect. The battle for control of the middle of the pitch pulsed, with Josh King a major part of it.

The No 10 threatened during a first half in which Fulham were the more urgent and creative team. King worked Lammens in the 32nd minute after buying a yard of space from Shaw and it was not the only time that United felt their hearts skip.

Fulham had to be annoyed that they did not score before the interval. Twice, Gonzalo García fluffed his finish when well placed; on the second occasion, Berge extended Lammens on the second phase of the move. There was also the moment when Bobb spun into a seam of space only to drag wide. King wanted a free‑kick on the edge of the area in the 45th minute after running into Harry Maguire but he was looking for the contact and was booked correctly for diving.

The Guardian view on AI v mathematicians: humans are still vital to the field, but tech firms refuse to see that

The Guardian Sun, 20 Sep 2026 16:58:03 GMT

OpenAI claims its agents have solved the Navier-Stokes problem. But questions remain about how useful and independent its work really is

On 8 September, OpenAI claimed that its AI agents had solved the Navier-Stokes problem, one of the most famous and difficult challenges in mathematics. Had a human solved it, they would have collected both prize money and plaudits from their fellows. The announcement instead ignited what some mathematicians have called an “existential crisis” in their field over the power of AI, and accusations that OpenAI misused human work.

The maths behind Navier-Stokes is difficult to understand, but the critiques levelled by mathematicians will be familiar to artists, office workers, or anyone else concerned about AI. OpenAI’s results, like any arising from a large language model, depend on digesting work by human mathematicians. The OpenAI paper cites sources, but many believe the company didn’t give sufficient credit, especially to several mathematicians believed to be very close to a solution – bad form that erases human ingenuity and hogs all the glory. The mathematician Tristan Buckmaster also has concerns that work he was doing on Navier-Stokes using OpenAI’s Codex model was seen by the OpenAI team. OpenAI has denied directly accessing this material, but could not rule out that data from Buckmaster’s use of their products “helped improve our model”.

This lack of attribution and compensation for the human labour that AI is built on has turned many against the companies that develop these systems. It has yet to be adequately addressed. This is a particular misstep in the case of mathematics. As many mathematicians have pointed out, AI firms are keen to use their models’ maths prowess as an advertisement. But they rely on mathematicians to check their – often sloppy and baffling – work, and to tell them if it is useful and how it might be applied. An AI-produced movie or vaccine would have a clear and obvious use, whatever its merits, but it will take time and human intellectual labour to tell whether OpenAI’s purported solution contains any novel mathematical tools or insights. This should be an opportunity for collaboration. It has instead become yet another source of alienation and resentment.

Despite this, mathematicians are remarkably open to the use of AI, even as they commit their names to open letters denouncing tech firms. Most recognise that the technology is undeniably powerful and particularly good at maths. There has been a nuanced discussion of how maths might change and integrate AI, with humans guiding and interpreting its work. There has also been some soul-searching as to whether celebrating the person – or machine – that achieved a flashy final result in the form of a mathematical proof is the best way to value contributions. As Bill Thurston, the Fields Medal-winning mathematician, put it in 2010, well before the age of AI: “The product of mathematics is clarity and understanding. Not theorems, by themselves.” These are still uniquely human qualities.

Some critics of AI are still stuck dismissing its outputs as uniformly useless “slop”. AI will not become good at everything. But more people may find themselves in the current position of mathematicians, confronted with the undeniable effectiveness of AI, while deeply concerned about how it is being used. This anxiety might not exist, the mathematician Nestor Guillen wrote recently, if we could separate the tech from the tech companies, and democratise its use. It is increasingly urgent that we find ways to do so.

Exclusive: Intelligence officers say Russian campaign could intensify ‘in months, not years’ – but that panic risks playing into Kremlin psy-ops

European intelligence officials have raised the possibility of an imminent Russian test of Nato, with one saying a potential attack could come in a matter of “months, not years”.

The warnings come after Poland’s prime minister, Donald Tusk, told parliament that intelligence assessments suggested Russia might launch an attack with drones or missiles on Nato territory in the coming months, as part of efforts to prove that “article 5 is more theoretical than practical”.

The French president, Emmanuel Macron, called Tusk’s warnings “sound and well-documented”, and on Friday summoned party leaders and 2027 presidential candidates for an emergency meeting in Paris, where they discussed – among other topics – intelligence of a growing threat from Russia.

The escalation fears come as the UN general assembly convenes in New York later this week, and amid intensifying airstrikes on both sides of Russia’s war on Ukraine. Kyiv hit Moscow and other Russian regions with hundreds of drones and missiles in the early hours of Sunday, in one of its biggest air attacks of the war.

In separate interviews with the Guardian over the past week, in different locations, three European intelligence leaders discussed their views of the potential threat from Moscow.

Michal Koudelka, the head of the Czech Republic’s BIS security service, said that as well as increased drone activity, a small-scale invasion of Nato territory that bordered Russia could be part of the Kremlin’s plans. “It’s possible. It could involve a limited incursion, false-flag provocations, a massive influence campaign,” he said, in a rare interview at the agency’s headquarters in Prague. He said this scenario could play out in a matter of “months, not years” but added that “a lot of people are doing everything they can to make sure this doesn’t happen”.

Officials in the three Baltic countries, which border Russian territory, have been more cautious about the prospect of an invasion or other serious escalation, citing Moscow’s stretched resources in Ukraine and warning that playing up the prospect of an attack might play into the Kremlin’s hands.

“We don’t see indications of an imminent attack,” said Normunds Mežviets, the director general of the VDD, Latvia’s state security service, in an interview at the agency’s headquarters in Riga. He conceded there were signs that Moscow was making preparations for more decisive action in Europe, but said it was not clear whether the plans were simply part of a destabilisation strategy.

“It’s still an open question if they have direct and concrete plans or if it’s just within the context of their overall attempts to spread fear and uncertainty in western society,” he said.

Baltic politicians, who for many years criticised western Europe for being soft on Russia, now find themselves in the strange position of telling some western leaders to calm down in their public messaging, fearing that talk of an imminent invasion could prove damaging to their societies and economies.

On Saturday, the secretary general of Estonia’s foreign ministry, Jonatan Vseviov, decried “panic on social media” in recent days about a possible attack. “If there is reason to fear an attack, rest assured: we will make that clear. Until then, keep calm, carry on and support Ukraine,” he wrote on X.

Mežviets said that, overall, it was good that western Europe had woken up to the threat from Russia. “Before 2022, we constantly warned our western European partners about the threat from Russia, but most of the time our voices were not listened to. In 2022, the approach of our partners changed. They said it turns out the Balts and the Poles had been right,” he said.

Neither Mežviets nor Koudelka would discuss what specific intelligence might have been obtained about Russia’s supposed planning for the coming months, nor would they comment on whether a surprise trip by the CIA director, John Ratcliffe, to Moscow last month – during which he stopped off in Riga – was partly to warn the Kremlin about the dangers of launching an attack on Nato.

After that visit, the Kremlin spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, dismissed rumours of a Russian attack on Nato. “It has nothing to do with reality and nothing to do with the intentions of the Russian Federation,” he said.

However, many in Europe will have the build up to the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 in the back of their minds, when US officials repeatedly warned Russia was preparing to invade and the Kremlin repeatedly denied it.

As the full-scale war that ensued approaches its fifth winter, US-led efforts to bring about peace in Ukraine show no signs of success, with Russia and Ukraine intensifying their drone and missile strikes on each other. Ukraine has destroyed much of Russia’s oil infrastructure, targeting refineries and other facilities over recent months.

Moscow has frequently said the provision to Ukraine of weaponry, intelligence and military advisers makes western countries participants in the war and legitimate targets, but has so far avoided action that might provoke a coordinated response from Nato. Instead, it has launched what western agencies describe as a campaign of sabotage against targets in countries that are the loudest backers of Ukraine, and one-off incidents apparently meant to test boundaries, such as when more than a dozen drones, flying without ammunition, veered into Polish airspace a year ago.

Koudelka said the current Russian tactic was “escalate to de-escalate”, with the Kremlin keen to push at weak points in western societies to tamp down their support for Ukraine’s war effort. “They believe if they escalate enough, then European countries will decide not to support Ukraine,” he said.

In recent weeks the Trump administration has made another attempt to kickstart peace negotiations in Ukraine. As well as the Ratcliffe visit to Moscow, the US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner made another trip to Moscow, as well as a first-time trip to Kyiv. While Donald Trump has frequently claimed the Russian president, Vladimir Putin, is interested in a deal, there is scepticism in Europe that the Kremlin has any interest in good-faith negotiations.

“I haven’t seen any signs that there is a serious consideration in Moscow about real negotiations,” said Thomas Nilsson, the head of Sweden’s military intelligence and security service, in an interview on the sidelines of a conference in Riga. “My assessment is that they are still thinking that they could achieve their strategic objectives, so they are just playing negotiation theatre,” he added.

All three intelligence bosses said that whatever else happened, Russia’s campaign of sabotage in Europe is likely to intensify in the coming months. Nilsson described as a “gamechanger” the recent armed drone incident at Leipzig airport, which German authorities have attributed to Russian intelligence.

“To have an armed UAV drone sent in to a busy airport in the middle of Europe … If you have attacks that could result in losses of life or losses of very critical infrastructure that have a huge implication for society, I think that is a gamechanger,” he said.

Mežviets said Russia was moving from randomised targeting of sabotage and arson attacks intended to sow panic to specific targets linked to western backing for Ukraine. “We see them looking to attack railway infrastructure, Ukraine support infrastructure. Right now we see a move towards defence industry targets,” he said. “If you do this then the psy-op effect is reached anyway, so you get both things in one,” he added.

Nilsson said there were several goals behind the recent intensification of Russian sabotage activity: to reduce support for Ukraine, to introduce splits in Nato and to alarm European populations. “I think Moscow would love Nato to have endless discussion about article 4 consultations, but coming up with no actions,” he said.

Koudelka said another effect of the sabotage campaign is the stretch on resources of intelligence services, as doubts often linger even when incidents are caused by other factors. “Now every fire or every malfunction needs to be investigated by intelligence services as a potential terror attack, and that is a good result for them,” he said.

The Guardian view on the last instalment of the Seven Up! series: growing up in public

The Guardian Sun, 20 Sep 2026 16:47:05 GMT

The compelling documentary series is drawing to a close. But following people from childhood raises difficult ethical questions

In 1963, a television crew documented the lives of 14 children. Michael Apted, then a young researcher, saw Seven Up! as an opportunity to expose the British class system, juxtaposing public schoolboys with counterparts from children’s homes and council estates. Seven years later, Apted returned to direct an update – then went back again, and again. For the most part, his subjects followed the socioeconomic paths one might have predicted. But what emerged over the decades was much more piercing and poignant than initially envisaged. It turned out – as its participants have noted – that the programme was as much about life itself as class.

The final instalment, 70 Up, currently being shown in two parts on ITV, is extraordinarily moving. We know that the children we see in the original footage will struggle with divorce, bereavement, depression, homelessness, redundancy and ill-health. Two of the original participants, and Apted himself, have died; Nick Hitchon, the boy from a Yorkshire farm who became an expert in nuclear fusion, gave a final interview days before his death. Yet these closing episodes, directed by Asif Kapadia, also capture deep joys such as parenthood, and the satisfaction of the self-knowledge they have earned. There are no simple arcs of redemption or tragedy, but something more muddled and nuanced.

To watch these lives unspool is a remarkable privilege. Yet it is not always a comfortable one, nor one which could easily be repeated. The loss of innocence that 70 Up captures is not only that of its youthful subjects, but of the society around them. Apted’s questions could be blunt, verging on cruel. But the seven-year intervals mean that while the series captured lives, it did not expose them as brutally as the relentlessness of today’s reality television and social media schedules, and the endless replay of clips and memes, would. No subject now could expect anonymity between the instalments. Most would want to shape their own narrative. At least one would surely establish their own supplements line, or become a streamer.

More children than ever are served up for the public gaze, directly by their families as well as the TV and film industries: at the same time, the viewer is increasingly aware of the toll that such attention has previously taken on children in the spotlight, from youthful Hollywood stars to those monetised from babyhood by their parents. Horrifying family influencer scandals underline the questions about who is benefiting and who is watching, in an age where the UK’s National Crime Agency has warned parents against putting their children’s images on public display online because of concerns over AI-generated images of sexual abuse.

Even in the best-case scenario, it is hard to know whether parents, as well as children, can truly understand what exposure to the public eye will mean not only in the moment, but later in life. Fictional versions are not immune to the challenges. Richard Linklater filmed scenes every year to construct his moving film Boyhood, which captures a childhood from five to 18 – but the director’s daughter Lorelei, who played the protagonist’s sister, wanted to opt out as a teenager.

Apted’s subjects pushed back at the director’s biases as they grew and in some cases quit the programme – though all but one returned, and several speak fondly about what it has meant to them. Viewers will be grateful. But it is harder to justify the greater toll of growing up in public these days.

‘I suck at breaks’: a day in the life of an aerial cellist

The Guardian Sun, 20 Sep 2026 16:00:19 GMT

Cellista, an aerialist who regularly performs upside down with her cello, shares what her life looks like training for the stage

Mastering the cello is hard enough, but Cellista also regularly performs upside down. She’s based in Las Vegas, but the aerialist spoke to us while traveling in Germany, and told us about what her life looks like training and writing for the stage.

I woke up at 7.10am and beat my alarm clock, which was set for 8.01am. I felt triumphant. The feeling lasted until 11am and then I was back to my usual self.

I fast. I really dislike eating in the morning and never have much of an appetite when I wake up. Although, technically I cheat because I have a nice big cup of coffee with ample milk and sugar.

I start every day by reading and journaling over coffee. I’ve been reading Nabokov’s love letters to his wife, Véra. He’s one of my favorite writers, but I now suspect from his letters that he was a neurotic love-bomber.

After reading, I write. I’m currently writing a book to accompany my aerial theater piece, Mémoire. It interlaces my writing, old journal entries, a film I direct and aerial cello into one stage poem or one-woman show.

I began the process of submitting the album that accompanies Mémoire for Grammy consideration. I also had to follow up with a client about their very overdue payments. It felt weirdly emotional for me. It’s the freelancer life: you feel guilty asking for what you’re worth, or requesting what is due to you, and you’re tempted to default to being nice because it feels easier in the moment.

I suck at breaks. I know that rest is better for my body and mind. But my mind just chatters away, and it feels incredibly difficult to take enough time off from training.

Our understanding of the slave trade is still evolving

The Guardian Sun, 20 Sep 2026 15:43:17 GMT

Readers respond to William Pettigrew’s article about the lasting significance of the slave trade to Britain’s politics, economy, institutions and culture

William Pettigrew’s book, Britain’s Slave Traders: A Forgotten History, adds a further dimension and depth to our understanding of how entrenched and significant Britain’s involvement in the transatlantic slave trade was. The landmark University College London’s Legacies of British Slavery project previously documented the “compensation” payments to 46,000 persons who, at the time of its abolition in 1834, had a financial interest in slave ownership – the £20m paid out is generally reckoned to be worth around £17bn at 2019 prices, or 40% of total government expenditure in 1834 – a vast national debt that was only fully amortised in 2015.

The earlier study thus highlighted the extensive involvement of sections of the British public in profiting from slavery, and the further financial benefit from “compensation”. The recent study tracks back into the prior history from the beginning of the transatlantic slave trade through the 18th century, and shows how its tentacles throughout that time reached out deep into the economy and society. The economic impact over this whole period should not be underestimated. As Pettigrew observes (Slavery was not a footnote to British history. It helped shape the nation, 14 September), the slave trade provided some of the seed funding for the Industrial Revolution. The flow of income back from the Caribbean sugar plantations provided capital surpluses to fund new industries, through an expanded banking system, not to mention personal wealth. Defending these assets in turn stimulated the growth of the British navy, and its eventual control of the seas.

Until American independence in 1776, the colonists relying on enslaved people for their cotton and coffee plantations were British settlers, paying taxes to the British exchequer. In the 19th century, “compensation” payouts fed into investments in the new railways; into banking; and into the funding of stately homes and the arts. Taken together, it could therefore be reasonably argued it was the slave trade that made Britain the cradle of the Industrial Revolution. Chris HendryEmeritus professor, City, University of London

William Pettigrew is right that slavery was not a footnote to British history. His account powerfully demonstrates how the slave trade was entangled with the state, finance, politics and culture. But there is a further question: what about class? Pettigrew speaks of “Britain” and says “we are all – in some way – connected to it”. Yet Britain was never a single social actor. The slave owner, merchant and investor had a fundamentally different relationship to slavery from the growing cotton-mill proletariat whose labour helped turn slave-grown cotton into commodities.

The danger is that “we are all connected” obscures the asymmetry of accumulation between those who owned capital and accumulated wealth from the system, and those who possessed only their labour and received wages. The question is not simply how slavery shaped Britain, but how its wealth entered an expanding capitalist economy – and was distributed through profoundly unequal class relations. David EatonSunderland

The Guardian’s excellent presentation of the findings of the Register of British Slave Traders (What is the Register of British Slave Traders and whom does it identify?, 14 September) highlighted what has been long known. It is also timely if it persuades anyone to question the thinking that underlies the philosophy shared by most western leaders that “western democracy” shines out in a challenging world, representing the best of humanity.

Historians know that this is based on contradictions. The world’s first known democracy, the dazzling civilisation of ancient Athens, was based both on slavery and on a thoroughly undemocratic empire, the Delian League. Slavery has been practised across history by all types of government from despotic monarchies to republics and democracies. Put this alongside the fact that the democratic rights we now enjoy had to be extracted, sometimes by force, from the ruling class, and we might have a more humble evaluation of the place of our civilisation in the world. As Gandhi famously said when asked what he thought of western civilisation, “It would be a good idea”. Dr Peter PurtonSouthall, London

As slavery was abolished, poor laws were enacted across England. A distinction began to be established between those deemed to be worthy of charity and those who were not. The workhouse consolidated the form and substance of these differences. Distinctions established then persist today in ideas about the undeserving and deserving poor, scroungers and strivers, immigrant and indigenous labour. Rod EarleGuildford, Surrey

It’s not just young people who need jobs

The Guardian Sun, 20 Sep 2026 15:38:46 GMT

There should be provision for people who find themselves out of work when they approach state pension age, writes Peter Wade

I am now in my 61st year, haven’t worked for more than two years and have stopped applying for jobs (‘I feel invisible’: over-50s reveal harsh realities of trying to get a job, 17 September). The bulk of my career was as an advice worker, specialising in debt, housing and energy advice.

Some years ago I worked with a client in her late 50s who had been a hospital cleaner. She had expected to retire earlier, but the changes to women’s state pension age meant that she faced several more years before retirement. She could no longer do the physical work of cleaning, yet starting a new career while managing her physical health seemed a daunting prospect. At the time I was looking at this situation from the other side of the desk. Now my perspective is rather different.

There quite rightly needs to be an emphasis on young people who are out of work, but I have felt for some time that there also needs to be an alternative route for people who find themselves out of work when they are approaching state pension age. Our current social security and pensions system has roots in the reforms of the early 20th century, developed through the Beveridge report of 1942 and the postwar reforms of the Attlee government.

Since then, the system has been adapted and tweaked many times. But perhaps we have reached the point where tweaking isn’t enough. What we need is Beveridge for the 21st century. Peter WadeLeeds

Victoria Starmer models clothes at London fashion week show

The Guardian Sun, 20 Sep 2026 15:16:01 GMT

Wife of former PM takes part in designer Edeline Lee’s show inspired by the Greek myth of Sisyphus

Victoria Starmer has taken part in a London fashion week show, in one of her first public appearances since her husband, Keir Starmer, stepped down as prime minister.

Lady Starmer appeared at Sunday’s Edeline Lee show. The London-based, Canadian British designer’s clothes are a favourite of the Princess of Wales, and have also been worn by celebrities including singer Taylor Swift and actor and screenwriter Phoebe Waller-Bridge.

Lee’s spring/summer 2027 show took place in the unusual setting of a north London school sports hall. Starmer wore a bright turquoise knitted midi dress with a high neckline, pleated detailing and short, sculptural sleeves, paired with white block-heeled shoes, with her hair worn in loose waves.

Rather than preparations for the show taking place backstage in the usual way, in Lee’s unique show, models were fitted and adjusted in full view of the audience, dancers rehearsed beside the catwalk, while a drone followed proceedings from the high ceiling of the gymnasium.

Starmer was photographed having her makeup done beside the catwalk, against a backdrop of a football net, with makeup and hair products spread out over a table in front of her. Ballerinas stretched beside the catwalk and synchronised swimming-inspired dancers performed in bright red costumes as part of the show, in the school in Chalk Farm.

The collection was based on the Greek myth of Sisyphus, in which a man is condemned to push a boulder uphill, only for it to roll back down again each time he reaches the top.

“There’s a general feeling right now of relentlessness, a sisyphean cycle,” Lee said. “I was already thinking about the ballet – dance is incredibly transporting, but the work behind it is so intense, the way dancers train for years, the endless repetition, for one ecstatic moment of performance, and then they’re back in the studio.

“I wanted to acknowledge the rigour and hard work behind that moment – much like the skill and artistry required of my team to present beautiful clothes.”

Throughout Keir Starmer’s time in office, Lady Starmer kept a low public profile, but her “political chic” and “modern British” sense of style was often admired. At London fashion week’s spring/summer shows in 2024, when her husband was prime minister, Lady Starmer took a front-row seat at Edeline Lee’s show, which took place at Millbank Tower, a former campaign HQ of Labour and the Conservatives, where Reform UK’s central office is now based.

She wore a borrowed £615 cream pussy-bow blouse with a navy polka dot print and matching £715 wide-leg trousers.

It came amid a row over free clothes for Lady Starmer, with Keir Starmer facing an investigation at the time over a possible breach of parliamentary rules around gifts.

He had failed to declare that some of his wife’s designer clothes had been bought for her by his biggest personal donor, Lord Alli. The Sunday Times reported that the Labour peer had paid for a personal shopper, clothes and alterations before and after Starmer became prime minister.

‘I feel betrayed’: inside Ed Sheeran’s controversial return to the stage

The Guardian Sun, 20 Sep 2026 15:12:36 GMT

Some fans were hesitant to turn the page after Sheeran’s tour resumed in Philadelphia after the removal of Macklemore, who spoke out in support of Palestine

“This is not usually how I would open the show,” Ed Sheeran told the crowd at Philadelphia’s Lincoln Financial Field on Saturday night, a humble preamble to a three-plus-minute speech addressing the greatest controversy of his career. Shaky-voiced and stealing glances at the monitor at his feet, he looked every bit the chastened superstar.

“I have tried in my career not to be a political commentator of any kind, because I want my music and shows to be about unity, not division, about humanity, not politics, but this is a humanitarian issue and I cannot hide how I feel about it any more,” Sheeran said. He described the Hamas-led attack at the Nova music festival in Israel on 7 October 2023 as “horrific”, and expressed heartbreak over civilian deaths in Gaza and the West Bank, describing the situation as “catastrophic and unjustified and disproportionate”.

He ended his speech with an appeal for “love, hope and unity”.

“Everyone here can stand by people that they don’t agree with on everything, but they can always agree on singing these songs,” he declared shortly before launching into Castle on the Hill, a rousing anthem about growing up in rural England. The guitar jangled, fireworks lit into the sky and pastoral scenes filled a giant screen behind the pop star as fans sang along. There was an overwhelming sense, between Sheeran and his ecstatic audience, of wanting to turn the page.

Cindy Lucente, a 73-year-old retiree who attended the show with her daughter and granddaughter, described the speech as “eloquent” and said that she was impressed by Sheeran’s mettle.

“People kept telling me I should probably get rid of my ticket because he’s going to cancel,” she said. “But I knew he wouldn’t.”

The night marked Sheeran’s return to the stage after the rapper Macklemore was removed from the tour after controversy erupted over his remarks during a performance at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey on 5 September. In a statement shared to Instagram last Tuesday, Sheeran said that he faced pressure from venue owners – including Robert Kraft, the billionaire who owns Gillette Stadium and the New England Patriots – to excise Macklemore from the lineup, but that his removal “was the promoter’s decision, it was not mine”. The statement was met with widespread condemnation, with detractors accusing Sheeran of cowing to corporate interests and putting profit over freedom of expression.

“I feel betrayed about how he handled this,” said Hillary Steinberg, a 34-year-old sociology PhD who was among the pro-Palestine protesters gathered outside the NRG metro station, a group that reached about 100 at one stage. “It has sort of soured how I think about him as an artist.”

After getting her ticket refunded earlier in the week, Steinberg decided to come to the stadium and try convincing others to do the same. She wore a black and white keffiyeh and held a sign that read: “If you leave now you will have more spine than Ed Sheeran.” By the end of the night, she said that she and her boyfriend had convinced “at least five” other people to get refunds.

Despite reported safety concerns and fears of an outright cancellation, the mood at Lincoln Financial Field was light and at times triumphant. The singer repeatedly invoked the controversy but spoke in broad terms and with an air of self-deprecation. He did not mention Kraft or Macklemore by name.

“I hope you enjoyed the opening acts – I heard they were great,” Sheeran joked early in the show, waving off concerns about having to carry the event alone. Per its moniker, the Loop tour mostly features Sheeran performing solo and utilizing a looping pedal to create his own soundscapes.

One of the night’s many standing ovations came after Sheeran brought out a group of musicians, led by the fiddler Alicia Enstrom, to back him on a number of songs including the lilting Galway Girl. The Irish folk band Beoga, which had played behind Sheeran during this section on earlier stops, was among the acts who dropped out in solidarity with Macklemore. They were joined by the Danish band Lukas Graham, the Irish singer Aaron Rowe, and Finneas – brother and collaborator to Billie Eilish and a musician in his own right – who was slated to join Sheeran for a South American leg later this year.

Sheeran made it clear that Enstrom and the others were to be Beoga’s replacement.

“They said yes to being on stage with the knowledge that the world thought that I was a certain type of person,” Sheeran said to rapturous cheers from the audience.

Melody Fillier, a 49-year-old who works in the pharmaceuticals industry, was among those who applauded the new backing band.

“They had balls,” she said. “The other ones didn’t.”

The other conspicuous change was the absence of a retractable bridge and smaller “B-stage”, which had positioned the singer much closer to the crowd during intimate sections of earlier shows. Sheeran explained that he didn’t want to risk having things thrown at him.

“I took the B-stage out because I was afraid what might happen if I stood in the middle, and I will admit that,” he said, grinning sheepishly.

Throughout the night, Sheeran returned again and again to themes of political harmony. The pop star appeared less defiant than humbled, repeatedly describing the concert as the greatest of his career. It seems unlikely that his words, which mostly served to justify the actions of the preceding week, will satisfy his critics. But in the city of brotherly love, where the stadium appeared mostly full even as the concert stretched past the three-hour mark, fans of the singer seemed more than satisfied.

“I didn’t come here for politics,” said Tim Matkosky, a 59-year-old entrepreneur who was among those who stayed to the bitter end, up on their feet and dancing as the bassline thumped and fire plumes filled the air. “I came here to get away from politics.”

Cody Gakpo was again the architect, the Dutchman the supplier for all four of Isak’s goals this season. Isak’s only other shot before scoring was to balloon a first-time effort high and wide but his second-half strike was sufficient to return Liverpool to winning ways in the Premier League.

Perhaps it was inevitable that these teams would neutralise each other. On Iraola’s final day at Bournemouth’s training base he spent an hour in the company of his successor, Marco Rose, who is yet to taste victory in the Premier League. The pair stopped talking only because Tiago Pinto, Bournemouth’s sporting director, interrupted to remind them there were other things on the agenda.

“We knew what we were going to get, they knew what they were going to get and maybe you could see it,” Rose said. “It is mostly the same after our games; I sit here after a good performance, but you don’t get points for good performances. You have to force wins.”

All the niceties, Iraola said, could wait until afterwards. Dominik Szoboszlai dropped a typically vicious free-kick wide of Djordje Petrovic’s post and Petrovic saved a deflected Bradley Barcola shot, but Liverpool spent much of the first half containing Bournemouth’s threats. Iraola conceded that his side were slow out of the blocks.

The kindness of strangers: I was a ball of stress taking my four children on an international flight – then a passenger tucked a blanket around my sleeping son

The Guardian Sun, 20 Sep 2026 15:00:20 GMT

Walking on to the plane with the kids in tow, I could almost hear people think, ‘Oh my God, I don’t want to be seated next to them!’

Read more in the kindness of strangers series

I won’t lie – I was having nightmares before the trip. When my family immigrated to Australia from Europe, my husband travelled ahead to organise a place for us to live. I followed him seven weeks later with our four children, all aged under seven. I was a ball of stress for weeks in the lead-up.

Walking on to the plane with four kids in tow, I could almost hear people think, “Oh my God, I don’t want to be seated next to them!” And I completely understand.

I had booked a window row and a seat in the middle row, thinking that I could put all the kids in the window row and then myself in the middle, where I could keep an eye on them. But when we got into the plane, the flight attendant told me that for security reasons we couldn’t do it that way. We had to rejig, my five-year-old son taking the middle-row seat alone, for what was to be a nearly 24-hour flight broken up into two legs.

There was a man seated next to my son. He didn’t display any of the annoyance he must be feeling about being seated next to a small child – a very kind act in itself, and one that brought me great relief. But his kindness didn’t end there.

At some point during the flight, after the cabin lights dimmed, the other three kids and I dozed off. When I woke up, I looked over to see my five-year-old had fallen asleep as well. The man next to him was pulling his blanket up and gently tucking him in. It was an unguarded moment of care and compassion.

I don’t think the man had any idea I saw him do that. We arrived safely and I never saw him again. But it was such a generous thing to do that, 20 years later, the memory remains magical.

From making your day to changing your life, we want to hear about chance encounters that have stuck with you.
