Adults with severe mental illness die 15 to 20 years earlier from diseases such as cancer

The Guardian Sun, 20 Sep 2026 15:00:19 GMT

Exclusive: Stark health inequalities in terms of deaths before age of 75, NHS data reveals

Adults with severe mental illness are nearly five times more likely than their peers to die from serious physical diseases before the age of 75, according to research.

The analysis of NHS data by the Rethink Mental Illness charity reveals that people with severe mental health problems die 15-20 years earlier than the wider adult population, largely due to preventable physical conditions.

Rethink’s calculations show that adults under 75 with serious mental ill health – defined as those referred to specialist secondary mental health services – are 6.3 times as likely to die from liver disease, 6 times more likely from respiratory illness, 3.8 times more likely from cardiovascular disease and 2.3 times as likely from cancer. They are also 14.6 times as likely to die due to suicide, compared with those who were not referred. Overall, they are 4.8 times more likely to die before the age of 75 than the general population.

For some conditions, these health inequalities are the starkest to date. For working-age adults living with a mental illness, the number of deaths from cardiovascular disease and cancer are at their highest levels since records began, each with more than 24,000 deaths in the 2022-2024 reporting period, the charity calculated.

Cancer, cardiovascular disease, liver disease and respiratory disease accounted for more than half (56.5%) of deaths for 18 to 74 year olds with severe mental health problems in England during this period. Cancer and cardiovascular disease each accounted for just under 19% of all deaths, respiratory disease 11%, and liver disease 8%. During the same period, suicide comprised 7% of these early deaths.

The report identifies a number of factors driving this excess mortality, including poverty, poor housing, higher rates of smoking, weight gain from medication, physical inactivity, and fragmented care. But the authors conclude that “diagnostic overshadowing” – where physical symptoms are wrongly attributed to mental illness – means potential illnesses are not always properly investigated and treated.

The findings come before the government’s independent review of mental health, autism and ADHD, which is expected to be published this week and recommend a more holistic approach to supporting patients with these conditions.

Mark Winstanley, the chief executive of Rethink, said: “It is a scandal that people living with severe mental health problems are so much more likely than the rest of the population to die from often preventable physical health conditions.

“Given that many are in frequent contact with health services throughout their lives, it is clear that opportunities to identify and treat physical health problems are being missed.

“These early deaths are not inevitable. The new cross-government mental health strategy … must prioritise physical health checks, improve access to mental-health informed interventions and bolster peer support, if it wants to reduce these terrible health inequalities.”

Responding to the findings, Prof Subodh Dave, the president of the Royal College of Psychiatrists, said: “Having a severe mental illness shouldn’t be an early death sentence. This stark inequality is unacceptable. People with severe mental illness deserve the same opportunity to live long, healthy lives as everyone else. We know that evidence-based solutions to close this gap exist – from smoking cessation to routine physical health checks. But what is lacking is concerted action to prevent these premature deaths.”

A Department of Health and Social Care spokesperson said: “People living with severe mental illness face stark health inequalities, and too many continue to experience poorer physical health outcomes.

“This government is taking immediate action to transform services for people with severe mental illness. We’re developing a new modern service framework to look at what action is needed to help people live healthier and longer lives through high-quality care, opening 100 new community mental health centres, and our mental health strategy will go further, outlining how we plan to build a more integrated system that responds earlier and reduces waiting times for support.”

In the UK and Ireland, Samaritans can be contacted on freephone 116 123. In Canada, you can call or text the Suicide Crisis Helpline on 988. In the US, you can call or text the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline on 988, chat on 988lifeline. org, or text HOME to 741741 to connect with a crisis counselor. In Australia, the crisis support service Lifeline is 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found at befrienders. org

Hungry for connection? This is what we lose when we stop eating together

The Guardian Sun, 20 Sep 2026 15:00:19 GMT

Mealtimes offer a pause in the day for parents and children to sit together, listen to one another and trade stories

Making sense of it is a column about spirituality and how it can be used to navigate everyday life

When I was growing up in a Muslim household, food was rarely just food. As the youngest child, my job was to bring out a large water jug with a matching basin pot and soap to help the family wash their hands. Mum would distribute freshly baked breads to everyone to have with the soup or curry. Dad would have me sit next to him as he presided over the gathering – asking questions, giving directions all the while passing food and utensils around. My older brother would take turns helping everyone wash their hands.

There was even a small ritual around something as ordinary as a piece of bread. If it fell on the ground anywhere in the house or was even seen on the ground outside, we would pick it up, clean it, kiss it respectfully and place it somewhere clean and safe. Food was not to be treated carelessly.

And sending a guest away without offering them a meal is unthinkable – almost a sin.

As a child, I didn’t think of any of this as “spirituality”. It was simply what you did. Eating alone felt like punishment. It still does.

Only later, after leaving Afghanistan and building a life in Australia, did I begin to understand what those ordinary habits carried with them: gratitude, hospitality and a sense that food was something to be celebrated – and shared.

Islam is hardly alone in this.

In Judaism, the Shabbat meal brings families together around food, prayer, conversation and ritual. Christianity has the shared meal at the centre of one of its most powerful religious symbols, while the Gospels repeatedly depict Jesus eating with others, including people considered outsiders.

Across Hindu traditions, food is associated with gratitude, hospitality and community. In Sikhism, the tradition of langar makes the social meaning of eating together particularly explicit. People sit together and share a free meal regardless of wealth, status or social position. Everyone is fed. Just as importantly, everyone eats together.

The traditions are different, of course. But across them runs a familiar idea: food can bring people together in ways that go well beyond satisfying hunger.

During a fieldwork assignment, a group of strangers and I were thrust together for an orientation meeting over lunch.

Nerves stopped everyone from taking the first bite. So our team leader smiled and said: “Buon appetito.” I replied with the Afghan equivalent: “Ishteha-e-khoob” – enjoy your meal.

Halfway through eating, our team leader suddenly apologised for his habit of eating quickly. He explained that he had grown up as the youngest of nine children in a poor Italian family, where you learned early to eat before the food ran out.

Others began opening up and telling their own stories about food.

For some, family meals were about far more than what was on the plate. They created a pause in the day when parents and children sat together, listened to one another and traded stories. In an era before smartphones, and when many families turned the television off at dinner, the table was the centre of family life.

I left that lunch thinking about how much can be contained in something as simple as sitting down to eat.

These days, more often than not, I find myself eating lunch on the go – in my car, on a Teams meeting or while scrolling on my phone. Once, amid community engagement work and endless spreadsheets and trackers, I forgot that I had left my lunchbox in the car.

That’s modern life, I suppose.

Food is easily reduced to fuel: something we need to get through the day before moving on to the next task. We don’t always have the time to wait for others to join us. We don’t always ask whether someone has eaten. And yet we seem to spend an extraordinary amount of time looking at photographs of food online.

Perhaps there is something slightly strange about that. We have never had so many pictures of beautifully presented meals yet so little time to sit down and enjoy our food with the people we love.

Buon appetito. Ishteha-e-khoob!

Semenyo helps chaotic Manchester City beat Sunderland despite Brobbey hat-trick

The Guardian Sun, 20 Sep 2026 14:59:02 GMT

Manchester City sent a message to Arsenal with this chaotic victory that takes Enzo Maresca’s team three points clear as leaders during the three-week international break.

Until the Premier League resumes on 10 October City can enjoy their status while Mikel Arteta’s champions have to stew following Saturday’s 3-0 humbling at Brighton.

Maresca will review this match because City lacked control and may not have enjoyed a 5-3 win that featured two Antoine Semenyo strikes for them, a Brian Brobbey hat-trick for Sunderland, with Enzo Fernández, Rayan Cherki and Erling Haaland the other scorers.

Maresca’s side are entertaining for the neutral and heart-palpitating for the manager. When the normally calm Rúben Dias hit the ball towards his goal and scrambled to hoof off the line, this was City in microcosm, versus Régis Le Bris’ potent visitors. The conclusion, though, from the season opening phase is that City will compete with the Gunners to the end of the title race – providing they become less fragile.

Sunderland conceded first by allowing a break at a corner that ended in Dayann Methalie chopping down Iliman Ndiaye. Next came a moment of Fernández skill from a free-kick along the right-hand edge of the box. City’s £125m deadline-day acquisition from Chelsea asked Ndiaye to alter position in the area, then guided the ball straight home, on the near side, his instruction to the winger hoodwinking Robin Roefs, Sunderland’s goalkeeper, who ended up on his backside. It was a first goal for Fernández since his equaliser in the World Cup semi-final for Argentina against England.

Having been excellent, City fell asleep seconds later. Enzo Le Fée is one of Sunderland’s star acts and the pinpoint pass into Brobbey that split Dias and Matheus Nunes showed why. The No 9’s first touch was smart, allowing him to then beat, with the outside of his right boot, the onrushing Gianluigi Donnarumma.

Maresca had billed the contest as City’s toughest so far and you saw now that this was not regulation respectful manager-speak. Le Bris’ side pinged the ball about and were quick to fire it into the danger area. Yet, when feeling too comfortable while playing out from the back, City pounced again. Kevin Danso’s loose pass from his area was nabbed by Ndiaye and the ball went instantly to Haaland near the penalty spot. Semenyo took over, tapped to Cherki and the Frenchman made space and threaded in.

That made it 2-1 to City with half an hour gone. Three minutes later a breathless opening period had another twist. Le Fée slipped in Thomas Meunier, the wide right forward crossed, and Brobbey could not miss. Following a prolonged video assistant referee check Sunderland’s second stood: Brobbey and Meunier being offside was the question and it appeared marginal.

Again, Maresca’s side suffered due to naivety. And, again, they roved upfield and breached their visitors’ rearguard. This time Cherki hit Marc Guéhi with a chip from the right that provoked a scramble in Sunderland’s area. The ball came out to Semenyo who powered in to restore City’s lead.

By the interval it should have been 4-2 but the normally lethal Haaland splayed wide after Ndiaye teed him up. The last bit of action had a mis-hit Brobbey effort nearly chipping Donnarumma who needed his 6ft 5in to tip over.

Maresca wanted the match slowed down in the second half, with the ball at City feet. Yet still holes were punched in them as when Elliot Anderson was caught upfield and Noah Sadiki ran into space and ballooned over.

Another goal looked to be needed because Sunderland were relentless. Cherki’s curving pass right to Ndiaye created a chance for the fourth but the winger’s touch was clumsy. Better was Semenyo’s decisiveness that made it 4-2. Cherki’s pass caused Nordi Mukiele a problem, the ball went to City’s Ghanaian international, and he arrowed into the far right corner.

The British team will next head to Bologna for the quarter-final knockout stage of the competition, which takes place between 24 and 29 November in the final week of the tennis season, for the first time since 2023. “There’s obviously a lot of tennis to be played before [the Davis Cup Finals], but it’s really a great thing to look forward to,” Smith said. “I’m really pleased how each of the players have gone about things in different ways yesterday and today. The way they prepare, their quality, their competitiveness. I thought they were excellent.”

Smith had warned on Saturday evening that there would probably be few breaks in the doubles match because of the fast indoor conditions inside the Copper Box. It was a source of great pleasure, then, when Patten and Skupski burst into the match with a brilliant opening return game, immediately breaking serve with no fewer than three lob winners, including a particularly sweet backhand from Skupski on break point.

The British pair did not face a break point in the match, finally breaking serve at 4-4 in the second set from a brilliant forehand return winner by Skupski. “Very happy to play with Henry,” Skupski said, smiling. “It’s a privilege to play with the world No 1.”

Patten responded to the compliment by rolling his eyes, drawing laughter from Skupski and Smith: “It’s a privilege for me to play with the US Open champion as well. Former world No 1.”

This has been a good weekend for the Davis Cup, with ties around the world attracting strong crowds and great atmospheres, including the sold-out Copper Box. This was undoubtedly a great draw for the British team – in the best tie of the weekend, the USA team were toppled 3-2 by an excellent Czech squad before 13,000 fans each day in Prague, while France fell against Canada in front of 10,000 Québecois fans led by Félix Auger-Aliassime – but this is still a good result.

It is also a good reflection of the Great Britain team’s overall depth, with five British players now inside the singles top 100. While Jack Draper has been sidelined for an extended period, Cameron Norrie could only passionately cheer on from the sidelines during the past week after he was forced to withdraw at the last minute because of injury.

The draw for the final eight will be made on Tuesday. In a world of wars and climate crisis, a new leader could save the UN. But would Trump allow it?

The Guardian Sun, 20 Sep 2026 13:38:46 GMT

As the organisation meets this week, it remains the best hope for restoring order. But it relies on goodwill from the US president – and that is lacking

If all goes to plan, at some stage in the coming weeks 15 diplomats will emerge from a small sound-proofed room deep in the bowels of the United Nations headquarters in New York and announce the organisation’s next secretary-general.

The person they choose will face a combination of challenges unlike any that their predecessors have had to deal with. Two of the security council’s permanent members, the US and Russia, are engaged in wars of choice that have no end in sight. A UN commission of inquiry has accused Israel of committing genocide in Gaza, but the UN has effectively been reduced to the role of bystander, pushed out by Donald Trump’s Board of Peace. The climate crisis is creating a cascade of new humanitarian disasters, while every day now seems to bring a new security threat caused by the unregulated rise of AI.

All of this is happening in a world in which the very principles of the UN – multilateralism, a rules-based order and international law – are under threat.

Secretary-general elections have rarely been this consequential and conversations about who should win will dominate the sidelines of the UN general assembly this week and next, as world leaders gather for the annual summit.

The UN, and the world it speaks for, desperately needs a new leader who is both charismatic and competent. Yet the five permanent members of the security council – the US, UK, France, Russia and China – hold a veto. Anyone who wants the job will need the approval of Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin and, most importantly, Trump.

It is not easy to argue you are best placed to save the UN when the man you need to persuade would rather it fails.

Three informal straw polls have taken place so far and no frontrunner has emerged, indeed opposition to the two leading candidates rose in last Friday’s vote. For the first time in the organisation’s 80-year history serious discussions are quietly taking place about what would happen if no secretary-general is chosen at all.

Ten years ago, the election of António Guterres of Portugal was widely welcomed as a shot in the arm for the UN after a decade of the low-energy leadership of the South Korean Ban Ki-moon. In his previous role as the UN’s refugee chief he had been an outspoken activist and had pledged to continue speaking up for the world’s most vulnerable people. Then, a month later, Trump took office as the US president.

Earlier this year, he announced the US’s withdrawal from 31 UN organisations, including the bodies responsible for dealing with climate change and women’s health, while in July his secretary of state, Marco Rubio, announced the administration’s desire to “dismantle” the international criminal court “brick by brick”. The abrupt closure of the US’s aid and development programme, USAID, led to deaths around the world.

Most controversially, the establishment of Trump’s Board of Peace sparked fears that it could be used to supplant the UN itself. The UN meanwhile is in the grip of a financial crisis, with Guterres warning during the summer that it faced “imminent financial collapse” due to unpaid dues, much of it owed by the US.

And yet, despite everything, the UN is still standing – and still matters. It is only the UN, through its Framework Convention on Climate Change, that manages to focus international attention on the greatest crisis the world is facing. Despite dramatic cuts in funding, there are still 11 peacekeeping missions staffed by more than 50,000 personnel in some of the most dangerous parts of the world. The UN’s office for the coordination of humanitarian affairs remains the best hope for negotiating access to deliver aid in war zones, including Sudan.

This year the general assembly passed two landmark resolutions: one recognising the transatlantic slave trade as a crime, another to adopt a new world map that correctly recognises Africa’s size.

We don’t know what the candidates think of these decisions, nor do we know where they stand on the war in Ukraine or what their stance is on Israel’s actions in Gaza. Despite the election’s importance – and despite the relatively recent transparency of “vision statements” and hustings – the candidates’ campaigns have been overwhelmingly cautious.

Part of the reason, of course, is that someone standing on an ambitious platform would stand no chance of getting the job.

UN experts believe there is a chance that the two current frontrunners, Guyana’s former foreign minister Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett and Costa Rica’s ex vice-president Rebeca Grynspan, might become good secretary-generals. But no one is blown away by the choice on offer.

For Andy Burnham and Ed Miliband, both of whom will be in New York this week at the UN general assembly, there is a choice to be made. The UK is yet to express a preference, indeed the UK team at the UN is said to be unimpressed with all the candidates. So far, it’s understood, they have not voted in favour of anyone in the first three straw polls. The UK and France are both hoping another candidate will emerge.

Whether they will be any better is an open question. The New York Post reported in July that Trump wanted Fifa president Gianni Infantino to get the job. There is next to no chance that would happen, but European diplomats fear a Trump-backed dark horse – possibly one without a diplomatic background – may emerge in the coming weeks. This is, after all, the man who has outsourced his nation’s diplomacy to his son-in-law and a real estate investor. So far, Trump has said nothing in public, although that may change on Tuesday when he gives his speech at the general assembly. Or a social media post spat out at two in the morning could upend the race entirely.

The chances of the “Permanent Five” failing to agree on a name remain slim, but plans are already being drawn up in case the worst happens. Guterres may be asked to stay on, while another possibility is that a collection of senior UN officials is asked to serve in administrative roles until a candidate is found. Either way, it would leave the UN rudderless at a time it needs to be anything but.

No one is getting this job without Trump’s say so. But once the new general secretary is in office, the US president will have less sway on their actions. They will potentially serve for 10 years, eight of which will be without Trump in the White House.

But even without Trump, this will be an almost impossible job. The UN’s financial crisis is not going away. Severe cuts are coming. There will be no easy return to the 1990s and early 2000s, when the UN was at the heart of world events. A new leader will need to reinvent multilateralism in a world where it’s going out of favour.

Depending on the choice they make, we could look back at this decision as the moment that the crumbling international rules-based order began to be rebuilt – or when it slid irretrievably into irrelevance.

Steve Bloomfield is the former international editor of the Observer and a previous winner of the Orwell prize

Trump claims triumphal arch will serve as a ‘top grade military complex’ to store weapons

The Guardian Sun, 20 Sep 2026 13:26:23 GMT

US president on Truth Social claims his new plan for the 250ft arch comes at the ‘strong request’ of the US military

Donald Trump is proffering a new argument for building his triumphal arch in Washington DC: it will be converted into a “top grade military complex” replete with drone and ammunition storage space and customised sniper facilities on the roof and plaza.

In a post on his Truth Social platform on Sunday morning, Trump claimed that his new plan came at the “strong request” of the US military. He said the 250ft structure would be able to “house, store, and have the rapid ability to use large quantities of sniper ammunition in storage”.

With the hyperbole that is his trademark, the president added that the arch would be unique. “There will be no facility like this anywhere in the world.”

The triumphal arch project has come under widespread criticism for its potential impact on the historic area of downtown Washington DC. Its intended location in a circle close to the Memorial Bridge could interrupt the sight lines of several of the most resonant structures, including the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery which would flank it.

The siting of the structure close to the Ronald Reagan Washington international airport has also prompted questions from Democratic Congress members.

Last week, the National Park Service warned that it could have “adverse effects to historic properties” and called for additional planning before the building work went ahead.

The arch is one of several construction projects that Trump has initiated which he claims are necessary to elevate the visual greatness of the US capital but which critics have slammed as thinly veiled efforts to promote his own legacy. They include the creation of a White House ballroom, the refurbishment of the reflecting pool at the Lincoln Memorial and the renovation of the Kennedy Center.

All those projects have run into big problems, ranging from criticism of their aesthetic qualities, structural difficulties and legal challenges. In the case of the John F Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, one of the world’s pre-eminent cultural venues, Trump has hinted that he might demolish the property altogether in a fit of pique at the courts blocking the addition of his name to its title.

The White House ballroom, which Trump has also been calling a “military complex”, was beset by legal wrangling until the US supreme court last month said the project could go ahead.

The ground breaking that will kick off construction of the arch is expected to begin this month. Trump has linked it to the 250th anniversary of the Declaration of Independence, and said in Sunday’s post that it would be “by far the greatest” triumphal arch in any of the world’s top cities and capitals.

It will be clad in granite, with three golden statues on top.

Singer Becky Hill looks back: ‘Aside from the music I was making, I hated every minute of my 20s’

The Guardian Sun, 20 Sep 2026 13:00:17 GMT

The Brit award winner on being scammed by a model agency, coming to terms with sexual assault, and wrestling with impostor syndrome

Born in Bromsgrove, Worcestershire, in 1994 and raised in Bewdley, Becky Hill is a singer and songwriter. She began making music at 14, performing in a band called Shaking Trees, before reaching the semifinals on the first series of The Voice UK. She has since had two top 10 albums and collaborated with David Guetta, Chase and Status, Joel Corry and Rudimental, and won the Brit award for best dance act in 2022 and 2023. Her latest album, Rebecca, is out on 13 November.

This was taken for a kids’ modelling agency, which we later discovered was a scam. Every stage of the process – getting pictures taken, sending them to the agency, getting them back – cost us more money. We’d wire over £100 and get nothing in return. Our family wasn’t rich, so Mum didn’t tell Dad what we were up to – he probably doesn’t even know about it to this day. As for my modelling ambitions, I never pursued it further. I was cute until the age of seven, then started to go on the turn.

I was a happy, chatty child, but my home life was quite dysfunctional. My parents were on their second marriages, I was their first baby together, and they had five children between the two of them – some lived with us, some didn’t. There was a lot of moving about – a lot of arguing, too, but I always, always felt loved. Everyone had their own taste in music: Mum listened to cassette tapes of Foreigner, Eric Clapton and the Eagles; my sister gave me her computer full of all her downloaded music; and my brother liked Eminem, Blink-182, Slipknot and drum’n’bass.

I was always a mummy’s girl, and she and I would go to acting, singing and dancing classes together. She wanted me to find something I was passionate about, as I was bullied at school. I kept my singing a secret mostly, but when I was 11 there was a talent show at school and I performed JoJo’s Leave (Get Out) in front of all the parents. I’ll never forget the feeling of singing that song and realising that everyone’s jaws were on the floor. I could see other parents turning around in their chairs and asking my mum and dad: “Did you know she could do this?”

On the car journey home, there was a conversation about my future. Dad asked Mum: “Do we send her to a stage school where her talent can be nurtured?” Mum knew we didn’t have the money or live in the right place. She said: “But if music is meant for her, music will find her,” which I thought was beautiful.

Luckily, I found some good support in Bewdley – from my music teacher and Andy Brown, a guy who was dating a friend’s mum. He had management experience and took me under his wing – buying me a guitar and paying for singing lessons and studio time. It was a rare taste of what it was like to be nurtured without expectation.

My teenage years were typically fraught – I got my braces off by the time I was 13, so at least my teeth were fixed, but I started smoking weed and was temporarily a bit of an angry kid. Discovering drum’n’bass was a real escape – when I was at a rave, I had music to focus on rather than the way I looked or felt. I remember going to [the London club] Fabric for the first time at 18, walking down the stairs and thinking, “I’m home.”

I was 17 when I entered The Voice. I was working two bar jobs and was depressed. I didn’t feel that I had much going for me, but I knew I wanted to get out of Bewdley. University wasn’t an option as I didn’t like hanging around with strangers, but The Voice ticked every box. The high pressure of the live competition each week didn’t bother me as I was so happy to be living in my own flat in London and grateful for this huge, strange experience. I didn’t win, but I came out with all the contacts I needed to start my career.

Aside from the music I was making, I hated every minute of my 20s. It was a decade of establishing myself as an artist, shaking off the stigma of coming from a TV show, as well as a lot of personal turbulence. In the same year, I got dropped by my label and raped by a friend. I was 21 and remember sitting in a writing session and telling these three men I was working with about the sexual assault that had just happened – trying to externalise some of the intensity of what I was feeling. A few hours later, I was being pulled into a meeting with my management team to be told I had no label.

Around this time, I also met the man who would become my husband – we broke up a few years later, then got back together again. I started having success on featured tracks, but I felt like it wasn’t my success – it was the producer’s. I was always fighting to be heard and seen.

After I signed my second record and publishing deal, I was finally able to take care of my parents. They were going through a lot of stress, and my mum’s parents had just died and she was struggling, so I said: “I’ll pay you not to work any more.” I bought them a house – which they have just paid me back for, even though I told them not to – and I’ve put some money into their pensions.

My brother’s family were living in a hovel, so I bought them a house, too. I was still renting my flat at the time and wasn’t on the property ladder, but it was important to me that my family was stable before I was. My brother even works with me now. He was in the Marines from the age of 16 and got shot in the head, but is now my security guy. He comes with me everywhere.

So far, I’m loving my 30s, but the landscape has changed for music, and I am probably not having the same level of success that I had in my 20s. At the start of my career, my ambition was to write songs that other people liked, whereas now I am writing songs about what I really want to say – the pressures of the job and of society. So I’m at peace if this new album isn’t as big as the others, because I’m proud of what I’ve made.

I’ve been in therapy since I was 22, and have done a decade of working on my internal voice – the impostor syndrome that still creeps in and is so hard to escape when you work in music. It’s hard to be gentle on yourself when you work in an industry that is so fickle and unpredictable. Even at the start of this year, I was panicking that my job was about to end and that I was going to have to work in McDonald’s or try to get a new qualification. I’ve always thought I would like to become an electrician, actually, but I know that I’d be electrocuted within the first five minutes.

Really, I can’t do anything else apart from what I’m doing now. So I am glad I am still here, and glad that I’m full of a new sense of kindness – something I lost in my 20s, and something that kid in the photo had an abundance of.

My mum has died - and every decision I make about her belongings feels wrong

The Guardian Sun, 20 Sep 2026 13:00:16 GMT

Until now I’d never realised how much work is involved in sorting out a parent’s affairs, and how much heartbreak

In all the talk of the five stages of grief, I don’t recall one of them being spending hours on hold to energy suppliers. Perhaps I misunderstood, though, and that’s entirely what they’re about. This call won’t take long (denial); aargh, are they ever going to answer? (anger); if I hang on for five minutes more, they’ll definitely pick up (bargaining); they are never, ever going to pick up (depression); and I live on hold now – this is my life (acceptance).

You hear the term “sadmin” bandied about, you understand there’s paperwork to do after somebody dies – but until it’s you who has to do it, you don’t realise how much, what it entails or how encompassing it is. My mum’s death has basically become my full-time job. The hours are terrible, the pay is worse and the promotion prospects sobering, to say the least.

Received wisdom is that you should ask your parents lots of questions while they’re still around. For me, this feels increasingly true. There’s so much I now wish I’d asked my mum – namely who her mobile phone provider was and the number of her milkman. I don’t know where the water meter in my own house is, let alone anyone else’s, so it would have been handy if that had come up, too.

I’m lucky my mother died after the introduction of Tell Us Once, the one-stop shop for notifying government departments and council services. But so far my experience is: tell them once, tell everyone else 47 times and prepare yourself for a variety of responses in reaction to the news.

I’ve previously covered the odd sentences people insert in the gap after “I’m calling to let you know that my mum has died,” a sentence that drives home reality sledgehammer-style whenever you hear yourself say it. In fairness, many call centre employees have been empathic and kind. However, this week, one responded: “That’s not a problem,” and I was too stunned to reply with any of the killer sick burns I’ve since thought of.

The DVLA staff, whom I’ve spoken to thrice and counting, did not react. On the last call, I’m afraid I snapped a bit – third time unlucky – and suggested that acknowledging what I’d said in a manner that was vaguely human was perhaps a tactic they could try in future. I was told that this was not policy: they were trained to stay silent. I wonder whether this is true, or just quick thinking.

On top of the sadmin, there’s the stuff. A whole homeful of it. Deciding what to keep and what to donate or – eek – chuck is a battle with nostalgia and sentimentality.

My house is full, but what am I supposed to do with the plates I ate off as a child? The table we sat around every Christmas? My mum’s diary, the old-fashioned, paper variety, full of appointments, meetings and get-togethers it turns out she’ll never attend, in handwriting as familiar as my own? A photo of my parents with nine of their friends, only two of whom are still alive? Here, they’re in their 40s or 50s, on holiday somewhere, laughing and mucking around, looking pretty similar to me and my frie … nope, let’s steer well clear of that, thanks.

Becoming an orphan attempts to force you to face your own mortality, when I would rather pack it away and give it to a charity shop. But as I sit with this picture in my hands for too long, which I’d do even if I didn’t have such a lengthy to-do list, I have to accept that, if I take it home, I’m merely ensuring my son will have to decide what to do with it when his turn comes. The circle of sadmin.

Every decision feels incorrect. Keeping this kind of photo is silly, but throwing away evidence of anniversary parties, minibreaks, school uniforms, long-departed pets, Wednesdays, is worse. These pictures are proof of life. But I don’t need proof: I was there, living it. I remember it well. And, realistically, I’m not going to frame them all, hang them on my walls, turn my house into a shrine to the past. They’ll gather dust in a drawer, letting me off my guilt on a technicality.

Is there a right way to do this? It seems extremely important not to get it wrong.

When my dad died, in 2012, I kept everything he had ever touched – and many things just in case he might have. There was an offcut of string he’d wound up in a precise, careful way that was so unmistakably him that I found it impossible to discard, or even use when I randomly needed a bit of string exactly that length, which would actually have pleased him immensely.

A while afterwards, I read a bedtime story to my friend’s son. It was a book called The Invisible String, which helps children process grief by reminding them they’re always linked with those they love. It was so on the nose, including the title, the parallels too obvious to ignore.

These bonds go well beyond the tangible. We don’t need a tea cosy we’ll never use, a collection we didn’t collect, a painting we wouldn’t have chosen ourselves. The connection is baked into our bones. It would remain even if we didn’t have a single worldly possession. It carries on, regardless.

Gradually, over the years that followed, I managed to do without many of the superfluous items of my dad’s that I’d clung on to. I do wear his watch, even though it stopped working years ago (it’s right twice a day). And I still have the neat little knot of string. Hey, nobody’s perfect.

What if my attitude to my mum’s belongings is all wrong? What if it isn’t a case of now or never? Not getting rid of an object immediately doesn’t mean I’m keeping it for ever; it could be that the lesson here is to give myself a bit of grace. Maybe sometimes it takes a little longer to let go.

Polly Hudson is a freelance writer

‘I have nothing in the UK at all’: British man torn from his Swedish wife and home

The Guardian Sun, 20 Sep 2026 12:02:43 GMT

Charles lands at Heathrow with just two bags and nowhere to go as a result of Brexit and Stockholm’s hardline immigration position

Doubled over a Heathrow baggage trolley, the former British business director is sobbing uncontrollably, exhausted emotionally and physically after being deported from Sweden.

Hours earlier the 65-year-old had been marched on to a plane in Stockholm, separated from his home and his Swedish wife after a five-year battle to stay in the country after Brexit came to an end.

An only child with no children and no property in the UK, Charles has in effect been made homeless. He was last in the UK in 2022 for one week, and before that not since 2017 when he emigrated.

“I have nothing, nothing in the UK at all,” says Charles as he shows a text from the British consulate explaining where in Heathrow those suddenly left homeless can get help.

“All I want is to return to my wife, my home and my friends in Sweden and to live a quiet, peaceful life,” adds Charles, who does not want to publicly share his full identity.

His forced flight on Tuesday shows that deportations of British citizens who lived in Sweden before Brexit are continuing. Stockholm has already deported 458 British people after rejected residency applications, a higher proportion in terms of its population than any EU member state.

The situation persists despite promises from opposition parties now on track to form a government that they will introduce urgent laws to give Britons a second chance to apply for residency.

“I’ve done nothing wrong but feel I’ve been treated like a criminal,” Charles says.

“Since arriving in Sweden nearly nine years ago, I’ve done everything I can to integrate myself into Swedish society. I’ve learned some basic Swedish, contributed to Swedish society and the Swedish economy, and for that, I’m being punished. Why are they doing this to good, honest, hard-working people like me and my wife?”

Shortly after disembarking in London, he is sitting down in an airport cafe processing what has just happened.

Pointing to a small holdall and a large reusable shopping bag, he says: “All I have is what my wife packed in my bag here with clothes and my little bag” – in which he has belongings handed back to him by the captain as he got off the plane.

The bag includes a plastic envelope sealed and emblazoned with the words Kriminalvården, the Swedish Prison and Probation Service, containing meagre belongings.

In it is a miniature tube of toothpaste, a toothbrush and earplugs given to him in the detention centre where he was locked up for two weeks.

A bright yellow envelope was also handed to him by the captain before disembarking, which he opens for the first time.

Inside is a police document saying he does not need to be “escorted”. Another says he is being deported over a failed residency application under the Aliens Act – his latest legal attempt to stay in Sweden after a pre-Brexit residency application, made on time, was rejected.

Charles’s plight started just over two weeks ago when he and his wife received a text requesting that they come to their local police station to discuss their migration case. They thought it was to discuss their five-year battle to persuade authorities they were in the country lawfully before Brexit. But he was immediately detained and told he would be deported.

“It was an incredible shock. I was distraught. This is not about leaving Sweden, this is about me being forced to leave my wife and my house. They are separating me from my wife,” he said. “They said we think that if we don’t detain you, you will abscond from Sweden because you are not cooperating.

“For the last nine years, all we’ve done is cooperate with them.”

He said he begged authorities not to detain him, telling them he would go of his own accord but they said no. He asked if he could drive back to Britain “so at least I could take some belongings with me because I have nothing in the UK, and they said: ‘No, the decision has been made.’”

Before Brexit, British citizens could live, work, study or retire in any other member state. Under EU law deportation was reserved for exceptional cases of criminality such as terrorism.

After Brexit, Britons and EU citizens who had exercised those free movement rights were told their rights to remain in their host country would be guaranteed in the legally binding withdrawal agreement.

The campaign group British in Europe has raised concerns about the hardline treatment in Sweden for years but this summer it became an election issue after a series of controversial cases emerged, including a removal order issued to a 78-year-old British widow, Joyce Thomas, who had been in the country for 21 years.

A 74-year-old British man with dementia in full-time care was also ordered to leave after 25 years while another British man, 34, in the country since he was 10 years old, was deported in January.

The cases raised questions about whether Sweden’s hardline immigration position had infected decision-making relating to Britons there before Brexit, a cohort with special protection.

Charles says the experience has been humiliating, particularly as he spent a career in public service helping prisoners and unemployed people to start up businesses.

“When I first moved to Sweden, I thought it was a wonderful place to live. Clean air. We were very close to the sea. Forests, nature, the people that I met when I first moved there were all generally very nice people. That did change,” he said.

“Only two friends know what’s happened in the last couple of weeks. And they’re disgusted by it. One of them said, ‘I’m ashamed, I’m ashamed of what we’ve done to you’.”

Jane Golding, the chair of British in Europe, says “it is another case that raises the question of whether Swedish implementation is in line with the spirit of the withdrawal agreement,” referring to the legally binding treaty that Michel Barnier, then the EU’s chief negotiator on Britain’s exit from the EU, and Boris Johnson, the then prime minister, promised would protect EU citizens in the UK and British citizens in the EU.

“This British man who has sufficient means and a home and a Swedish wife in Sweden now faces homelessness in the UK where he has nothing,” she says. “This wasn’t the intention of the EU and UK negotiators of the agreement who said that citizens should broadly be able to continue their lives as before,” she adds.

She points out that, unlike the UK, there is no statutory body in any member state to oversee correct implementation of the withdrawal agreement. “Monitoring and support resources for UK citizens in the EU trying to enforce their rights are not commensurate with those in the UK, where there is a dedicated independent monitoring authority. Unfunded volunteers trying to help are overwhelmed,” says Golding.

Caitlin Moran: social media went from utopia to hellhole in a decade – if you want to feel hopeful again, get offline

The Guardian Sun, 20 Sep 2026 11:00:15 GMT

Fourteen years ago, Twitter was the fastest, funniest game on the web. Now I’ve been driven out by so-called ‘online activists’. The only answer is to unplug and try this instead

God, I love social media! I cannot believe my exquisite luck – to exist in a time when it was invented! Bliss it is in this dawn to be @live! If you’ve not been on Twitter yet – please join! It’s kind of like a cross between your best ever pub, and the bit on Live & Kicking where celebrities like Duran Duran were doing the phone-in, and you could ring in and talk to them. Literally! Because Duran Duran are on Twitter! Well, Simon Le Bon is. And Spandau Ballet, too! Well, Gary Kemp. And they’re really funny. During the royal wedding with Kate and William, when all the lesser royals were herded on to some shitty coaches, Kemp was horrified.

“Spandau would never have got into a coach!” he posted sniffily.

“Yeah – limos all the way for Duran,” Simon replied, with palpable distaste.

For a certain kind of person – by which I mean someone raised on Smash Hits magazine – the idea of Spandau Ballet and Duran Duran doing live, bitchy commentary on a royal wedding, on a new communication device in your pocket? This is all our dreams come true.

But it’s not just Camp Old New Romantics Tweeting During a Royal Wedding, though. It’s also a community. Everyone’s so nice on there. Everyone is their best selves. Last year, there was a mother in Welwyn Garden City whose child had lost its teddy bear. She was, understandably, desperate to get it back – begging everyone to keep an eye out for it on the streets.

Obviously, everyone reposted her tweet, and it went super-viral. Then the deputy prime minister, John Prescott, got involved. He wrote a little poem about the bear! And then that went viral! Because everyone really wanted to find that bear! And, by the end of the day, the bear was found – and it was like a breaking news event, but with actual good news. Everyone went bananas!

For a certain kind of person – by which I mean someone who wishes our newspapers and news bulletins contained more good news – it’s like a dream come true. Online, every day has a moment where it feels like It’s a Wonderful Life.

But the thing is – the fun and the community of Twitter aren’t even the best bit. No! Because the killer thing is: it’s kind of like the revolution on there. Seriously. For the first time ever, people can communicate with each other, across the world – unmediated by newspapers or TV. We all have the power to broadcast, and be heard, now. And do you know who’s basically taken over Twitter in the UK? The women. They’re on there, every night, reviewing the state of feminism through the day’s media – and being Chris Morris-level amusing about how ridiculously male-dominated everything is. And, gradually, they’ve got so pissed off about it, it’s turned into action.

For instance, this year, after the Today programme had two days in a row with, madly, all-male panels talking about female issues – first teenage girls and contraception, then breast cancer tests – Caroline Criado-Perez, who wasn’t a journalist, or a media person, but just someone with a job in the pharmaceutical industry, complained to the BBC – and was told it was because the Today programme could not find a female expert in time. She then spent the next month on Twitter, asking for female experts to volunteer to be on a list, titled it The Women’s Room, and sent it to the BBC.

And now – they use it! She has been the change she wants to see! She saw a problem, crowdsourced a solution – and fixed it! She has altered female representation, overnight, on the biggest broadcasting platform in the world – just by being able to coordinate a campaign on this new-fangled social media thing!

And this will, clearly, be the first of many campaigns like this. This is how everything will change now. We all have our hands on the levers of power, now that Twitter is here. This is the future! This is true equality! We can all be activists now! And at the same time as hanging out with Duran Duran, and Spandau Ballet!

We are, clearly, about to enter the most equal, humane, progressive, amusing and adorable era of humanity the world has ever known. Twitter is going to solve everything. Huzzah!

Well. It’s been quite the 14 years. Like they say on social media – or what’s left of it, now it’s mutated beyond all recognition from what it was in 2012 – that escalated quickly.

In 2012, I truly believed social media – and particularly Twitter: back then, the fastest, funniest game on the internet – was the greatest force for progressive change the world had seen. I spent hours every day on it – keeping up with the news, signing petitions, mucking around, making a whole new bunch of friends who are still my primary social circle, and, quite frequently, laughing more than I had before or since.

Obviously, part of my love for it was that I was, to use the parlance of the time, totally winning the internet: I had 800k followers and, in 2014, my Twitter feed was added to the list of English A-level set texts, as an example of “modern digital communication and contemporary rhetoric”. Let’s gloss over the fact that this was alongside the Twitter feed of Russell Brand. After all, back then, the worst thing we knew about him was that he had chosen to write something called My Booky Wook.

Of course, it was all exciting and new, then. No one knew what it would turn into. But it was, we can see now, a gigantic, unprecedented experiment: not just one in “digital communication and rhetoric” but also in the behaviour of crowds; in exercises of power; in what “the democratisation of communication” really means – especially when it’s incredibly easy for hostile foreign governments to covertly infiltrate, and sabotage, it.

It was also an experiment in witch-hunts, and shitposting. In bullying, purity-spirals, public shaming, cancellations and algorithmic radicalisation. In what happens when there’s a form of mass communication in which the majority of the context has been stripped out; escalating rhetoric is financially rewarded; bad faith becomes rampant; and no one has made eye contact with the majority of people they have been talking to.

And some of the findings of this experiment are, finally, in: public health services and governments now have so much evidence of its deleterious effects on both mental health and social cohesion, they are banning our children from using it. There are whole subjects – trans rights, DEI, vaccines, Gaza – once seemingly settled, or marginal, but on which social media has now all but obliterated a calm centre-ground. And families, and whole social groups, have imploded – after online skirmishes became unsolvable, and each side slowly migrated to utterly different, algorithm-dictated “realities.”

As I look through the list of the people I was chatting to on Twitter in 2012 – people who went to early Twitter meetups; people who were part of my everyday conversation in this imaginary pub/club in the ether – the attrition rate is startlingly high. I would say that fully one-third of them have been fundamentally changed by social media. Like some modern-day version of the rhyme about Henry VIII’s wives – “Divorced, beheaded, died, divorced, beheaded, survived” – the tally reads: “Cancelled, radicalised, now offline; cancelled, radicalised, survived.”

Caroline Criado-Perez? Who, in 2012, looked as if she was changing the face of feminism with a brilliant, amateur, smart, one-woman online campaign? Six months after her success with The Women’s Room, she had received so many rape and death threats online – more than 50 per hour – that she could not eat or sleep, lost a stone in weight and felt utterly driven to despair.

When MP Stella Creasy tried to highlight Criado-Perez’s problem she, too, received a bombardment of rape and death threats – as did any other woman trying to help. Including me: 2013 was the first time on social media I was told someone wanted to kill me, or rape my children, or find my house and burn it down. And it was not, by a very long chalk, the last.

But as anyone who has been subject to mass abuse on social media will tell you, the rape and death threats are, genuinely, not the worst thing that can happen to you online. No – the worst part of being engaged in “activism” online, even in its most mild, polite and humorous form, is what you might term “your own side” turning against you.

A mild skirmish with someone you thought like-minded – a classic case of the vanity of small differences – gradually snowballing, thanks to the algorithm, into a pile-on of thousands, until you don’t know whose “side” you’re on any more.

Until – seemingly now ostracised by your own community – you’re faced with a stark choice. Carry on batting for “your” side, even though they have denounced you as wrong, toxic and problematic? Or – rejected – go over to “the other side”, who welcome outcasts, and potential new converts, with open arms?

If you want to see the most famous instance of this, look at the man who eventually bought Twitter – Elon Musk. In 2012, he was the goofy, Democrat-funding stoner guy – a real life Tony Stark – who was going to save the world with his electric cars. A couple of leftwing backlashes later, and Musk – stung and rejected – had begun a classic journey to “the other side” that saw him first radicalised by his own algorithm, and then overseeing a darkly re-badged X being flooded with child pornography, “libtard tears” and actual Nazis. It all feels a long way away from John Prescott writing poems about teddy bears.

This is why, in 2026, my primary piece of advice to someone who wants to make the world a better place is: don’t become an online activist. In fact – seriously – don’t be online at all.

Three years ago, and while in the midst of my menopause, my lifelong, well-concealed anxiety disorder became so out of control I attempted to buy a remote farmhouse in Wales. In many ways, I still think this was a sensible decision: after all, the billionaire tech-bros are buying apocalypse bunkers in Hawaii, New Zealand and remote parts of Argentina. They obviously know something we don’t know. They clearly believe that civilisation will fall, and soon. Follow the money!

Unfortunately, six weeks after putting in my offer, and while tits-deep in planning a life of total self-sufficiency – Goats! Wells! An iron-making forge, so I could be in control of my own supply of eg: rakes! – I realised just how much money you actually have to have to follow the money. The surveyor’s estimated renovations bills prompted my mortgage company to withdraw their offer, and the whole deal collapsed.

If civilisation was to fall, it became clear, I would have to do it in my old house, in my old life. And if I was to ever get a handle on my rampaging anxiety, I would have to work out just what it was about modern life that was causing it in the first place.

This is a peerlessly anxious age, we are constantly informed. The last 15 years or so have seemed so fast, chaotic, polarised and without precedent, we are all frazzled and reeling. The cry of gen X and boomers is: “When will things calm down? When will things be normal again?”

On hearing this, I have noticed – with no little sorrow – that millennials and gen Z and alpha will reply, curiously, “What do you mean – ‘normal’? What would we get back to?” For they, obviously, have no memory of a time before … all this. Before all conversations were about how things are getting worse; before the news of things getting worse pinged, 24/7, in your pocket. Before “responding” to the news, online, became some kind of social duty, but one that could, very easily, if you said the wrong thing, ruin your life.

Trying to remember what “before” was like – and why it definitely felt better than what we have now – I drew up a list of ways to improve my life. Some seemed quite random, and all of them were either cheap, or free, but they all made it on to the list because they were things that, I hoped, would help me do two things.

The first – fall back in love with humanity again. To truly believe – as I once had – that most people are, by and large, good. And then second? To be hopeful again. Hopeful about making the future better.

Of the things I tried, I can tell you which ones were a roaring success. Getting a dog. Buying a litter-picker, and regularly acting like a middle-aged Pac-Man, gobbling up the empty vape and vodka bottles of the neighbourhood and depositing them in a big bin bag. Donating blood. Rewilding the garden: “eco grief” is real, but so is “eco relief” when a new pond, and a stretch of unmown grass, sees your previously lifeless garden explode with dragonflies, goldfinches, frogs, and – on what was one of the best days of my life – a peregrine falcon, washing its wings in my homemade waterfall.

I was also unexpectedly affected by accidentally losing my headphones, and starting to “rawdog” on public transport. It’s far easier to believe the doom-laden pronouncements of Donald Trump and JD Vance – that London is a seething cauldron of hatred, on the verge of sharia law – if you never leave the house without pumping an “emergency” news podcast through your Bose. It’s far harder when you sit on the bus with what I began to call “naked ears”, actually listening to what people are saying in London in 2026. Turns out, they’re not seething with plans to begin vigilante mobs at all. They’re just on their phones, talking to their mums (“Press the button at the bottom. The bottom! You’ve got the camera on reverse!”), or planning whether to have chicken, or sausages, for tea. They’re singing to the baby across the aisle, or giggling about some boy they fancy. If you are feeling paranoid, or dolorous, about your fellow man, I can heartily recommend going sans headphones for a spell. It really drops your anxiety rates.

However. Without doubt, the biggest change in my life has been changing my attitude to social media. As a middle-aged, feminist lefty on Twitter, I had genuinely bought into the idea that social media was the water-cooler/town square of our times, and that we all had something bordering on duty to be on it. In this, I was helped by a common online trope – being peevishly reminded, by others, to do so.

“Your silence on this topic has been notable.” “I am disappointed you have not used your platform to centre this subject.” Or – the big trebuchet of prompts – “Your silence is violence.” Each person saying this was utterly convinced of the righteousness of their cause, of course – but possibly unaware of just how many other people were also convinced by the righteousness of their cause – and how, ultimately, impossible and mad it would be for everyone to speak out about everyone’s causes, every day.

Additionally, I had started to notice a definite, recurring event: people whose conversation had previously roamed over multiple subjects, and in multiple tones, gradually becoming fixated on just one, single cause. Usually, this was defined by the cause – or, more specifically, the Tweet – which had gone mega-viral. Suddenly faced with a deluge of new followers, Tweeting “My hero!” or “You speak for all of us!” the poster would start posting more and more on this subject – until, one day, it finally became the only thing they posted about. I started referring to this phenomenon as “The Omnicause”: the moment where someone’s online life becomes defined by a single subject.

One acquaintance – “A” – took on the Omnicause of homelessness. What happened next was the classic Omnicause domino-effect: viral Tweet; new followers; “You’re my hero!”; escalation; until, finally, febrile, manic obsession. By Christmas Day – just six months after their big, viral Tweet – A was posting videos at 4am, sobbing about how terrible they felt about all the “hate” they were getting from “traitors” whose “silence is violence”, and screaming about government inaction – “These politicians are vermin! They should hang from lamp-posts!” – while their children slept, upstairs, in their parent’s lovely house.

As I knew a bit about A, I had a deeper contextual understanding of their Omnicause: a bad childhood, a failing marriage, ongoing mental health problems. To me, it seemed obvious what was fuelling the greater part of this – and, to be honest, so many other – Omnicauses: it was a proxy fury/sorrow about their own life. But of course, not one that could ever be admitted, on modern-day social media – where there is always someone, no matter how bitter your own sorrows, ready to shout “Check your privilege!”, “Stop whining!” or “Think how lucky you are, compared with those in Sudan!”

Over the years, I’ve observed just how many of those ostensibly passionate about a cause are, in fact, subtweeting just a single person – a wife; a friend who has turned against them; an alienated social group. And they are often so distressed by their online experience that they don’t realise how, if we are being honest, there is a terrible form of narcissism, which they are blind to, in their posts.

I have lost count of people who say they are having a “genuine mental health crisis” about, say, Gaza, or Ukraine. I wonder how distasteful someone actually in Gaza, or Ukraine, would find these posts: someone in Leytonstone or Brighton claiming to be “broken” by a foreign war in which people are actually being bombed.

Or – worse – people allowing their “passion” for a subject to become so intense they are willing to watch whole friendship groups and families divide over the issue and implode. Even to the point – at the most extreme end – of violent marches, and bricks through shop windows.

Surely, the first response to any brutal conflict, thousands of miles away, is to do whatever it takes not to import that conflict back into your own, fortunately peaceful country? You don’t spread the kind of ideological contamination that has set another country on fire. You just offer up your most profound and humble thanks you were born in a country currently experiencing far better luck – and then?

And then. For what do you do if you really do want to make the world a better place? How does a 21st-century person make conversations about the 22nd-century flip to the presumption it will be better than this one – and not, as we currently presume, so much worse?

Well, first of all – as I said before – get off the internet. Or at least ration it way down. If you want to do online activism – if you are on a platform you still, perhaps bafflingly, believe can be used to spread news, information and ideas for a better world – then, 20 minutes a day, tops, seems optimal. Enough to put something useful, and good, out there – but not long enough to get caught up in snark, and fights, or get co-opted into factional wars in which at least a third of the participants will – and we can now observe this to be true – eventually burn out, radicalise, or go, to use the technical term, “completely crackers”.

And secondly? Well, the old Al-Anon saying is popular for a reason: you can only keep your side of the road clean. No one can actually change the world – like Zara’s infamous “death trousers”, it’s both controversial, and far too long. But we can change our days. We can change our lives – just enough to change those of others.

Pick litter. Donate blood. Volunteer. Fund a local community centre. Mentor. Flower-bomb wastelands. Clear a river. Raise funds for overseas aid. Talk to someone lonely. Babysit for an exhausted friend. Join an organisation you believe in. Turn up and show solidarity with a local mosque, synagogue or abortion clinic. Read a proper history book on a subject you’ve only read tweets about. Then read another one – as there’s nothing more dangerous than someone who’s only read one book on a subject. Seriously – if I have to explain what “from the river to the sea” actually means to another ardent 21-year-old, I will genuinely lose my mind.

Stop listening to emergency podcasts; stop doomscrolling; go for a walk and talk to people; buy your local newspaper – and, finally, stop believing that we are living “through one of the most difficult, anxious and chaotic times in human history”. Sure, it’s not a golden age – housing, the NHS, the climate crisis, inequality and the rise of intolerance nix that – but, if you’re British, you must keep hold of a solid historical perspective: there are no bombs in our skies. There is no plague stalking our streets. We are not living through a Depression so bleak children are abandoned outside churches.

For the truth is, the world is, still, largely, as it was, “back then”, when things were “normal”: a big old mixed-grill of awful things and wonderful things; steps back and steps forward. In reality, there are only two big things that have changed. The first is climate change – something which, as every expert will wearily explain, we already have the solutions to tackle - but still lack enough bracing top-level panic to implement. And this leads to the second, and arguably biggest, change in our times: how we are being told about the world. Who is telling us about the world – and why. You only need to see footage of well-funded bot-farms – thousands of phones and laptops, blankly using AI to argue with real, angry, despairing, crying people – to realise something deeply disruptive is happening here.

And if you take your headphones off, put your phone down, and turn all those newly freed-up hours into actually doing something – however small – then maybe you, like me, will realise that you’ve now passed through Peak Despair. And have, yes, started to become, well, hopeful again.

The writer’s fee has been donated to charity. How to Be Hopeful by Caitlin Moran is published by Ebury at £22. To support the Guardian, order your copy from guardianbookshop. com. Delivery charges may apply.

Star Trek is turning 60 – and the vision it promised feels more distant than ever

The Guardian Sun, 20 Sep 2026 11:00:15 GMT

The US’s deployment of weaponry in space marks the latest backward step from the show’s optimistic conception of the future

Who among us doesn’t dream of space in their youth?

OK, maybe some of us. Like the ones with lives. While you were out playing hopscotch with little Jimmy and Susie, I was locked in my room mainlining episodes of Star Trek or the weird, sanitized version of Aliens that aired on broadcast TV. Fantastical science-fiction adventure seemed to offer more than playground games and actual human connection. Spaceships over relationships.

Star Trek, celebrating its 60th anniversary this month, offered a utopian vision of the future. Highly competent scientists traveling the galaxy solving moral and ethical quandaries with grace and intelligence. It was a vision of Earth that had overcome greed and selfishness to pursue a more peaceful world Kirk and Spock. Picard and Data. These were characters that were ethical, witty and heroic. Better that than little Jimmy burning ants with a magnifying glass.

The Alien franchise, on the other hand, was the complete opposite. In the second film, Aliens, which coincidentally is turning 40 this year, the characters are mostly brain-dead killing-machine soldiers and venal corporate stooges. This one sounds a bit more familiar, doesn’t it? The entire known universe is controlled by a diabolical company whose only aim is profit at the expense of the average person. Both Star Trek and the Alien films offered the requisite thrills and whiz-bang action to titillate a young boy like myself back in the 1990s, but they were also diametrically opposed visions of what the world might look like when I became an adult. Would it be along the lines of a lush beige carpet and colorful pajamas or a soaking wet murder machine covered in KY Jelly grinding the working class into the ground? It took a few decades, but I think I found my answer.

The US air force announced on Monday that it had deployed weapons into space, thumbing its nose at the unwritten rule that space is for peace, not for war. The US rationale is, well, everyone else is doing it! Officials point to the increased militarization of space, including a 2024 Biden administration report claiming Russia was developing the capability to detonate nuclear weapons in space to disable or destroy orbiting satellites, which are crucial pieces of global infrastructure.

The air force secretary, Troy Meink, referred to the deployment as “on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the joint force against hostile adversary action”. He wouldn’t say what they were, what they could actually do, or even what they look like. Which is always so comforting when futuristic space guns are involved. Is it a giant laser beam? Missiles? A claw that can grab satellites out of the sky? A large hammer? A Trump-shaped robot gollum that could swallow the International Space Station with the ease and gusto of the real person chowing down on a Big Mac? My imagination, stoked by years of sci-fi television, is running rampant. At the very least, I hope it has a series of blinking lights all over it. And an off-switch.

Back in the 1980s, when Star Trek was at its creative peak, the idea of weaponizing space was considered such a joke that President Reagan struggled to amass a consensus around his Strategic Defense Initiative (derisively nicknamed “Star Wars”), which would have created a US orbiting missile deterrent. But now, Donald Trump is making fantasy space battles a key element of his rapidly deteriorating legacy. The US space force, his absurd brainchild, presented new uniforms that look like they were leftover from a Paul Verhoeven movie. If one wants to conquer a lifeless galaxy full of dirt, rocks and little else, one must be wearing the shiniest black boots possible. Also a hat.

The space force uniforms are certainly lightyears away from the ones on Star Trek, where everyone wears bright colors that immediately make the viewer think they’ve accidentally stumbled onto a rather unique discotheque. The Star Trek creator, Gene Roddenberry, made sure that the phaser weapons depicted on the show had a non-lethal stun setting. I think if anyone proposed a non-lethal weapon for the US space force, they’d be A) fired immediately and B) called woke to their face (and on Fox News in front of millions of people).

Looking back six decades at the world Star Trek was born in, there was optimism in the world, mixed in with the chaos of political assassinations, riots, a war in Vietnam, and the ever-present threat of nuclear annihilation. The idea of going to space and landing Apollo 11 on the Moon was inspiring to a world that needed more cheering up than Ed Sheeran trying to find an opening act for his tour. Star Trek posited that life on Earth might be bad now, but fear not, the good guys would win in the end. Humanity would overcome itself.

Countless modern scientific achievements – cellphones, tablets, the internet, medical advancements – can be attributed to Star Trek beaming ideas of benevolent futurism into homes around the globe for 60 years. But did society actually learn anything from Star Trek? The Federation and the Klingons made peace in the film Star Trek VI: The Undiscovered Country, but could their real-world analogues – the United States and Russia – be any further apart? Of course, if you know anything about the future-history depicted on Star Trek, you know utopia doesn’t occur until after a global nuclear holocaust, in case you want to be even more depressed today.

Star Trek’s impact is immense, especially for a TV show that only lasted for three years and often deployed styrofoam rocks, wobbly models, and dodgy rubber aliens in its design. That impact is a testament to the writing, acting, and film technique that grabbed millions of people and changed their lives. But I’ve never been more pessimistic about humanity achieving the beautiful dream of Gene Roddenberry. With every fascist-looking spacesuit or space laser, I feel like we’re progressing backwards, step by step. Given the proliferation of pandemics, climate change, species extinction, and contaminated food supplies, I’m more apt to wake up expecting to have an HR Giger-inspired genetic abomination gnawing at my face. At least my years staring at my TV screen alone prepared me for what’s to come.

Dave Schilling is a Los Angeles-based writer and humorist

AI slowdown calls justified but collapse of bubble may be more immediate threat

The Guardian Sun, 20 Sep 2026 10:38:51 GMT

Scale of debt issuance being used to fund the hectic pace of the datacentre rollout by tech firms is a worry

Warnings about powerful and uncontrolled AI have dominated the headlines this past week. But even amid the omens of apocalypse, it is still worth asking if the entire AI-industrial complex is sailing towards a financial iceberg.

It will hardly be our most pressing concern if the bots are poised to take over the world, but a collapse of the AI bubble would have repercussions far beyond the US.

AI bosses have united in recent days to warn us the immensely powerful product they have sunk billions into creating may or may not destroy the human race.

Some are also calling for limits on how rapidly the technologies should be allowed to progress, and how they can be used.

There is ample evidence that AI urgently needs regulating – from the ability of Meta’s pervert glasses (sorry, smart glasses) to film us without consent to the lack of adequate safeguards that allowed swarms of chatbots to go on a hacking spree.

Some of the suggestions currently being mooted, including independent analysis of AI models, seem important improvements on the ungoverned status quo.

But we should also be alert to the risk that a small number of intricately linked megafirms that have racked up multibillion-dollar debts are hoping the state will throw a regulatory moat around them.

Perhaps a government-backed AI “pause” could prevent cheaper Chinese options from encroaching on Silicon Valley’s market dominance, for example.

Away from the risk that their product might obliterate human life, there are more old-fashioned reasons for tech bosses to be fearful – including the fundamental one of whether the economics of their businesses work.

The first worry is the sheer scale of debt issuance being used to fund the hectic pace of the datacentre rollout by the hyperscalers building them – Google, Amazon, Microsoft, Meta and Oracle – $132bn (£99bn) this year alone on one estimate.

In a world of fragile bond markets with yields on 10-year US treasuries, a global benchmark for borrowing costs, hovering at about 5%, the size of these debt piles could be one potential trigger for a market rethink.

That is especially true given the second reason for concern: the fact that the “unit economics” of AI continue to be questionable and aren’t moving in the right direction.

As a recent Bloomberg report put it: “The price of AI is collapsing, while the cost of building it is not.” It pointed out that OpenAI has repeatedly cut its fees to hang on to customers, for example.

An index by the research company Silicon Data that aims to track how much customers are paying for a million tokens – the units of data processed by large language models – shows it more than halving since June, to less than $1.

Yet at the same time, frenzied demand for the real-world components of datacentres – semiconductors, for example – is keeping costs elevated.

The maths only works, it seems, on the assumption of epic revenue growth. Anthropic apparently told investors recently that its “adjusted operating income” was positive – the only problem being that this measure effectively excludes many of its costs.

As the digital rights campaigner Cory Doctorow puts it: “These companies are claiming that they are so cool that their profitability can only be measured using a novel, secret form of mathematics.”

Some aspects of this edifice may seem familiar to veterans of the global financial crisis: masters of the universe, with a business model that is so clever mere mortals can’t be expected to understand it, all propped up with ample dollops of leverage.

A frankly terrifying recent research note from the financial analyst Groundbreaker made this analogy clear, by unearthing a third reason to worry – just totting up debt underrepresents the financial promises underpinning the boom.

It sets out the $1.5tn “compute commencement wall” faced by the AI labs over the next couple of years, drawing a comparison with the moment when cut-price “teaser” mortgage rates began to run out in 2007 and 2008.

When those rates ended, flipping low income homeowners on to much higher rates, borrowers began defaulting in their droves, lighting the touchpaper on what became the global financial crisis.

According to Groundbreaker’s analysis, in many cases datacentres are being built and kitted out on “take or pay” contracts, with not a dollar due until a deadline is hit (often two to three years), and they hum into life.

In the interim, the hyperscaler building the datacentre books the value of the contract as expected future revenue, and shareholders cheer. Meanwhile, the buyer, (a frontier lab such as OpenAI or Anthropic) doesn’t yet have to account for the costs it will have to pay, once it starts using it.

The analysis suggests the abrupt jump in costs, as contracts mature and datacentres come online, could be an eye-watering $700bn next year and more than $800bn in 2027.

That could all be just fine if revenue continues to rocket. Or perhaps not so much, if AI’s end users aren’t prepared to pay enough to cover the costs – perhaps because cheaper options arise.

This isn’t, technically, debt – but the impact, if obligations can’t be met in full, would shake the foundations of the entire edifice.

Given the spate of recent revelations about revolting bots, the focus on AI safety and the risks to humanity may well be justified, and should be tackled.

But that should not prevent us from fretting about the delicate, interlinked financial structures that underpin the AI boom, and the risks for us all if they crumble.
