As White House shields the AI gold rush, Trump family and other allies strike it rich – with few guardrails

The Guardian Sun, 20 Sep 2026 10:00:13 GMT

It’s not clear that financial interests are driving White House policy, but they run parallel even as resistance mounts

Donald Trump’s sons, through a series of AI-linked defense and technology ventures, have picked up a $620m Pentagon loan, a Marine Corps robotics contract and an undisclosed air force drone deal in the past year. His longtime friend Michael Dell won a Pentagon contract worth nearly $9bn. And this week, as public support for artificial intelligence sinks to some of the lowest levels ever recorded, the president went to bat for the industry.

“The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U. S. A. has that, in spades,” he posted on Truth Social Monday. “There is a SICK conspiracy going on against AI and Data Centers.” It was the first of many aggressively pro-AI posts he would make this week.

Trump is resisting new restrictions on AI at a moment when his family and some of his closest allies have accumulated financial interests in the infrastructure and defense-technology ecosystem expanding alongside the AI boom, an overlap that has now drawn scrutiny from Democratic lawmakers, government ethics watchdogs and, by some accounts, his own senior aides. It’s not clear that financial interests are driving Trump’s policy, but the two have moved in close parallel.

The administration frames its resistance chiefly as a matter of competitiveness. Trump and officials including David Sacks, who co-chairs his Council of Advisors on Science and Technology, have repeatedly argued that new rules could slow US AI development when the country is racing China for dominance of the technology. Sacks said at a Politico summit on Wednesday that recent warnings from Anthropic and OpenAI about the technology’s risks amounted to political theater, manufactured by advocacy groups and the press, and said existing laws were largely sufficient.

But many concerns are coming from inside the industry itself. In early September, Jacob Coxon – a researcher who spent three years working on the foundational training of AI models at both OpenAI and Anthropic – resigned and published a stark warning.

“Neither company is acting responsibly,” he wrote. “They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.” He said colleagues privately believe the technology “could kill us all by the end of the decade”. Anthropic’s head of AI safety, Mrinank Sharma, separately resigned the same week, writing that “the world is in peril.”

Those warnings coincided with a concrete demonstration of AI-enabled risk. A California cybersecurity firm disclosed this month that it had used artificial intelligence to build a self-spreading worm capable of hijacking WeChat accounts through a single unanswered call, and then automatically spreading through the victim’s contact list. The firm estimated the technology could compromise more than a billion devices within hours.

Tencent, the Chinese tech giant that owns WeChat, patched the vulnerability before it was deployed and said no accounts were affected, but the firm noted that building the exploit, work it said would once have taken a larger team months, took roughly 10 days with AI assistance. Around the same time, JD Vance, speaking on a Christian podcast, described certain uses of AI as carrying “really, really weird spiritual dark energy” and said there are “things about the world” that leave him “not shocked if the Antichrist was walking among us”.

Polling shows how far out of step Trump’s posture is with the public, particularly once AI’s costs become tangible. A poll released on Wednesday found just 11% of Americans support an AI datacenter being built in their own community, while 65% oppose one – including 52% of Republicans – and 57% say Trump has handled the issue of AI poorly, up seven points since March. The same day, the House voted 417-3 to require datacenters to bear the costs of the electricity-grid upgrades their operations demand, underscoring how concerns about AI’s infrastructure costs have moved from polling into Congress.

If the federal government did enact regulations that ultimately damaged AI profits, it’s possible some members of the Trump family would feel the pain. Donald Trump Jr and Eric Trump joined the investment firm Dominari Holdings last year and helped launch American Data Centers Inc, an AI infrastructure venture in which Dominari holds a minority stake. The deal came weeks after their father unveiled an expected $20bn datacenter pledge from Emirati billionaire Hussain Sajwani, and $500 bn in planned private sector AI investment, alongside an executive order unwinding Biden-era AI safeguards.

Since then, the brothers have moved from infrastructure into defense contracting, most notably through Vulcan Elements, a rare-earth magnet startup whose products are used in AI datacenters, drones and defense systems. Three months before the Pentagon announced its $620m loan to Vulcan in December – the largest the defense department’s office of strategic capital has ever issued – 1789 Capital, the venture firm where Trump Jr is a partner, quietly took a stake in the company. A ProPublica investigation found the loan request came not from Vulcan or the Pentagon but from Peter Navarro, a senior White House adviser and close friend of Trump Jr’s, and that Pentagon staff were told to move at an “unusually rapid pace”.

“The call came from the White House: We have to get this done,” one person involved in the deal told the outlet.

Trump Jr’s spokesman, the Pentagon and Vulcan have all said he played no role in the deal and that the company received no political favoritism. Eric Trump, separately, serves as chief strategy adviser to Foundation Future Industries, the robotics startup behind the $24m Marine Corps contract; senator Elizabeth Warren called that award “corruption in plain sight”. A third venture, the drone maker Powerus backed by both brothers and having signed a new agreement with Pakistan’s army, also holds a $90m air force contract, and has separately pitched its technology to Gulf states amid Iran’s striking of US bases across the region. Drones are widely expected to increasingly utilize AI technology in the coming years.

A Washington Post analysis in July found 15 companies tied to the brothers’ investment funds have generated at least $3.2bn in direct federal business since they got involved, but SpaceX and Anduril, the latter an AI-powered defense technology firm behind Lattice account for 97% of that figure, and 10 of the 15 companies already had government business before the Trump sons invested.

Excluding SpaceX and Anduril, the remaining 13 companies had received $103m in direct federal funding and nearly $1.8bn in long-term commitments after the brothers’ investments.

The pattern extends beyond Trump’s family to some of his closest technology allies. Sacks’s influence over Trump’s regulatory decisions has been substantial: in May, he reportedly persuaded the president in a last-minute call to scrap a planned executive order that would have subjected AI models to extended government review, overriding the chief of staff, Susie Wiles, and treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, who had spent months negotiating the stronger version.

His own financial position has drawn scrutiny inside the administration as a result. Sacks’s venture firm holds stakes in SpaceX and a range of AI startups, along with earlier investments in Meta, Palantir and Airbnb; federal ethics rules required him to divest only some of those holdings while he served as the White House’s AI and crypto czar, a post he left in March. Some administration officials have privately looked into whether Sacks could personally benefit from blocking new AI rules, the Wall Street Journal reported.

The outlet reported that Musk pushed in the same direction, joining Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg and Nvidia’s Jensen Huang last month in personally lobbying Trump against a proposed industry-funded AI oversight body, helping shelve the plan. Dell, a member of Trump’s science and technology advisory council and a longtime friend and donor to the president, saw his company win the nearly $9bn Pentagon contract in May, prompting ethics watchdogs to question whether his advisory role created an unaddressed conflict.

The technology industry is not uniformly aligned behind Trump. Federal filings on OpenSecrets show the broader communications and electronics sector still sends roughly two-thirds of its political money to Democratic candidates and committees this cycle. Trump’s support among industry figures has come instead from a narrower group: OpenAI’s Sam Altman and Greg Brockman have given tens of millions of dollars to a pro-Trump super Pac and Trump’s inaugural committee, though have also donated to Democrats in the past.

The Pentagon’s own account of its safeguards makes no distinction between a routine contractor and a company whose investors include the president’s son, which is a gap Democratic lawmakers asked the Pentagon’s inspector general to investigate last month.

Next week, Trump is set to host the leaders of the country’s leading AI companies at the White House, a meeting arranged with the House speaker, Mike Johnson, that will coincide with a visit from the Chinese president, Xi Jinping.

In the meantime, the investments continue.

This is how we do it: ‘As a Catholic monk, I was celibate. But sex with Orla feels so natural’

The Guardian Sun, 20 Sep 2026 10:00:12 GMT

Rory left the monastery after feeling lonely; with Orla, herself a Catholic, he’s been making up for lost time

How do you do it? Share the story of your sex life, anonymously

double quotation markWe had sex after a week. I remember thinking afterwards wow, everything has changed

On our first date, last October, I asked Rory how conservative he was and he said: “I have premarital sex, but I’d rather die than eat meat on a Friday.” I’d been single for almost three years and wondered if I’d ever meet someone who understood both sides of me: Catholic but liberal. When we told each other we were bisexual, I felt a huge sense of relief.

He introduced me to his friends straight away and we had sex after a week. I remember lying in bed afterwards and thinking wow, everything has just changed.

I usually struggle to feel present during sex, but I can lose myself with Rory. I orgasmed from oral sex for the first time with him – I’d never felt comfortable enough before. In past relationships, I’d use sex to gain affection and attention or I’d withdraw it to say: please show me you still love me.

Sex was a way to prove I was enough, and so the focus was always on the other person’s pleasure. But with Rory I feel safe, and I don’t use sex as a bargaining chip. If I can’t come, it’s not a big deal.

While training to become a Catholic monk, Rory was celibate for three years, so he’s proven he can go without sex – there’s never any pressure. We have it three or four times a week, sometimes twice on a Saturday morning. That’s my favourite time, when we can take it slow.

In Catholicism, premarital sex is considered a mortal sin, so you’re not supposed to take communion. At mass, when everyone goes up to receive communion and we stay sitting, sometimes I worry about being judged. Rory wonders whether sex will feel less exciting when we’re married.

The sex we have is fairly standard, but emotionally it feels new. Had he continued his training, Rory would have become a priest this year. Knowing how different our lives could have been – that we could so easily never have been together – makes what we have feel even more meaningful.

When I left the monastery, I thought I’d never get married; I’m a bisexual ex-monk – too weird.

From Lizzie Borden to Myra Hindley, why are we still so fascinated with female killers?

The Guardian Sun, 20 Sep 2026 09:00:12 GMT

Another true-crime drama about a woman accused of murder is hitting our screens, feeding into our culture’s unhelpful obsession with ‘female rage’

On 20 June 1893, in New Bedford, Massachusetts, a packed courtroom waited with bated breath for the jury to return its verdict following a gruelling double-murder trial. Against a backdrop of intense media interest, they had heard the prosecution argue that the accused had hacked to death their own parents with a hatchet, had burned their clothing to hide evidence of blood, and had done so out of hatred. The question the jury was asked to answer was simple – was Lizzie Andrew Borden guilty of murdering her father and stepmother? Jurors took just one hour to reach a decision: not guilty.

Yet, almost as soon as the trial came to an end, the mythmaking around Borden began – from fevered speculation about her motives and the infamous nursery rhyme to the many film and TV retellings of the story. The latest incarnation, Netflix’s Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story, opens with an axe-wielding Borden committing the murders, and frames the crimes around a fictionalised queer romance between her and the family’s housemaid, Bridget Sullivan.

Why, after 130 years, are we still enthralled by the Borden murders? Part of the answer, I think, speaks to a wider obsession with female killers (or alleged female killers in Borden’s case) and the way in which society ties itself in knots to try to explain, excuse or justify violent women. Statistically, globally and historically, homicide is a largely male crime – in terms of both perpetrators and victims. Female killers are rare: they represented just 7% of convicted homicide suspects in England and Wales between 2019 and 2022. It is precisely this rarity that sees homicides with female perpetrators (or alleged perpetrators) disproportionately sensationalised, mythologised and forced into recognisable tropes – the femme fatale, the wrongfully accused, the passive victim or the monstrosity.

That is not to say there isn’t some truth in each of these ideas. But very often a female perpetrator of a violent crime will also trigger or become the face of wider societal debates about crime, punishment, justice and womanhood. History is littered with examples.

The execution of Marie Manning in 1849, alongside her husband, for the murder of her lover, Patrick O’Connor, was followed by tens of thousands of Londoners, including Charles Dickens, and spawned close to 2.5m broadsheet sales. The shock of seeing a woman hanged triggered a nationwide debate about the ethics of public executions (they were abolished in Britain less than 20 years later). So notorious did Manning become that Madame Tussauds created a wax model of her, dressed in the black satin dress the killer supposedly wore at her execution. The statue remained in its chamber of horrors until 1971.

Similarly, the trial of the chocolate poisoner, Christiana Edmunds, forced Victorian society to confront the idea that a single middle-class woman could intentionally cause indiscriminate harm. When an attempted plea of insanity failed and she was found guilty of the murder of Sidney Barker and attempted murder of Mrs Beard, she was sentenced to death. But the home secretary stepped in, asked for her to be reassessed and granted her a reprieve. She spent the rest of her days at Broadmoor psychiatric hospital.

As the historian Jill Newton Ainsley attests, “Declaring her insane and therefore not responsible for her actions provided a bizarre and unprecedented crime with a relatively simple explanation.” This reluctance to acknowledge women’s agency when it comes to violent crime plays out in statistics too. Newton Ainsley has shown that between 1832 and 1901 women were twice as likely as men to be granted an acquittal on the grounds of insanity – even when charged with similar crimes.

For very different reasons, the acquittal of Beatrice Pace in 1928 captured public attention. She had been accused of murdering her abusive husband by arsenic poisoning, only to become the poster girl for wronged women. Upon her acquittal, newspapers reported emotional scenes where “women clasped one another by the hands and some cried”. Hundreds of women later wrote to her expressing their well wishes for her future. A few decades later, in 1955, after shooting her abusive lover, David Blakely, five times with a revolver, there was no such sympathy for Ruth Ellis at her trial. She was found guilty of murder, but her subsequent execution shone a spotlight on the ethics of capital punishment.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

after newsletter promotion

Perhaps the most chilling manifestation of female violence in the 20th century comes in the person of the child killer Myra Hindley. Despite conducting the crimes alongside Ian Brady, the criminologist Mark Pettigrew has noted that the press coverage of Hindley, with the infamous mugshot, far exceeded that of Brady. Additionally, her unsuccessful parole attempts opened a wider debate about whether “life” should mean life. More recently, the case of the convicted murderer Lucy Letby has become deeply political with regard to whistleblowing, medical care and the role of expert witnesses.

When it comes to this latest iteration of the Lizzie Borden story, the Netflix show appears to make a connection between Borden and 20th-century serial killer Aileen Wuornos, who received her own Hollywood treatment in a film starring Charlize Theron, also called Monster. This seems designed to, as the publicity materials state, tap into a “legacy of female rage” and provide an “exploration of why women kill”. From the opening episode, the show takes a highly sexualised and graphic approach to the story of the killings.

Was Borden guilty? We may never know. What we do know is that there were four people in the Borden household on the morning of 4 August 1892: Andrew Borden, Abby Borden, Lizzie Borden and Bridget Sullivan. By lunchtime, Andrew and Abby were hacked to death; Abby’s body was abandoned face-down on a bedroom floor and Andrew’s lay on a blood-drenched sofa. The brutal reality is that this was a horrific crime – whether a result of “female rage” or not.

Rebecca Rideal is a historian and the author of 1666: Plague, War and Hellfire. She co-hosts the historical true-crime podcast series Buried Evidence, and writes on history, true crime and culture

Pizza dough and TV prison dramas: how Nazanin Zaghari-Ratcliffe survived jail in Iran

The Guardian Sun, 20 Sep 2026 07:44:09 GMT

Former charity worker tells Big Brue festival in Somerset of the strange comforts that helped her during imprisonment

It is a TV show about women confined to prison in the US, but Nazanin Zaghari-Ratcliffe found watching Orange is the New Black with her fellow inmates a strange comfort after smuggling episodes into her Iranian jail cell, downloaded on to an illegal USB stick.

The British-Iranian former charity worker was detained in 2016 for more than five years and kept in the notorious Evin prison in Tehran.

She told an audience at the Big Brue festival in Bruton, Somerset, that she thought she would never be released, so did not mind risking her freedom by sneaking in contraband.

This included USB sticks preloaded with Netflix shows. She said: “We watched Breaking Bad, Prison Break and Orange is the New Black. It was very unusual, but it kind of connected us to the life we had before. Orange is the New Black is a whole different kind of genre of somebody who’s in prison.”

Zaghari-Ratcliffe also danced with her fellow prisoners to contraband Zumba videos and cooked pizza for them in an oven she managed to cobble together money for and have sent to the prison. “I was the queen of the pizza dough in prison,” she said.

She also discussed how she got permission to use the prison sewing machine, which helped her pass the time as she sewed clothes for her young daughter and her friends, the other prisoners.

This newfound artistic hobby spawned a collaboration with London’s Imperial War Museum and the fabric department of Liberty, creating three new prints that explored her experience as a prisoner.

The riskiest item of contraband she snuck into prison was a Swiss Army knife. She said: “I realised, they don’t care what I do. I’m just a political hostage. So I can basically do anything in prison. I can be naughty. I can smuggle things, and once I smuggled this massive whopping Swiss knife.”

She placed it in her shoe, but said: “It was so chunky, I just couldn’t walk. Having a knife in prison is a real crime. But I felt if they had found it, they would have given me what sentence? I was already in prison, and they couldn’t have done anything else to me.”

Zaghari-Ratcliffe was released in March 2022 after the then Conservative government paid back a multimillion debt the UK owed to Iran. The Iranian regime had accused her of spying – a charge she denied and for which no evidence was ever produced.

It became increasingly clear she was being held as a state hostage to try to force the UK to pay back its debt arising from a military deal struck with the deposed Shah of Iran.

Though she is still traumatised by her time in prison and is visiting a therapist, Zaghari-Ratcliffe said she had continued to find solace in sewing.

“When the military attack on Iran happened at the end of February, for five days, I didn’t do anything. I just couldn’t do anything. The only thing that I could do was sit at my sewing machine and sew,” she said.

“I thought, I don’t even know where my parents are. There was an internet blackout for a good two months, and I just couldn’t control the world around me, but I could control my own world. Sewing was the only thing that could calm me down. So yes, still, that’s still my refuge.”

‘We miss her the same every day’: Olivia Cusack on her late footballer sister Maddy

The Guardian Sun, 20 Sep 2026 07:00:10 GMT

Family is determined to ensure her ‘legacy lives on’ three years after the Sheffield United player’s death

Olivia Cusack says her sister, the late Maddy Cusack, is on her mind every single day and she is determined to ensure her “legacy lives on” three years after the former England youth international midfielder’s death.

Olivia, together with family and friends of Maddy, walked 29 miles from Bramall Lane, Sheffield United’s home, to their family’s home in Horsley, near Derby, on Saturday to raise funds and awareness. Maddy’s loved ones are still enduring a “frustrating and confusing” wait for answers about the circumstances surrounding her death on 20 September 2023.

An inquest into the death of the 27-year-old Sheffield United player was adjourned again in July and has been scheduled to resume on 7 December after fresh evidence came to light. Cusack, a former England under-19 international, was the first player to appear in 100 matches for the Sheffield United women’s team.

Olivia says the walk on Saturday, “Bringing Maddy Home”, was motivated by some of the evidence during the inquest. “After the inquest we wanted to bring her home from Bramall Lane, back to our family home,” she says. “Many people know Maddy as the professional football player and the name on the back of her shirt, the number, the colours she wore, the club she was associated with.

“But I felt in the inquest it was lost that she was a person, she wasn’t an object that we were discussing. She’s a person, she’s a family member of ours [and] a person that’s sometimes been lost within the chaos surrounding her death really, so that’s the notion behind the walk. To claim her back, bring her home and protect her.”

A minute’s applause will be held before kick-off on Sunday at the Women’s Super League 2 fixture between Newcastle and Sheffield United. Discussing that anniversary, Olivia says: “We miss her the same every day, as I will on Sunday. The anniversary is always something that creeps up on us. It’s very emotional and it’s a time where we just reflect, but we do so much throughout the year so she really is at the heart of pretty much every single day. Not a day goes by where we don’t think about her.

“There can be days when you just feel absolutely drained and you know you don’t quite know what the right thing to do is, but I think the way that we just get through it is that we remember who she was as a person. She loved her life, she loved trying new things and just enjoying life’s simple pleasures, we try and embody that on every day, not just the anniversary.

“I really do encourage people to, as difficult as it can be sometimes, share the photos, share the memories, bring her up in conversation wherever you can, talk about her, and between all of us, you know her legacy will live on.”

The family have already endured eight full days of evidence, after the hearing began belatedly on 29 June, but the discovery of additional documents led the proceedings to be paused until December. The coroner apologised to the family for yet another delay. The case had been set previously to start being heard on 5 January 2026 after additional postponements in 2025.

“It’s been really difficult,” Olivia said of the delays. “It’s not something that any of us anticipated to happen. It’s very confusing and it can be very frustrating, the length of time it’s taken, it can be difficult to work that out and to know how you should be feeling and the process of it. However, we know that for the right outcome it has to be taken seriously. They need the time to come together and really get an outcome.

“It feels as though she can’t be at peace until it’s finished. And I do feel that’s quite upsetting to think about and to work through. It needs to come to a conclusion.”

Olivia said she would “channel Maddy’s energy” during the 29-mile walk on Saturday, when a group of about 15 family and friends travelled in the reverse direction to another fundraising walk in February 2024 from Pride Park to Bramall Lane.

We were really keen to get involved in this as Maddy was really passionate about education.”

Don’t discount Reform because it’s had a bad year. In our angry, fragile democracy, anything can happen

The Guardian Sun, 20 Sep 2026 07:00:09 GMT

Nigel Farage’s tactics are to play up the anxiety and resentment that people feel. Labour’s job is simple: to offer hope and change

Despite the energised start Andy Burnham has made as prime minister, plenty of his party’s MPs and hardcore activists are still haunted by a familiar sense of insecurity. Underpinned by a political version of impostor syndrome, it runs deep – and, bar the odd spell of Labour optimism, it always has. So it is with the battle between Labour and Reform UK that will define an election that could arrive much sooner than some people think, and a widely held ambivalence on the left about the possibility of Nigel Farage’s party taking power. Reform is apparently in deep trouble, yet also still in with a serious chance. How come?

Investigations into the party and its leadership’s finances by both the Metropolitan police and parliament’s standards commissioner may worsen Reform’s woes. Those investigations predate the two recently announced £36m donations from the crypto tycoons Christopher Harborne and Ben Delo, which themselves risk being backdatedly ruled illegal and are reportedly already being spent on 400 “field agents”. The two mega-donations symbolise two connected stories. One is about the possible buyout of our fragile democracy. The other centres on how, from much of the public’s perspective, all the allegations about Farage and his party might have already turned into an indecipherable blizzard. So, although Reform is down, it is still far from out.

But the reasons for that extend much further than money. Reform still has a serious chance of either leading or forming the next government because of the same basic fact that Burnham says he has come to avenge: that since the crash of 2008, millions of British lives have pinballed from one crisis to the next, leaving many people resentful, insecure and plain scared.

If anyone hadn’t already noticed, ours is an age of fear: of economic insecurity, wildfires and unprecedented weather, seemingly unending wars, and massed and chaotic human movement. Reform – and the Tories – lean into all that anxiety, offering the kind of crass solutions (witness Farage’s recent promise of a state of “national emergency” as soon as he takes office) that only heighten people’s sense of crisis. Labour, meanwhile, can only offer another variation of its age-old answer: modest hope and constructive change. Such will be the choice sooner or later presented to voters. And in that sense, the next election will be more emotional than political.

Make no mistake: the campaign has effectively already begun. If, for instance, John Healey’s first budget is not peppered with vivid symbols of a different approach to the economy, it will threaten to be a very serious dud, with lasting consequences. Moreover, at some point during the autumn – presumably beginning at the Labour conference – we will start to get a sense of Burnham’s 10-year plan. He will have to talk about AI, and its dire threats and huge opportunities, and the climate emergency – a subject he has so far been strangely reluctant to address. But he will also need convincing answers to less apocalyptic problems. Right now, I can think of no better example than the million or so young people not in education, employment or training (Neet) who have mums, dads and grandparents terrified – fear, once again – on their behalf.

He is also going to have to walk some very precarious tightropes. We all know what sits behind much of the public’s feelings about immigration: as well as misapprehensions about the relevant numbers – which are actually going down – and straight-up racism, too many working lives sit on the borderline between the official and illicit economy, and are defined by “employers being able to import cheap agency labour to undercut existing pay and conditions in the name of free-market orthodoxy”. Those last words were once uttered by that sainted socialist Jeremy Corbyn: they were intended as a rational explanation for yet another example of people’s deep sense of worry.

From that vantage point, footage of so-called small boats is bound often to spark a callous and fearful response. To many people, such sights look – look – like proof of even more people who have come to disappear into the cracks that run through our labour market, and then surface offering to work longer hours than you, for a lot less money. That makes you feel even more scared than you already were. And as any student of the 20th century knows, nothing warps politics – and helps demagogues – like that kind of anxiety.

A visceral dread is now the basis of the picture of modern Britain – and England in particular – offered to the public by Reform, the Tories and their allies in the press and online. We are, in fact, living through the comprehensive reinvention of English rightwing politics as a byword for angst, fury and paranoia. Anything that could reasonably be termed conservatism is nowhere to be seen: their England is now a country where summers are spent willing on unrest, and where quasi-paramilitaries menace our ports. Last week saw that Passport to Pimlico-esque village of Piddington in Oxfordshire hold a referendum on leaving the UK – with 92% of votes in favour – because of what the Telegraph calls a “migrant camp”. From Reform in particular, one often gets the sense that any degree of contentment is seen as being tantamount to complacent wokeness; as they see it, England is – or should be – a righteously stroppy little country, prone to the raging, nihilistic impulses that Farage et al seem to see as the essence of our national character.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

As much as Labour needs a solid, credible approach to immigration, it is going to have to remind people of the truth. We are a country with problems, for sure, but one whose people have not abandoned hope and largely get along with one other – and where, to quote July’s bulletin from the Office for National Statistics, “The cost of living (88%), the NHS (78%) and the economy (70%) were the most commonly reported issues facing the UK today.” Whatever our fears, earlier this month, YouGov reported that 57% of us are “fairly satisfied” with life. Labour should attack Farage, Badenoch et al for their lack of faith in the essential moderation and calm of most Britons; Burnham is the first senior Labour figure in a long time who may have the authenticity, energy and principle to make such talk actually ring true.

And then there are more solid, tangible matters. A fortnight ago, the new prime minister announced £1bn of investment in a new fleet of trains that are going to be built in Derby, “supporting over 350 jobs … and almost 6,000 across [the] UK supply chain”. Self-evidently, we need a lot more of that kind of stuff. Highly visible sites should be quickly set aside for new council housing, so Labour can point at the plots and promise people transformed and secure lives. In our further education colleges, money must soon be spent on teaching the absent skills that will help revive the economy, not least in construction, and provide good, dependable jobs.

The list inevitably goes on, but it may soon mark the difference between the meaningful survival of our democracy and the arrival of a munificently funded barbarism. Labour high-ups ought to remind themselves that that great Labour godhead Aneurin Bevan titled his only book In Place of Fear: in those four words lie this new government’s basic mission, the high stakes involved, and the almost impossibly hard work it will take to even begin to achieve it.

John Harris is a Guardian columnist

Are global stock markets heading for a crash?

The Guardian Sun, 20 Sep 2026 05:00:07 GMT

Economies thrown into renewed turmoil as AI debt, Iran war and soaring government bond yields fuel alarm

At the height of the summer, the mood was optimistic in the world’s financial capitals. Powered by the AI revolution, the US stock market had rallied to a fresh all-time high, as investors bet the multitrillion-dollar investment spree would overshadow the hit from the Iran war.

Now the warning lights are flashing red. As the fighting in the Middle East intensifies without clear sign of a resolution, financial markets have been thrown into renewed turmoil. A slowdown looms in the AI arms race, and tinderbox conditions in the market for government debt are fuelling alarm.

In the past week the US government’s borrowing costs climbed to the highest level since 2007, with knock-on consequences for the finances of households, businesses, and other governments worldwide. The fear is that Donald Trump’s war is igniting higher levels of inflation. The president’s tax and spending plans – driving Washington’s debt levels above $40tn (£29.9tn) – also have investors worried.

But as the soaring global oil price to above $100 a barrel stokes heavy selling pressure in the bond market, could shares be the next in line for a crash?

With the S&P 500 index of leading US companies 3% below an all-time high, and a combined value of more than $20tn for the “magnificent seven” tech stocks – Nvidia, Apple, Google, Microsoft, Meta, Amazon and Tesla – the concern is that markets are overextended just as the storm clouds gather for the world economy.

“These are febrile times,” Albert Edwards, a senior analyst at the French investment bank Société Générale, wrote in a note to clients. “The key worry for investors and policymakers alike is the extent to which the current oil price ‘shock’ will ripple through the global economy and whether it will necessitate sharply higher, recession-inducing, interest rates.”

Famed for his gloomy predictions, Edwards thinks the ingredients for a financial crisis could be coming together.

Such is the worry over the Iran war stoking inflation that the US Federal Reserve defied Trump this week with its first interest rate rise since 2023. As households and businesses come under pressure from rising energy bills and surging fuel prices, central banks elsewhere are also taking action.

Financial markets suggest the Bank of England will raise interest rates four times before the end of next year, even after it kept borrowing costs on hold this week. The European Central Bank raised rates last week, highlighting the hit to the eurozone from the escalating conflict, and the Bank of Japan raised its policy rate to a 31-year high on Friday.

The rationale is that adding to the cost of borrowing will weigh on the economy – limiting the potential for short-term higher rates of inflation from becoming entrenched. However, it will hit households and businesses already struggling with a cost of living crisis. Job losses will probably rise, in-turn compounding the challenges facing governments swimming in debt.

A US recession has historically followed about three to 3.5 years after the first rate rise, on average, Deutsche Bank’s Jim Reid has calculated. Markets have a habit of falling, or even crashing, before a recession begins, and often start to recover before the economy does.

However, the big concern among investors is that the main hope of economic redemption – AI – could also turn out to be a dud, amid fears it has fuelled an almighty bubble in the US stock market.

One popular measure used by investors to assess whether a market is overvalued – the CAPE ratio – or cyclically adjusted price-to-earnings ratio – has risen to its highest level since 2000, showing that the US stock market is unusually highly valued compared with its profits.

The CAPE ratio for the S&P 500 share index is almost 41 points, more than double its long-term average of about 17 points, and approaching the record high of 44.19 points in December 1999, just before the dotcom crash.

Highlighting the challenge, research by Fathom Consulting shows that for the multitrillion-dollar AI boom to turn a profit, it would need the AI-related sales of the tech companies involved to rise by between $600 and $800bn within two years.

Against a febrile backdrop as investor patience is increasingly tested, the consultancy gives a 30% chance that the AI bubble pops next year.

Brian Davidson, an economist at the consultancy, said: “For all the impressive advances in AI technologies in recent years, the economics behind the current capex boom do not work.

“Yes, recent AI advances could yet unlock huge productivity gains; but sales of AI models need to increase by hundreds of billions of dollars per year over the next two years to justify the current spend. Such growth appears unlikely.”

Investors are clearly worried. More than 1,000 investors registered for an analyst call conducted by Jefferies this week into “AI Extinction Warnings”, after the bosses of the world’s top tech companies called for a slowdown in “reckless” development.

The situation has parallels with the dotcom crash of the year 2000, when many internet companies that had been billed as the next big thing dramatically tumbled in value. That was a reminder that even if a technology is going to be revolutionary, investors can still lose their money if they finance too much infrastructure too early.

“It took a decade or more for demand to catch up with the infrastructure laid down in the British canal and railway and US telecoms and fibre booms – and many investors never recovered their capital,” points out Adrian Cox of the Deutsche Bank research team.

There are also sobering comparisons with the buildup to the great crash of 1929. A hundred years ago, many small US investors were buying stocks “on margin” – acquiring them with borrowed money. They blew up in the market turmoil that preceded the Great Depression.

This year, South Korea’s army of traders have been buying shares in AI-linked chip makers on margin – doubling the value of the blue-chip Kospi index. But once the market started to fall, they were hit by a massive wave of margin calls – when investors are told to stump up more cash to keep borrowing. Many were forced to sell their shares. According to Goldman Sachs, 1.2 million South Korean retail investors were hit by margin calls – which is the equivalent of one in 30 adults getting a nasty call from their broker asking them to hand over more money.

The huge spending plans announced by AI companies are causing concerns that they may simply borrow too much.

One firm with ambitious AI plans is Oracle, the database software vendor. Oracle’s shares surged a year ago after it announced a cloud computing deal with OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT.

However, they have halved since, as investors have fretted that Oracle could be borrowing too much to fund datacentres.

There are other signs of rising stress in the credit markets. The Bank of England reported this summer that the spread between the riskiest and safest high-yielding debt has widened since the Iran war began, showing that investors are warier of holding risky debt.

Government bonds have been sold off in recent weeks, and that fall in prices pushes up the yield (or rate of the return) on sovereign debt. Those higher bond yields make owning shares less attractive – an investor has less incentive to buy equities (which are riskier) than bonds, which are seen as safer.

For the US this week the rise in borrowing costs involved the yield – or interest rate – on 10-year bonds, known as Treasuries, climbing above the psychologically key threshold of 5%.

That level is “seen by some as a threshold above which financial markets might go into meltdown,” said John Higgins, the chief economic adviser at Capital Economics.

“While we aren’t convinced that 5% is that ‘magic’ number, higher Treasury yields would certainly pose a risk to the sustainability of the US public finances as well as threaten equities,” Higgins told clients.

Bloomberg macro strategist Simon White argues that trouble would really start if the US 10-year Treasury yield rose above 5.25%. He has calculated that this is the “inflection point” where, historically, stocks and bonds have reinforced losses in one another.

Despite the turbulence there are still hopes that a crash can be avoided, including optimism that markets are overestimating the inflation risk from the Iran war.

“A major downturn would need a trigger. Further geopolitical instability could be the catalyst, but we’ve long argued that the impact of geopolitical shocks on economic activity is overstated,” analysts at Oxford Economics wrote in a note to clients.

“Resurgent inflation and policy rate hikes by the Fed and other central banks are another candidate. However, our view on inflation is less alarmist – we think market expectations overstate the risk of further policy tightening.”

For many investors a slowdown in feverish AI investment will guard against the danger of a bubble.

There are signs that AI is beginning to power economic growth. The US economy has recorded a rise in productivity growth, while AI is also among reasons the UK economy has beaten expectations to grow at the fastest rate in the G7 in the first half of this year.

Such a turnaround in productivity could help the companies with sky-high share prices to begin justifying their valuations. However, it is a high-stakes play at a time of intense global volatility.

“Do I think there’s a significant dose of reality though in that productivity miracle in AI? Yes,” Andy Haldane, the former Bank of England chief economist, told LBC this week. Still, he warned the situation is fragile.

“I don’t think outright collapse in a dotcom bubble type fashion. But could I see a slow release of air that doesn’t collapse the world economy, but slows it down? Yes, I could.”

Our children may be surprised by what’s in our will – should we tell them now?

The Guardian Sun, 20 Sep 2026 05:00:06 GMT

You don’t have to reveal the contents, but I’ve seen families torn apart by unexpected inheritance plans

My wife and I have three children and several grandchildren. Our will may contain some surprises for them. Is it better to reveal its contents while we are still alive, or let our beneficiaries discover them when we die?

We gave our children considerable financial help, enabling them to buy their first homes. We have also made sizeable contributions to our grandchildren’s education funds.

Our thinking is that our descendants will need more assistance when they are young: for their education, setting up home, starting a family. And we want to give them the gift of knowing that my wife and I loved them enough to help with these challenges, and that the bequests came from us, not through the generosity of their parents.

My wife’s jewellery goes only to our granddaughters, and the mothers of our grandsons could feel aggrieved that their sons have been passed over. However, we don’t consider the jewellery to have any financial value, as it should never be exchanged for cash.

The financial value of our estate is to be divided one-third to each of the next three generations, with each third divided equally between the members of that generation. We have also stipulated that no generation’s members will receive more than their parent.

If we tell our children the contents of the will now, they may think we are asking for their opinions, which we emphatically are not. Making this clear may result in ill feeling. On the other hand, if they discover the will’s provisions only when we die, there may be room for misunderstanding, again resulting in ill feeling. We have explained our thinking in a document that accompanies the will. I wonder if others have wrestled with these questions and arrived at satisfactory conclusions?

What riches you have with all these children and grandchildren!

I am assuming you live in England and Wales, where you can leave your estate to whomever you want.

I went to lawyer and wills specialist Gary Rycroft, who advised that “there is no legal requirement to tell anyone, including your children, what’s in your will. It is your money, your property and, ultimately, your decision. A will is not decided by a family committee.”

That said, Rycroft and I both advocate discussing things ahead of time. “I’m a fan of transparency,” said Rycroft. “No one likes surprises in wills, especially if the surprise is getting less than expected. And while the will is clear about who gets what, families can be left very unclear about why.”

So, yes, we think you should explain ahead of time. I have seen families torn asunder by unexpected wills. Also, who knows what might happen between now and when the will becomes active. What if you have an argument with a family member and they think the will is retribution (even if it was clearly dated before the row)? Also, remember that it is likely that either you or your wife will die first, so if you decide to talk about it beforehand, it’s best done together.

Sign up to Inside Saturday

after newsletter promotion

Rycroft said to make sure the extra document you mention is a “more formal ‘memorandum of wishes’. The will is still the legally operative document and the memorandum does not rewrite or trump it. Its value is in explaining the decisions.” This stands even if you have a meeting to explain, as people tend to forget what was said or recall only what they want to.

“Remember,” counselled Rycroft, “an inheritance is not just about what you leave behind. It’s also about how a person will be remembered.”

And don’t forget that anyone you leave things to who is over 18 can vary their inheritance, within a time limit, with a deed of variation and change who gets their share. A reminder that, after death, we cannot control those we leave behind.

After 20 years of my school dinners campaign, I’m a happy man. At last, we’re going to feed kids properly

The Guardian Sat, 19 Sep 2026 07:00:40 GMT

This week’s government announcement on school food standards is huge. It’s based on common sense and science. Beautiful!

More than 20 years ago, when I started the campaign and TV series School Dinners, I couldn’t believe that we had standards for dog food but no standards for the food we fed our children at school. I have never, and will never, stop banging that drum – even after this week’s momentous announcement on school food standards in England. Because it is so important we remember where we started from.

Children in the state sector are at school for 190 days a year. And if they’re eating breakfast and lunch there, the majority of what they consume each day is in the hands of their school. When we know that children are consuming less than half the recommended fruit and vegetables, but twice the recommended sugar, school food is a massive opportunity to directly improve diets at scale.

But eating good food around a shared table isn’t just important for children’s health. It’s a core part of a child’s social connection and sense of belonging. Well-fed kids are happier, have more energy and fewer days off school due to sickness, and their learning and behaviour improve, too.

It’s no surprise that 80% of teachers agree that unhealthy food at lunch and breaktime can lead to disruptive behaviour, and 85% say diet affects pupils’ ability to concentrate.

But we didn’t need scientific evidence to tell us that – who doesn’t feel and perform better when their bellies are full of the good stuff? Get school food right and the prize is massive. Not just for children today, but for the adults they will become. Feed children well and we give them a better chance of healthier lives, greater productivity and less long-term pressure on the NHS and social care from diet-related disease. That’s no small change when current estimates are that obesity, and its knock-on consequences, costs the UK economy about £126bn each year.

That is why it’s so great to see the government announce new standards, based on the latest science. It’s the first time in a decade. And it means, for this generation of kids, they will be nourished with more fruit and vegetables, fibre-rich proteins and whole grains. Beautiful stuff.

It’s a big and much-needed update, but we know that amazing schools, caterers and chefs can rise to the challenge. Through my Good School Food awards, we have shown amazing school food is possible and affordable, and it’s happening right now in schools across the UK.

Take Chef Russ in Bournemouth. Working out of a cupboard-sized kitchen, he has transformed the food at his school. Not only has the school increased the uptake of meals from 28% to 98%, there’s a waiting list of parents keen to nab their kids a place there.

We see this pattern in schools up and down the country, and we have to keep telling these stories again and again because it goes against what many people think they know – that kids simply won’t eat the “good stuff”. We have heard that for decades. And we get it, because the food environment we all struggle with makes it hard to eat well, and so this seems to chime with our experience. But school is different. It’s a rare, protected space where that noise can be stripped away.

And when it is, remarkable things happen. Children eat – and enjoy – delicious, nutritious food. The evidence is clear: when the food is good and the environment is supportive, over time school meal uptake increases.

What makes me excited is these standards won’t just sit on a piece of paper. There will be proper monitoring to make sure they are actually followed. Not to nit-pick. Not to catch schools out. But so we know what’s working, where schools are doing brilliantly, and where we need to deploy care, love and support to help them get it right. That’s where the School Food Project comes in. We know not all lunch trays are created equal, which is why we are partnering with Bite Back, Chefs in Schools, School Food Matters and the Food Foundation to help to make sure these new standards can really be for everyone.

These new school food standards will finally fix what is on children’s school plates, but it’s only half the job we have to do. A delicious lunch nourishes a child for the afternoon, but teaching them how to cook nourishes them for the rest of their life. You can serve the best meals in the world, but if a child leaves school without knowing how to feed themselves, that’s where it stops.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

That is why food education must be absolutely central to transforming school food. And it’s why I’m passionate about giving kids (and adults) the skills, knowledge and confidence to cook from scratch. My dream has always been simple: I want every single child to leave school knowing 10 core skills that will save their life.

My free 10 skills food education programme teaches kids basic, bulletproof culinary foundations – how to chop safely, balance flavours, cook a nutritious staple meal from scratch, and stretch simple, fresh ingredients into something delicious. If kids leave school knowing how to cook a fast vegetable stir-fry, a simple soup, or how to make a loaf of bread, not only will they be healthier now, but they have options in the future.

With this cooking superpower they can feed themselves, and their future families, on a budget. That isn’t just a life skill: it’s health insurance for life.

Jamie Oliver is a chef, restaurateur and campaigner

Why Tucker Carlson Is Defending This Democrat in a Key Senate Race

The New York Times September 20, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Mr. Carlson, the far-right podcaster, has promoted Abdul El-Sayed’s comments and sharply criticized his Republican rival in Michigan. Strategists are scratching their heads.

By Tim Balk

Tucker Carlson, the influential far-right podcaster, lives in Maine and spent more than three decades defending the Republican Party before leaving it this year over his opposition to the war with Iran. He is known for his nativist rhetoric and once said immigrants were making the United States “poorer and dirtier.”

Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, a son of Egyptian immigrants, lives in Michigan and has spent his adult life pushing for progressive causes. Now Dr. El-Sayed is the Democratic Party’s nominee in a pivotal Senate race, running on a left-wing platform that calls for universal health care and abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

Yet, in a striking twist that underscores his shifting politics, Mr. Carlson has taken to defending Dr. El-Sayed. Both are vocal critics of the Israeli government and the war with Iran.

In recent weeks, Mr. Carlson has repeatedly spoken in positive terms about Dr. El-Sayed and castigated his Republican opponent, former Representative Mike Rogers, a critic-turned-ally of President Trump with hawkish foreign policy views.

“I wouldn’t vote for Mike Rogers at gunpoint,” Mr. Carlson said on his podcast this month, adding, “There’s no one who should be farther from a position of power than Mike Rogers.”

As the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11 attacks approached, Mr. Rogers targeted Dr. El-Sayed for saying in 2021 that the military actions of the United States after the attacks had “scarred millions” around the world.

Mr. Carlson stepped in to defend Dr. El-Sayed.

“El-Sayed did not celebrate airplane hijackings or cheerlead Al Qaeda,” Mr. Carlson wrote in his newsletter, “he simply said that the U. S. conducting terrorism of its own in response to 9/11 was not exactly an appropriate reaction. He is obviously right.”

Political consultants were puzzled. Could Mr. Carlson really be endorsing Dr. El-Sayed?

In text messages with The New York Times, Mr. Carlson would not go that far.

“I’m a podcaster,” he wrote. “I don’t make endorsements.”

But Mr. Carlson continued to assail Mr. Rogers, a former chair of the House Intelligence Committee who was an early, vocal supporter of the war with Iran, and who has long been a supporter of Israel. Mr. Carlson called Mr. Rogers the “embodiment of the cruelty and stupidity of the national security state.”

“He’s a toady to Israel and an enemy of civil liberties,” Mr. Carlson told The Times, noting that Mr. Rogers had previously lost a Senate race in 2024. “I can hardly believe Republicans nominated him."

Mr. Rogers’s campaign did not respond to requests for comment.

To some, Mr. Carlson’s defense of Dr. El-Sayed is an example of what political commentators regard as a horseshoe alliance, a nod to the theory that both ends of the spectrum bend toward each other on some major issues. During Mr. Trump’s second term, some unlikely partnerships between the left and the right have sprung up.

Just last week, Senator Bernie Sanders, the progressive Vermont independent, and Stephen K. Bannon, an architect of the MAGA movement, delivered back-to-back speeches at a convention calling for A. I. regulation. Last year, Representative Ro Khanna, a progressive from California, and Representative Thomas Massie, a conservative libertarian from Kentucky, teamed up to press for more information related to the Epstein files.

“American politics isn’t really aligned on a single continuum,” said Josh Pasek, a professor of political science and communication at the University of Michigan, adding that the left and the right seemed to be aligning more regularly.

Still, Professor Pasek added that such alliances should not be understood as evidence that the far left and the far right were starting to “believe the same thing.” Mr. Carlson’s commentary was more likely a “marriage of convenience,” he said.

Despite their drastic differences, including Mr. Carlson’s frequent embrace of conspiracy theories, he and Dr. El-Sayed can find some common ground in their shared criticism of interventionist foreign policy and the Israeli government. Dr. El-Sayed has called for ending U. S. aid to Israel and made criticism of the American Israel Public Affairs Committee a major theme of his primary campaign.

But Mr. Carlson has gone much further in his criticism of Israel, making baseless suggestions that the country may have known about the Sept. 11 attacks in advance and claiming that it wants to “destroy Europe.” Mr. Carlson also conducted a friendly interview with Nick Fuentes, a Holocaust denier. Mr. Carlson has faced accusations of antisemitism, which he has repeatedly rejected.

“El-Sayed is harshly critical of Israel and its supporters in ways that some Jews find uncomfortable or offensive, and may even make some feel unsafe,” Aryeh Tuchman, the director for the Nexus Center for Antisemitism Research and a former director of the Anti-Defamation League’s Center on Extremism, said in an email. “But Carlson’s opposition to Israel is bound up with classic antisemitic ideas.”

Some Republican consultants in Michigan said that Mr. Carlson’s posture toward Dr. El-Sayed was somewhat startling.

“It’s one of those things where people tilt their heads and go: Well, why?” said Dennis Darnoi, a Republican strategist in Michigan. “It doesn’t seem to have any rhyme or reason.”

Mr. Darnoi questioned why Mr. Carlson was attacking Mr. Rogers now after not having done so in 2024.

Some things have changed since 2024, though. Back then, Mr. Carlson was often at Mr. Trump’s side as he ran for president. Mr. Carlson even lobbied Mr. Trump to select JD Vance, then a senator from Ohio, as his running mate.

Now, Mr. Carlson spends much of his time railing against Israel and the war in Iran. He has said he is “tormented” by his role in helping Mr. Trump return to the White House. And he has discussed helping to start a new political party, which he has said would support ending all immigration.

Democratic strategists say Mr. Carlson’s commentary might help Dr. El-Sayed make inroads with conservative voters. But it could also carry risks.

Dr. El-Sayed, who has been trailed by criticism of his decision to campaign during the primary with the provocative left-wing streamer and Israel critic Hasan Piker, has ruled out having Mr. Carlson join him on the campaign trail in the fall.

Asked about the idea on the “Pod Save America” podcast this month, Dr. El-Sayed said, “Unlikely — by unlikely, I mean no.”

Still, Dr. El-Sayed said that Mr. Carlson was casting a light on the “corruption inside MAGA.” He said he disagreed with Mr. Carlson on “a lot of things,” but that they agreed that Mr. Rogers “never saw a war he didn’t like” and that he never saw a “corporate contribution he didn’t like.”

Political strategists were split on how — or if — Mr. Carlson’s input would affect the race in Michigan.

“It’s really hard to know,” said Adrian Hemond, a Democratic strategist in Michigan. He added, though, that “the entire theory of the El-Sayed candidacy has been that he can change the composition of the electorate, and he did that to some extent in the primary.”

Still, repeating the feat in November would be more difficult, Mr. Hemond said.

Joe DiSano, another Democratic strategist in Michigan, who does not plan to vote for Dr. El-Sayed because of his positions on Israel, said he saw a “clear advantage” for the Democrat in having Mr. Carlson weigh in on the race. Dr. El-Sayed might be able peel off some disaffected conservative voters who share Mr. Carlson’s views, he reasoned.

“He has to do something to pick up voters he’s losing,” Mr. DiSano said of Dr. El-Sayed.

White House Moves to Take Control of N. I. H. Grants

The New York Times September 20, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

Federal officials are drafting an executive order that would place grants under review by an outside panel, the latest effort to redirect billions of dollars in research spending.

By Carolyn Y. JohnsonSheryl Gay StolbergTony Romm and Michael C. Bender

The White House has begun drafting a new executive order that could further cement President Trump’s ability to control billions of dollars in scientific grants funded by the National Institutes of Health and expand the administration’s pressure campaign against elite universities.

Discussed at a highly contentious meeting at the White House on Friday, the order aims to create a new external committee with the power to veto awards in the nation’s vast biomedical research portfolio that do not conform to Mr. Trump’s political agenda, according to people with knowledge of the effort.

During the meeting, Mr. Trump repeatedly complained about his administration’s failure to bring Harvard University to heel. The administration has been unable to hammer out a deal with the nation’s oldest and wealthiest university, a central plank of his broader push against “woke” ideology in higher education.

The White House has also lost a pair of lawsuits to Harvard, including one ruling that blocked cuts to the university’s existing federal research grants. The government has said it plans to appeal.

Inside the White House, some of Mr. Trump’s top lieutenants have expressed frustration about a perceived slowdown in the administration’s attempt to force conservative cultural changes on academia.

The meeting, in the Oval Office, was called in part to discuss why the N. I. H. hadn’t done enough to push the administration’s agenda on academia in general and Ivy League schools in particular, said two administration officials familiar with the planning.

The meeting was first reported by The Washington Post. Officials at the Office of Management and Budget, which is drafting the executive order, declined to comment. A spokesman for the N. I. H., Joshua Pradko, declined to discuss details of the meeting.

“N. I. H. remains committed to its mission of funding biomedical research to benefit the health of the American people,” Mr. Pradko said in a text message.

Referring to reports that Russell T. Vought, director of the O. M. B., wants to rescind N. I. H. funding, Mr. Pradko added, “There will be no rescissions to N. I. H. grant monies. All N. I. H. grant monies will be spent.”

If the order moves forward, it would mark the latest attempt by the Trump administration to usurp the scientific autonomy of the N. I. H., a $48 billion agency that distributes a majority of its budget to labs across the country for research into areas such as heart disease, cancer and infectious diseases.

Traditionally, the N. I. H. selects projects based on expert review of their scientific merit. But Mr. Trump has sought through a series of recent directives in his second term to bring that process under political review, arguing in part that the government has been funding “woke” liberal priorities.

Friday’s meeting brought to a head months of conflict between two of the attendees: Mr. Vought of the O. M. B., who wants to impose greater political control over N. I. H. grant approvals, and Dr. Jay Bhattacharya, the N. I. H. director, who is resisting those efforts, according to two people close to Dr. Bhattacharya.

Their relationship has grown so contentious that Mr. Vought had refused to meet with Dr. Bhattacharya, the people said. During the session on Friday, Mr. Vought accused the N. I. H. director of funding projects that were in conflict with administration priorities, such as supporting research related to diversity and equity.

One of Mr. Trump’s executive orders, issued on his first day back in office, ended all administration programs involving “diversity, equity and inclusion.” It has had far-reaching effects on N. I. H. studies, including those investigating “health disparities” — why people of certain races and ethnicities may be more or less prone to certain diseases or to suffer worse outcomes.

As a Stanford University economist, Dr. Bhattacharya conducted research on health disparities and has been trying to find a way to preserve N. I. H. funding for such work. In 2011, for instance, he and colleagues reported on “persistent racial disparities in survival after heart transplantation.”

The study, funded by the N. I. H., found that Black heart-transplant patients were at higher risk of death than similar white patients were.

The Times would like to hear about your experience as a federal worker under the second Trump administration. We may reach out about your submission, but we will not publish any part of your response without contacting you first.

But as N. I. H. director, Dr. Bhattacharya has also supported eliminating funding for work he regards as low-quality or ideologically driven. In a brief conversation with reporters early in his tenure, Dr. Bhattacharya said the cancellations were targeting “politicized expressions of devotion to a particular ideology” as opposed to “good science.”

The Harvard confrontation has placed Dr. Bhattacharya in an awkward position. Dr. Alan M. Garber, president of Harvard University, is his mentor and longtime friend. Both are physicians and health economists; they have authored academic papers together and remain close, according to The Harvard Crimson.

On Friday, Mr. Vought also sought access to funds for the current fiscal year that have not yet been spent, but he did not succeed.

The fundamental disagreement, however, appears to reflect a philosophical difference: Mr. Vought wants to cut federal spending for research; Dr. Bhattacharya does not.

Nor does Congress, which overruled Mr. Trump’s proposal to cut biomedical research spending last year.

Moreover, Dr. Bhattacharya opposes Mr. Vought’s push to give political appointees the final say over all federal spending, including health and scientific research.

A proposed rule earlier this year would have integrated political review into the entire federal grant-making process, calling for “ending government sponsorship of gender ideology and other radical doctrines,” such as diversity, equity and inclusion projects.

The changes were widely denounced by the scientific and medical research community, and drew bipartisan rebuke in Congress, where lawmakers blocked the White House from proceeding.

The White House has issued a number of executive orders to stop scientific research into areas that conflict with administration priorities. Thousands of grants were terminated for being in conflict with these priorities.

Even before Friday’s meeting, the administration was entangled in multiple lawsuits that challenged those actions.

Last week, a class-action lawsuit was filed in California district court by the American Civil Liberties Union on behalf of scientists alleging that the N. I. H. was unconstitutionally censoring scientific research.

The lawsuit, on behalf of researchers who study health disparities, Alzheimer’s disease and sexual harassment, among other topics, argued that measures the agency was already using to screen grants for compliance with political priorities were a violation of the free-speech rights of scientists.

“What the First Amendment does not allow is the government’s use of its funding power to target or silence the expression of disfavored viewpoints within the biomedical research community,” the lawsuit said.

Sheryl Gay Stolberg is a correspondent based in Washington for The Times, covering Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and President Trump’s health agenda.

Tony Romm is a reporter covering economic policy and the Trump administration for The Times, based in Washington.

Michael C. Bender is a Times correspondent in Washington.

Russia Barred Their Party, but These Antiwar Voices Are Still Standing

The New York Times September 20, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

The liberal party Yabloko is fielding 98 candidates in this weekend’s elections, a small miracle for antiwar Russians who cannot openly express their views.

By Valerie Hopkins and Paul Sonne

Valerie Hopkins reported from Moscow, and Paul Sonne from Berlin.

They have almost no chance of winning. Their party, Yabloko, was formally removed from the nationwide ballot in this weekend’s elections. Their fellow party members have been sentenced to years in prison for their antiwar positions.

None of that is stopping them.

The fact that Yabloko, Russia’s oldest liberal opposition party, is fielding 98 candidates in 42 regions feels like a small miracle for antiwar Russians whom restrictive laws have prevented from openly expressing their views. As wartime repression deepens, the country may not see such candidates on the ballot again.

“There were times in Russian history that were worse,” said Grigory Grishin, a Yabloko candidate running for the State Duma, Russia’s lower house of Parliament, in Moscow. “So, as the saying goes, ‘The eyes are afraid, but the hands do the work’ — we are participating. What else is there to do?”

The fate of Yabloko has been the most consequential story line in an election the Kremlin engineered to be as uneventful as possible.

The party, long considered irrelevant by the Russian authorities, became a Kremlin target this summer after it unexpectedly turned into a vessel for antiwar sentiment. The Russian Supreme Court barred the party at the last minute, citing minor copyright infringements and indirect foreign financing that it said violated the law.

Still, the decision left open one avenue for Yabloko candidates to run.

At the ballot box, Russians choose a party and then a candidate from their district. Half of State Duma seats are filled through the party vote — parties must clear a 5 percent threshold — and the other half through the votes for candidates in districts, as in elections for the U. S. Congress.

While the Supreme Court barred Yabloko from the party-list vote, many of the party’s candidates in individual districts remained on the ballot. The authorities later disqualified them in many regions, but as voting began on Friday, nearly 100 were still standing.

Why they were allowed is unclear. There may not have been enough time to drum up cases against every one of them, analysts said. Or the authorities may feel confident that they have disqualified all of the Yabloko district candidates with a good chance of winning and that any unforeseen victories could be fixed with ballot falsifications.

Recent data from ExtremeScan, a Russian pollster, suggested that the authorities may have had reason to fear rising support for Yabloko, the only party running on an antiwar platform.

In a survey this month, 18 percent of respondents said they would have voted for Yabloko on a party-list ballot. It was a surprising figure for a party that has not cleared the threshold to enter the Duma since 1999. The idea that any Yabloko candidate would be allowed to take a seat in the legislature and use the platform to question the war openly is considered unthinkable in today’s Russia.

Aleksei Minyailo, an opposition activist in Moscow and the founder of the independent pollster Chronicles, said one of the most important steps that autocratic authorities took to shape election outcomes was limiting the field of candidates.

“This is the essential thing,” he said. “It’s more essential than who gets what result.”

The Kremlin could ultimately try to use the remaining Yabloko candidates to its advantage, Mr. Minyailo said, presenting a poor showing by them as evidence that antiwar Russians are a marginal minority.

In recent polling, the share of Russians who say they do not support the war has ranged from about 20 to 35 percent.

While the mere presence of Yabloko candidates on the ballot may be a victory for them, Mr. Grishin, the district candidate in Moscow, said it was always going to be an uphill battle.

The candidate running against him from the pro-Kremlin governing party, United Russia, had a budget that Mr. Grishin estimated at 40 million rubles, or $500,000. His own budget, raised through donations, was about one-tenth of 1 percent of that.

“We could only print 5,000 leaflets,” he said, proffering one with his portrait and a dove carrying an olive branch. It bore the party’s campaign slogan: “For peace and freedom! For a life without fear!”

Financial troubles were just one of Mr. Grishin’s worries. This month, a day after his newborn daughter arrived at home from the hospital, Mr. Grishin was detained and taken to a police station. He was later accused of “displaying extremist symbols,” a common pretext for removing candidates from the ballot. In Mr. Grishin’s case, the charge referred to a reference he had made on Telegram to the deceased opposition politician Aleksei A. Navalny, whom the Russian authorities branded an extremist.

Had the accusation come three months earlier, Mr. Grishin would have been automatically disqualified from running in the election. But because it occurred so late in the election cycle, the authorities could not remove him from the ballot.

Some candidates have been disqualified after parties loyal to the Kremlin brought cases against them. Iya Boronina, who leads Yabloko’s regional branch in the central Russian republic of Udmurtia, was barred after being accused of copyright infringement, echoing the case that the party itself faced in the Supreme Court.

Her campaign video featured the 1982 rock anthem “Bad to the Bone.” Representatives of the nationalist party A Just Russia contended that Ms. Boronina, because of sanctions against Russia, could not have paid in U. S. dollars for the legal right to use the song.

Eight Yabloko members are currently in prison for their antiwar stances. One deputy chairman, Maxim Kruglov, is serving a seven-year sentence, and another deputy, Lev Shlosberg, is serving 11 years.

Yabloko’s leader, Nikolai I. Rybakov, said that despite the harsh penalties faced by its leaders, the party had become a beacon for Russia’s youngest voters, who dislike the increasing government restrictions on the internet, speech and culture. More than 13,000 people applied to become party members during the election cycle, he said.

“They removed us from the election list because real support belongs to Yabloko, and they cannot defeat us in an election,” Mr. Rybakov said in an interview in his party’s library as his shelter dog, Morty, sat quietly by his side.

Mr. Rybakov pulled a book from the piles around him. It was Roberto Carnero’s essays on the gay Italian filmmaker and writer Pier Paolo Pasolini. About 15 percent of its words were blacked out. On some pages, only a few words were visible.

“The young people who come here are absolutely free people,” said Mr. Rybakov, who himself was disqualified from the election because of a post he wrote after Mr. Navalny died in prison in what five European countries said was a poisoning.

“They want nobody telling them what color their hair should be, what clothes to wear, what to say, what to think, who to love, where to work, or which professor to study with,” he added.

Several young people who attended Yabloko meetings spoke of the psychological solace of speaking with others who opposed the war.

Many of the questions Mr. Rybakov fielded addressed a growing rift between the opposition forces inside Russia centered around Yabloko and those forced into exile, including Mr. Navalny’s team. They have differed over the best strategy for voters to try to express discontent in the election.

As Mr. Rybakov was speaking on a recent night, news broke that another Yabloko candidate, Aleksandr Muravyov, had been barred from the election. Another party had filed a complaint alleging that Mr. Muravyov’s use of the slogan “For a free internet without blocks” created a negative image of other candidates and parties.

Valerie Hopkins covers the war in Ukraine and how the conflict is changing Russia, Ukraine, Europe and the United States. She is based in Moscow.

Paul Sonne is the Moscow bureau chief, leading coverage of Russia, the Caucasus and Central Asia. He is based in Berlin.
